During the [Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"), Moses, along with Mayor [Fiorello H. La Guardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiorello_H._La_Guardia "Fiorello H. La Guardia"), was especially interested in creating new pools and other bathing facilities, such as those in [Jacob Riis Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Riis_Park "Jacob Riis Park"), [Jones Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jones_Beach_State_Park "Jones Beach State Park"), and [Orchard Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard_Beach_(Bronx) "Orchard Beach (Bronx)").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-NY1930-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974456-47) He devised a list of 23 pools around the city.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-49) The pools would be built using funds from the [Works Progress Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Works_Progress_Administration "Works Progress Administration") (WPA), a federal agency created as part of the [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal") to combat the Depression's negative effects.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974456-47)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-nydn19340723-50)

Eleven of these pools were to be designed concurrently and open in 1936. These comprised ten pools at [Astoria Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astoria_Park "Astoria Park"), [Betsy Head Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_Head_Park "Betsy Head Park"), [Crotona Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crotona_Park "Crotona Park"), [Hamilton Fish Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Fish_Park "Hamilton Fish Park"), [Highbridge Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highbridge_Park "Highbridge Park"), [Thomas Jefferson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_Park "Thomas Jefferson Park"), [McCarren Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCarren_Park "McCarren Park"), [Red Hook Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hook_Park "Red Hook Park"), [Jackie Robinson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Robinson_Park "Jackie Robinson Park"), and [Sunset Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset_Park_(Brooklyn_park) "Sunset Park (Brooklyn park)"), as well as a standalone facility at [Tompkinsville Pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tompkinsville_Pool "Tompkinsville Pool").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-NYC_Parks_Pools_History-51) Moses, along with architects [Aymar Embury II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymar_Embury_II "Aymar Embury II") and [Gilmore David Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilmore_David_Clarke "Gilmore David Clarke"), created a common design for these proposed aquatic centers. Each location was to have distinct pools for diving, swimming, and wading; bleachers and viewing areas; and bathhouses with locker rooms that could be used as gymnasiums. The pools were to have several common features, such as a minimum 55-yard (50 m) length, underwater lighting, heating, filtration, and low-cost construction materials. To fit the requirement for cheap materials, each building would be built using elements of the [Streamline Moderne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streamline_Moderne "Streamline Moderne") and [Classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_architecture "Classical architecture") architectural styles. The buildings would also be near "comfort stations", additional playgrounds, and spruced-up landscapes.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-NYC_Parks_Pools_History-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-52)

Construction for some of the 11 pools began in October 1934.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-53) By mid-1936, ten of the eleven WPA-funded pools were completed and were being opened at a rate of one per week.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974456-47) Combined, the facilities could accommodate 49,000 swimmers.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGutman2008p._532,_note_6-54) The eleven WPA pools were considered for [New York City landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_designated_landmark "New York City designated landmark") status in 1990.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-55) Ten of the pools were designated as New York City landmarks in 2007 and 2008.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-56)

Moses allegedly fought to keep African American swimmers out of his pools and beaches. One subordinate remembers Moses saying the pools should be kept a few degrees colder, allegedly because Moses believed African Americans did not like cold water. Caro alleged that Moses built low bridges across his parkways to make them inaccessible to buses, thereby restricting "the use of state parks by poor and lower-middle-class families" who did not own cars. However, both the pool and bridge claims have been challenged as fabrications by other authors.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-:0-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974318%E2%80%93319-58)

### Public housing and urban renewal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Public housing and urban renewal")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/NYCHA_Grant_Houses_WTM3_The_Fixers_0021.jpg/330px-NYCHA_Grant_Houses_WTM3_The_Fixers_0021.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NYCHA_Grant_Houses_WTM3_The_Fixers_0021.jpg)

Riis Houses in 2008

As chairman of the Mayor's Slum Clearance Committee, and as City Construction Coordinator, Moses employed [Title I of the Federal Urban Renewal Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_Act_of_1949 "Housing Act of 1949") to become the dominant force in determining which neighborhoods would be cleared and what would replace them.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974801-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974707-60) In the seven years after the war, it was estimated that some 170,000 people had been evicted from their homes in New York City for public projects—mainly Robert Moses public projects. [[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974967-61)

The projects Moses built or initiated included some of the largest public housing developments in the country. [Manhattanville Houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattanville_Houses "Manhattanville Houses") and [Grant Houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Houses "Grant Houses") rose in [West Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Harlem,_Manhattan "West Harlem, Manhattan"). The [Jacob Riis Houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riis_Houses "Riis Houses") and [Lillian Wald Houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Wald_Houses "Lillian Wald Houses") were built on the [Lower East Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_East_Side "Lower East Side"). Washington Houses went up in [East Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Harlem "East Harlem"). In the Bronx, a succession of developments followed the corridor cleared by the Cross Bronx Expressway.

Title I provided federal funding for cities to acquire and clear "blighted" land, which could then be transferred to private developers or used for public housing. Moses controlled the designation of blight in New York—a power whose scope was effectively unreviewable—and used it to clear vast swaths of neighborhoods in Manhattan, Brooklyn, and the Bronx.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-The_Cross-62) The communities displaced were disproportionately poor, black and Hispanic.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974967-61)

What Moses built on the cleared land were the "[Towers-in-the-park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Towers_in_the_park "Towers in the park")" type projects that still define large sections of the city's landscape. Departing from the traditional street grid, these developments erected tall residential towers on "[superblocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superblock_(urban_planning) "Superblock (urban planning)")" that eliminated the streets, small businesses, and sidewalk life that had characterized the neighborhoods they replaced.

### Post-war influence of urban development and projects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Post-war influence of urban development and projects")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/United_Nations_HQ_-_New_York_City.jpg/330px-United_Nations_HQ_-_New_York_City.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:United_Nations_HQ_-_New_York_City.jpg)

The [headquarters of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headquarters_of_the_United_Nations "Headquarters of the United Nations") in New York City, viewed from the [East River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_River "East River"). The [Secretariat Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Secretariat_Building "United Nations Secretariat Building") is on the left and the [General Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_Building "United Nations General Assembly Building") is the low structure to the right of the tower. This set of buildings straddles the [FDR Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FDR_Drive "FDR Drive"), another of Moses's creations.

Moses's power increased after Mayor LaGuardia retired in 1946 and a series of successors consented to almost all of his proposals. Named city "construction coordinator" that year by Mayor [William O'Dwyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_O'Dwyer "William O'Dwyer"), Moses became New York City's _de facto_ representative in [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."). He was also given powers over [public housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Housing_Authority "New York City Housing Authority") that had eluded him under LaGuardia. When O'Dwyer was forced to resign in disgrace and was succeeded by [Vincent R. Impellitteri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Impellitteri "Vincent R. Impellitteri"), Moses was able to assume even greater behind-the-scenes control over [infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure "Infrastructure") projects.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro789-63) One of Moses's first steps after Impellitteri took office was halting the creation of a citywide Comprehensive Zoning Plan underway since 1938 that would have curtailed his nearly unlimited power to build within the city and removed the Zoning Commissioner from power in the process. Moses was also empowered as the sole authority to negotiate in Washington for New York City projects. By 1959, he had overseen construction of 28,000 apartment units on hundreds of acres of land. In clearing the land for high-rises in accordance with the [towers in the park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Towers_in_the_park "Towers in the park") concept, which at that time was seen as innovative and beneficial by leaving more grassy areas between high-rises, Moses sometimes destroyed almost as many housing units as he built.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22)

From the 1930s to the 1960s, Robert Moses was responsible for the construction of the [Triborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triborough_Bridge "Triborough Bridge"), [Marine Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Parkway%E2%80%93Gil_Hodges_Memorial_Bridge "Marine Parkway–Gil Hodges Memorial Bridge"), [Throgs Neck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Throgs_Neck_Bridge "Throgs Neck Bridge"), [Bronx-Whitestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronx-Whitestone_Bridge "Bronx-Whitestone Bridge"), [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson_Bridge "Henry Hudson Bridge"), and [Verrazzano–Narrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verrazzano%E2%80%93Narrows_Bridge "Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge") bridges. His other projects included the [Brooklyn-Queens Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn-Queens_Expressway "Brooklyn-Queens Expressway") and [Staten Island Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island_Expressway "Staten Island Expressway") (together constituting most of [Interstate 278](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_278 "Interstate 278")); the [Cross-Bronx Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-Bronx_Expressway "Cross-Bronx Expressway"); many New York State [parkways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkway_(New_York) "Parkway (New York)"); and other highways. Federal interest had shifted from parkway to [freeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeway "Freeway") systems, and the new roads mostly conformed to the new vision, lacking the landscaping or the commercial traffic restrictions of the pre-war highways. He was the mover behind [Shea Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shea_Stadium "Shea Stadium") and [Lincoln Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Center "Lincoln Center"), and contributed to the [United Nations headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_headquarters "United Nations headquarters").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22) On November 25, 1950, Governor [Thomas E. Dewey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_E._Dewey "Thomas E. Dewey") appointed Moses along with former Secretary of War [Robert P. Patterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_P._Patterson "Robert P. Patterson") and former New York State Supreme Court Justice [Charles C. Lockwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_C._Lockwood "Charles C. Lockwood") as a member of the Temporary Long Island Railroad Commission, installed after the [Richmond Hill train crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_Hill_train_crash "Richmond Hill train crash") on November 22, 1950, that claimed 79 lives.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-nyt261150-64) The Commission recommended the state purchase and operation by non-profit public authority of the railway service.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-gdt080351-65)

Moses had influence outside the New York area as well. Public officials in many smaller U.S. cities hired him to design road and highway networks in the 1940s and early 1950s. For example, [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon") hired Moses in 1943; his plan included a loop around the [city center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Portland "Downtown Portland"), with [spurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spur_route "Spur route") running through neighborhoods. Of this plan, only [I-405](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_405_(Oregon) "Interstate 405 (Oregon)"), its links with [I-5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_5_in_Oregon "Interstate 5 in Oregon"), and the [Fremont Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fremont_Bridge_(Portland) "Fremont Bridge (Portland)") were built.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-66)

Moses himself did not drive an automobile.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-asimov-67) Moses' highways in the first half of the 20th century were parkways—curving, landscaped "ribbon parks" that were intended to be pleasures to travel on, as well as "lungs for the city". However, [post–World War II economic expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post%E2%80%93World_War_II_economic_expansion "Post–World War II economic expansion"), and notion of the [automotive city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_city "Automotive city"), led to the creation of [freeways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeway "Freeway"), most notably in the form of the vast, federally funded [Interstate Highway network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Highway_System "Interstate Highway System").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22)

#### Brooklyn Dodgers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Brooklyn Dodgers")]

When the owner of the [Brooklyn Dodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Brooklyn_Dodgers "History of the Brooklyn Dodgers"), [Walter O'Malley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_O'Malley "Walter O'Malley"), sought to replace the outdated and dilapidated [Ebbets Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebbets_Field "Ebbets Field"), he proposed building a [new stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Dodgers_proposed_domed_stadium "Brooklyn Dodgers proposed domed stadium") near the [Long Island Rail Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Rail_Road "Long Island Rail Road") on the corner of [Atlantic Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Avenue_(New_York_City) "Atlantic Avenue (New York City)") and [Flatbush Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flatbush_Avenue "Flatbush Avenue") (at the current site of the [Atlantic Terminal Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Terminal_Mall "Atlantic Terminal Mall"), across from the [Barclays Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclays_Center "Barclays Center"), home of the [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA "NBA")'s [Brooklyn Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets")). O'Malley urged Moses to help him secure the property through eminent domain, but Moses refused, having already decided to build a parking garage on the site. Moreover, O'Malley's proposal—to have the city acquire the property for several times as much as he had originally said he was willing to pay—was rejected by both pro- and anti-Moses officials, newspapers, and the public, as an unacceptable government subsidy of a private business enterprise.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-68)

Moses envisioned New York's newest stadium being built in Queens' [Flushing Meadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flushing_Meadows "Flushing Meadows") on the former (and as it turned out, future) site of the [World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_New_York_World's_Fair "1964 New York World's Fair"), where it would eventually host all three of the city's major league teams of the day. O'Malley vehemently opposed that plan, citing the team's [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn") identity. Moses refused to budge and, after the 1957 season, the Dodgers left for [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") and the [New York Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Giants_(baseball) "New York Giants (baseball)") left for [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22) Moses was later able to build the 55,000-seat multi-purpose [Shea Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shea_Stadium "Shea Stadium") on the site. Construction ran from October 1961 to its delayed completion in April 1964. The stadium attracted an expansion franchise, the [New York Mets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Mets "New York Mets"), who played at Shea until 2008, when the stadium was demolished and replaced with [Citi Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citi_Field "Citi Field"). The NFL's [New York Jets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Jets "New York Jets") also played its home games at Shea from 1964 until 1983, after which the team moved its home games to the [Meadowlands Sports Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meadowlands_Sports_Complex "Meadowlands Sports Complex") in New Jersey.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-Murphy-69)

### End of the Moses era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: End of the Moses era")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Unisphere.jpg/330px-Unisphere.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Unisphere.jpg)

View of the 1964–1965 New York World's Fair as seen from the observation towers of the New York State pavilion. The Fair's symbol, the [Unisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unisphere "Unisphere"), is the central image.

Moses's reputation began to fade during the 1960s. Around this time, Moses's political acumen began to fail him, as he unwisely picked several controversial political battles he could not possibly win. For example, his campaign against the free [Shakespeare in the Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare_in_the_Park_(New_York_City) "Shakespeare in the Park (New York City)") program received much negative publicity, and his effort to destroy a shaded playground in [Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park") to make way for a parking lot for the expensive [Tavern-on-the-Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tavern_on_the_Green "Tavern on the Green") restaurant earned him many enemies among the middle-class voters of the [Upper West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_West_Side "Upper West Side").

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/30_years_of_progress%2C_1934-1964_-_Department_of_Parks_-_300th_anniversary_of_the_City_of_New_York_-_New_York_World%27s_Fair._%281964%29_%2816478136350%29.jpg/250px-30_years_of_progress%2C_1934-1964_-_Department_of_Parks_-_300th_anniversary_of_the_City_of_New_York_-_New_York_World%27s_Fair._%281964%29_%2816478136350%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:30_years_of_progress,_1934-1964_-_Department_of_Parks_-_300th_anniversary_of_the_City_of_New_York_-_New_York_World's_Fair._(1964)_(16478136350).jpg)

A 1964 Parks Department map showing numerous Robert Moses projects, including several highways that went unbuilt or were only partially completed.

The opposition reached a climax over the demolition of [Pennsylvania Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Station_(1910%E2%80%931963) "Pennsylvania Station (1910–1963)"), which many attributed to the "development scheme" mentality cultivated by Moses[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-70) even though it was the impoverished [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad") that was actually responsible for the demolition.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-The_Nation-71) This casual destruction of one of New York's greatest architectural landmarks helped prompt many city residents to turn against Moses's plans to build a [Lower Manhattan Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Manhattan_Expressway "Lower Manhattan Expressway"), which would have gone through [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village") and what is now [SoHo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoHo "SoHo").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-72) This plan and the [Mid-Manhattan Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Manhattan_Expressway "Mid-Manhattan Expressway") both failed politically. One of his most vocal critics during this time was the urban activist [Jane Jacobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Jacobs "Jane Jacobs"), whose book _[The Death and Life of Great American Cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Death\_and\_Life\_of\_Great\_American\_Cities "The Death and Life of Great American Cities")_ was instrumental in turning opinion against Moses's plans; the city government rejected the expressway in 1964.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-73)

Moses's power was further eroded by his association with the [1964 New York World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_New_York_World's_Fair "1964 New York World's Fair"). His projections for attendance of 70 million people for this event proved wildly optimistic, and generous contracts for Fair executives and contractors made matters worse economically. Moses's repeated and forceful public denials of the fair's considerable financial difficulties in the face of evidence to the contrary eventually provoked press and governmental investigations, which found accounting irregularities.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-Nexus-32) In his organization of the fair, Moses's reputation was now undermined by the same personal character traits that had worked in his favor in the past: disdain for the opinions of others and high-handed attempts to get his way in moments of conflict by turning to the press. The fact that the fair was not sanctioned by the [Bureau of International Expositions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_International_Expositions "Bureau of International Expositions") (BIE), the worldwide body supervising such events, would be devastating to the success of the event.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-74) Moses refused to accept BIE requirements, including a restriction against charging ground rents to exhibitors, and the BIE in turn instructed its member nations not to participate.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-learn.columbia-75) The United States had already staged the sanctioned [Century 21 Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_21_Exposition "Century 21 Exposition") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle,_Washington "Seattle, Washington") in 1962. According to the rules of the organization, no one nation could host more than one fair in a decade. The major European democracies, as well as Canada, Australia, and the Soviet Union, were all BIE members and they declined to participate, instead reserving their efforts for [Expo 67](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_67 "Expo 67") in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal").

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Verrazano-Narrows_Bridge-_The_Beginning_%2815097870444%29.jpg/250px-Verrazano-Narrows_Bridge-_The_Beginning_%2815097870444%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Verrazano-Narrows_Bridge-_The_Beginning_(15097870444).jpg)

Robert Moses gives a salute after the ribbon-cutting ceremony to open the [Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verrazzano%E2%80%93Narrows_Bridge "Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge") on November 21, 1964

After the World's Fair debacle, New York City mayor [John Lindsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lindsay "John Lindsay"), along with Governor [Nelson Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller "Nelson Rockefeller"), sought to direct toll revenues from the [Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triborough_Bridge_and_Tunnel_Authority "Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority")'s (TBTA) bridges and tunnels to cover deficits in the city's then financially ailing agencies, including the [subway system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway"). Moses opposed this idea and fought to prevent it.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-The_Nation-71) Lindsay then removed Moses from his post as the city's chief advocate for federal highway money in Washington.

The legislature's vote to fold the TBTA into the newly created [Metropolitan Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Transportation_Authority "Metropolitan Transportation Authority") (MTA) could have led to a lawsuit by the TBTA bondholders. Since the bond contracts were written into state law, it was unconstitutional to impair existing contractual obligations, as the bondholders had the right of approval over such actions. The largest holder of TBTA bonds, and thus agent for all the others, was the [Chase Manhattan Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chase_Manhattan_Bank "Chase Manhattan Bank"), headed then by [David Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Rockefeller "David Rockefeller"), the governor's brother. No suit was filed. Moses could have directed TBTA to go to court against the action, but having been promised a role in the merged authority, Moses declined to challenge the merger. On March 1, 1968, the TBTA was folded into the MTA and Moses gave up his post as chairman of the TBTA. He eventually became a consultant to the MTA, but its new chairman and the governor froze him out—the promised role did not materialize, and for all practical purposes Moses was out of power.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-Murphy-69)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Robert_Moses%2C_in_office%2C_Randall_Island%2C_N.Y.%2C_1978_-_gtfy.02744.jpg/250px-Robert_Moses%2C_in_office%2C_Randall_Island%2C_N.Y.%2C_1978_-_gtfy.02744.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Moses,_in_office,_Randall_Island,_N.Y.,_1978_-_gtfy.02744.jpg)

Robert Moses, in office, Randall Island, N.Y., 1978

Moses had thought he had convinced Nelson Rockefeller of the need for one last great bridge project, a span [crossing Long Island Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Crossing "Long Island Crossing") from [Rye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rye_(town),_New_York "Rye (town), New York") to [Oyster Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyster_Bay_(hamlet),_New_York "Oyster Bay (hamlet), New York"). Rockefeller did not press for the project in the late 1960s through 1970, fearing public backlash among suburban Republicans would hinder his re-election prospects. A 1972 study found the bridge was fiscally prudent and could be environmentally manageable (according to the comparatively low environmental impact parameters of that period), but the anti-development sentiment was now insurmountable and in 1973 Rockefeller canceled plans for the bridge.

#### _The Power Broker_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: The Power Broker")]

| External videos |
| --- |
| [![Image 18: video icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg/20px-Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg)[Presentation by Robert Caro on Robert Moses and urban development at the Brookings Institution, September 28, 1998](https://www.c-span.org/video/?112640-1/power-broker-robert-moses), [C-SPAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-SPAN "C-SPAN") |

Main article: [The Power Broker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Power_Broker "The Power Broker")

Moses' image suffered a further blow in 1974 with the publication of _[The Power Broker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Power\_Broker "The Power Broker")_, a [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize")–winning biography by [Robert A. Caro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_A._Caro "Robert A. Caro"). Caro's 1,200-page book (edited down from 2,000 or so pages) showed Moses generally in a negative light; essayist [Phillip Lopate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillip_Lopate "Phillip Lopate") writes that "Moses's satanic reputation with the public can be traced, in the main, to ... Caro's magnificent biography".[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-76)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22) Caro's book won both the Pulitzer Prize in Biography in 1975 and the [Francis Parkman Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Parkman_Prize "Francis Parkman Prize") (which is awarded by the [Society of American Historians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_American_Historians "Society of American Historians")), and was named one of the 100 greatest non-fiction books of the twentieth century by the [Modern Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Library "Modern Library").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-learn.columbia-75)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22) Upon its publication, Moses denounced the biography in a 23-page statement, to which Caro replied to defend his work's integrity.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-Boeing2017Moses-77)

As illustrated by the book's subtitle, "Caro [...] doesn't pretend to be neutral" in his treatment of Moses.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-78) According to Caro's website, the biography depicts Moses as an "idealist" in his youth who "first created a miraculous flowering of parks and parkways, playlands and beaches—and then ultimately brought down on the city the smog-choked aridity of our urban landscape", having made power "an end in itself". The biography holds Moses responsible for "the endless miles of (never sufficient) highway, the hopeless sprawl of Long Island, the massive failures of public housing, and countless other barriers to humane living."[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-79) It concludes that it is impossible to know how New York would have developed without Moses's influence.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22)

Particularly enduring criticisms made in the biography relate to Moses's alleged racist tendencies (for instance, his toleration of [MetLife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetLife "MetLife")'s [Stuyvesant Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuyvesant_Town%E2%80%93Peter_Cooper_Village "Stuyvesant Town–Peter Cooper Village") being restricted to white residents,[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-:1-80) or his alleged lowering of parkway bridges to keep public buses off of beaches)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-nyt2cities-81), his insensitive methods of construction and disfavoring of public transit, and his fraught relationship with his brother and mother.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22) Additionally, _The Power Broker_ brought discussion of urban displacement into the public consciousness through its coverage of Moses's infrastructure projects: Caro calculated Moses's projects altogether displaced around 250,000 people.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-:2-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-83)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Death")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Robert_Moses_Crypt_1024.jpg/250px-Robert_Moses_Crypt_1024.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Moses_Crypt_1024.jpg)

The crypt of Robert Moses

During the last years of his life, Moses concentrated on his lifelong love of [swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_swimming "Human swimming") and was an active member of the Colonie Hill Health Club.

Moses died of [heart disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_disease "Heart disease") on July 29, 1981, at the age of 92 at [Good Samaritan Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Samaritan_Hospital_(West_Islip) "Good Samaritan Hospital (West Islip)") in [West Islip, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Islip,_New_York "West Islip, New York").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-The_New_York_Times-84)

Moses was interred in a crypt in an outdoor community mausoleum in [Woodlawn Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlawn_Cemetery,_Bronx "Woodlawn Cemetery, Bronx") in [The Bronx, New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx,_New_York_City "The Bronx, New York City") following services at St. Peter's by-the-Sea Episcopal Church in [Bay Shore, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Shore,_New_York "Bay Shore, New York"). [[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-86)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Legacy")]

Various locations and roadways in New York State bear Moses's name. These include two state parks, [Robert Moses State Park – Thousand Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses_State_Park_%E2%80%93_Thousand_Islands "Robert Moses State Park – Thousand Islands") in [Massena, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massena_(village),_New_York "Massena (village), New York") and [Robert Moses State Park – Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses_State_Park "Robert Moses State Park"), the [Robert Moses Causeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses_Causeway "Robert Moses Causeway") on Long Island, and the [Robert Moses Niagara Power Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses_Niagara_Power_Plant "Robert Moses Niagara Power Plant") in [Lewiston, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewiston,_New_York "Lewiston, New York"). The [Niagara Scenic Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Scenic_Parkway "Niagara Scenic Parkway") in [Niagara Falls, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls,_New_York "Niagara Falls, New York") was originally named the Robert Moses State Parkway in his honor; its name was changed in 2016. The [Moses-Saunders Power Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses-Saunders_Power_Dam "Moses-Saunders Power Dam") in [Massena, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massena,_New_York "Massena, New York") also bears his name. Moses also has a school named after him in [North Babylon, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Babylon,_New_York "North Babylon, New York") on Long Island; there is also a [Robert Moses Playground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses_Playground "Robert Moses Playground") in New York City. There are other signs of the surviving appreciation held for him by some circles of the public. A statue of Moses was erected next to the [Village Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_hall "Village hall") in his long-time hometown, [Babylon Village, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon_(village),_New_York "Babylon (village), New York").

During his tenure as chief of the state park system, the state's inventory of parks grew to nearly 2,600,000 acres (1,100,000 ha). By the time he left office, he had built 658 playgrounds in New York City alone, plus 416 miles (669 km) of parkways and 13 bridges.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-The_New_York_Times-84) The proportion of [public benefit corporations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_state_public-benefit_corporations "New York state public-benefit corporations") is greater in New York than in any other [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state"), however, making them the prime mode of infrastructure building and maintenance in New York and accounting for 90% of the state's debt.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-87)

## Appraisal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Appraisal")]

### Criticism and _The Power Broker_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Criticism and The Power Broker")]

Moses's life was most famously characterized in [Robert Caro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Caro "Robert Caro")'s 1974 award-winning biography _[The Power Broker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Power\_Broker "The Power Broker")_.

The book highlighted his practice of starting projects certain to cost more than the initial funding approved by the [New York State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Legislature "New York State Legislature"), knowing the legislature would eventually have to fund the full project to avoid appearing to have provided ineffective oversight (_[fait accompli](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/fait%20accompli "wikt:fait accompli")_). He was also characterized as using his political power to benefit cronies, including a case in which he secretly shifted the planned route of the [Northern State Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_State_Parkway "Northern State Parkway") large distances to avoid impinging on the estates of the rich, but told owners of the family farms who lost land that it was an unbiased decision based on "engineering considerations."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22) The book also charged that Moses [libeled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libel "Libel") officials who opposed him, attempting to have them removed from office by calling them [communists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communists "Communists") during the [Red Scare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Scare "Red Scare"). The biography further notes that Moses fought against schools and other public needs in favor of his preference for parks.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22)

Moses' critics charge that he preferred automobiles over people. They point out that he displaced hundreds of thousands of residents in New York City and destroyed traditional neighborhoods by building multiple expressways through them. The projects contributed to the ruin of the [South Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx "South Bronx") and the [amusement parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amusement_park "Amusement park") of [Coney Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island "Coney Island"), caused the [Brooklyn Dodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Brooklyn_Dodgers "History of the Brooklyn Dodgers") and the [New York Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_New_York_Giants_(NL) "History of the New York Giants (NL)")[Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") teams to relocate to Los Angeles and San Francisco respectively, and precipitated the decline of public transport from [disinvestment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinvestment "Disinvestment") and neglect.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22) His construction of expressways also hindered the [proposed expansion of the New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposed_expansion_of_the_New_York_City_Subway "Proposed expansion of the New York City Subway") from the 1930s to well into the 1960s because the parkways and expressways that were built replaced, at least to some extent, the planned subway lines. The 1968 [Program for Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Program_for_Action "Program for Action") (which was never completed) was hoped to counter that.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22) Other critics charge that he precluded the use of public transit, which would have allowed non-car-owners to enjoy the elaborate recreation facilities he built.

#### Racism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Racism")]

Criticisms of Moses and his work, particularly _The Power Broker,_ characterize Moses and his planning decisions as racist. Generally, these criticisms rest on the perceived disproportionate racial impact of Moses's decisions and instances where Moses is said to have explicitly made decisions to the disadvantage of black and brown residents.

Critics charge that Moses used various methods to keep black and brown New Yorkers away from the parks and beaches he built. Caro writes that Moses attempted to discourage black people from visiting Jones Beach, the centerpiece of the Long Island state park system, by such measures as making it difficult for black groups to get permits to park buses, and assigning black lifeguards to "distant, less developed beaches".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974318%E2%80%93319-58) While the exclusion of commercial vehicles and the use of low bridges where appropriate were standard on earlier parkways, where they had been instituted for aesthetic reasons, Moses appears to have made greater use of low bridges, which his aide Sidney Shapiro said was done to make it more difficult for future legislatures to allow access for commercial vehicles.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974952-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-Campanella-89) Steve Woolgar and Geoff Cooper refer to the claim about bridges as an "urban legend", and [Kenneth T. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_T._Jackson "Kenneth T. Jackson") similarly refutes that there was nefarious intent.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-90)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-:0-57)

Regarding Stuyvesant Town, a Manhattan residential development complex created to house World War II veterans, Moses and the LaGuardia administration defended the [Metropolitan Life Insurance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetLife "MetLife")'s decision to exclude black residents from the development, regarding it as a private project despite its public subsidization. Moses believed that public supervision of MetLife's tenant selection would make it "impossible to get insurance companies and banks to help us clear sub-standard, run-down, and cancerous areas in the heart of the city.”[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974-22)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-:1-80)

Additionally, there were allegations that Moses selectively chose locations for recreational facilities based on the racial compositions of a neighborhood, such as when he selected sites for eleven pools that opened in 1936. According to one author, Moses purposely placed some pools in neighborhoods with mainly white populations to deter African Americans from using them, and other pools intended for African Americans, such as the one in Colonial Park (now [Jackie Robinson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Robinson_Park "Jackie Robinson Park")), were placed in inconvenient locations.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-91) Another author wrote that of 255 playgrounds built in the 1930s under Moses's tenure, only two were in largely black neighborhoods.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-92) Caro wrote that close associates of Moses had claimed they could keep African Americans from using the [Thomas Jefferson Pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_Pool "Thomas Jefferson Pool"), in then-predominantly-white [East Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Harlem "East Harlem"), by making the water too cold.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaro1974512%E2%80%93514-93)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-nyt2cities-81) Nonetheless, no other source has corroborated the claim that heaters in any particular pool were deactivated or not included in the pool's design; Kenneth T. Jackson asserted these claims were "just wrong."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-:0-57)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGutman2008537%E2%80%93538-94)

On March 26, 1952, Moses gave a speech at an event in New York City which commemorated [Lady Randolph Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Randolph_Churchill "Lady Randolph Churchill"), the mother of [Sir Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Winston_Churchill "Sir Winston Churchill"). In the speech, Moses claimed that [Rudyard Kipling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudyard_Kipling "Rudyard Kipling") foresaw "the rise of lesser breeds without the law", a comment described as "excruciatingly racist" by the journalist Glen Jeffries.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-97)

In response to the biography, Moses defended his forced displacement of poor and minority communities as an inevitable part of urban revitalization: "I raise my [stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_stein "Beer stein") to the builder who can remove [ghettos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghetto "Ghetto") without moving people as I hail the chef who can make omelets without breaking eggs."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-Boeing2017Moses-77) Defenders of Moses and critics of _The Power Broker_ say that that there is "little evidence in Mr. Moses’ urban planning practices that he singled out the city’s relatively small Black and Puerto Rican populations for particular punishment".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-:2-82) Some of the racist incidents documented in _The Power Broker_, including the overpass-lowering and pool-cooling episodes, have been called fabrications by critics.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-:0-57)

### Reappraisal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Moses&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Reappraisal")]

Some scholars have attempted to rehabilitate Moses' reputation by contrasting the scale of works with the high cost and the slow speed of public works in the decades following his era. The peak of Moses's construction occurred during the economic duress of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"), and despite the era's woes, Moses' projects were completed in a timely fashion and have been reliable public works since then, which compares favorably to the delays that New York City officials have had in redeveloping the [Ground Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Center_site "World Trade Center site") site of the former [World Trade Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Center_(1973%E2%80%932001) "World Trade Center (1973–2001)") or to the delays and technical problems surrounding the [Second Avenue Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Avenue_Subway "Second Avenue Subway") and Boston's [Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig_(Boston,_Massachusetts) "Big Dig (Boston, Massachusetts)") project.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-Glaeser2007-98)

Three major exhibits in 2007 prompted a reconsideration of his image among some intellectuals, as they acknowledged the magnitude of his achievements. According to the [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University")[architectural historian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_architecture "History of architecture")[Hilary Ballon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilary_Ballon "Hilary Ballon") and colleagues, Moses deserves a better reputation. They argue that his legacy is more relevant than ever and that people take the parks, playgrounds, and housing that Moses built, now generally binding forces in those areas, for granted even if the old-style New York neighborhood was of no interest to Moses himself. Moreover, were it not for Moses' public infrastructure and his resolve to carve out more space, they argue that New York might not have been able to recover from the blight and flight of the 1970s and the 1980s to become today's economic magnet.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-nyt-2007-01-28-99)

"Every generation writes its own history," wrote Kenneth T. Jackson in the _New York Times_ in 2007. "It could be that _The Power Broker_ was a reflection of its time: New York was in trouble and had been in decline for 15 years. Now, for a whole host of reasons, New York is entering a new time, a time of optimism, growth and revival that hasn't been seen in half a century. And that causes us to look at our infrastructure," said Jackson. "A lot of big projects are on the table again, and it kind of suggests a Moses era without Moses," he added.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-nyt-2007-01-28-99) Politicians are also reconsidering the Moses legacy; in a 2006 speech to the [Regional Plan Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Plan_Association "Regional Plan Association") on downstate transportation needs, New York Governor-elect [Eliot Spitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Spitzer "Eliot Spitzer") stated a biography of Moses written today might be called _At Least He Got It Built_: "That's what we need today. A real commitment to get things done."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Moses#cite_note-Spitzer_speech-100)

[![Image 19: There’s a difference between a house and a work of art. Los Angeles is lucky to be littered with some of the greatest architects to have ever lived, and while not all Angelenos live in one, the layout of their kitchens or the way their windows look was probably inspired by one of these legends. THE GOATS Frank Lloyd Wright: He turned concrete into high art, think of the Ennis House as LA’s own ancient temple. Paul R. Williams: The king of Hollywood elegance who designed breathtaking homes. Julia Morgan: A total trailblazer who brought massive scale and soul to California’s most famous estates. THE MASTERS Richard Neutra: The reason we’re all obsessed with glass walls and that “indoor-outdoor” lifestyle. Rudolph Schindler: The bohemian master who made raw wood and concrete feel like a luxury vibe. John Lautner: If a house looks like a futuristic UFO perched on a hill, it’s a Lautner. Pierre Koenig: He perfected the “Glass Box” look that every modern developer is still trying to copy. Craig Ellwood: The master of clean, sharp lines; he made “Industrial” look like a million bucks. A. Quincy Jones: He focused on how we actually live, making high design feel smart and functional. Frank Gehry: The ultimate disruptor (1929–2025) who proved a house could be a sculpture, not just a box. Oscar Niemeyer: He only left us one home in LA, but its curves are a masterclass in pure grace. THE LIVING LEGENDS Barbara Bestor: The queen of “Stealth Modernism,” she’s the reason the Eastside looks so effortlessly cool. Thom Mayne: His work is bold and metallic; it’s for the people who want to live in the future. Michael Maltzan: A geometric genius who treats a hillside like a canvas for his sculptural homes. Lorcan O’Herlihy: The master of the “Small Lot,” proving you can have a masterpiece even on a tight footprint. Gus Duffy: My personal favorite, he’s the “New Traditionalist” who knows how to make a classic home feel brand new. # Architecture of Frank Gehry | Top 9 Gehry Works

By

[Archeetect](https://archeetect.com/author/kzxm241l-sadx/)

 - 

21 April 2022

Frank Gehry, whose real name is Ephraim Goldberg, is a Canadian born architect of Jewish origin. He had moved with his family to California before he went to college. After completing his undergraduate education at the University of Southern California, he was accepted to the Harvard School of Architecture. However, he abandoned his education and started to create a furniture series called Easy Edges. This design experiment he got in early ages has made a powerful impact on the **architecture of Frank Gehry**.

At his Easy Edges business, he was designing furniture from thick cardboard. Later, he released a second furniture design series and named it Experimental Edges.

## Architecture of Frank Gehry

[![Image 4: Life and buildings of Frank Gehry, famous Canadian architect](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/architecture-of-frank-gehry-works-buildings-archeetect.com_.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/architecture-of-frank-gehry-works-buildings-archeetect.com_.jpg)

Architect Frank Gehry – ©Eager, Flickr

Gehry started his professional architectural career by founding his own office, [Frank Gehry and Associates](https://foga.com/), in 1963. In 1989 he won the Pritzker Architecture Prize, the most prestigious award in the field of architecture. Then, he received a gold medal from the American Society of Architects in 1999 and from the British Royal Family in 2000. Throughout his career, he has produced designs in various typologies such as museums, public buildings, residences and concert halls.

### Characteristics of Frank Gehry Architecture

*   Frank Gehry has outstanded with the architectural designs he produced in the neo-modern period. Gehry started his career by designing furnitures. There, he was designing furnitures that was far from the usual forms by shaping cardboard. By this way, he had been disclosing his reaction against the usual and static designs of the modernism.
*   Gehry used to love functionalism and admired Louis Kahn, one of the leading architects in this field.
*   At the end of the 70’s, he designed various buildings by blending his architectural experience and mentality with deconstructivist thought.
*   In buildings of Frank Gehry, the form is freely shaped by cutting loose from the norms.
*   Frank Gehry often prefers to use curvy and fluid forms in his structures.
*   His designs leave a sculptural impact.
*   **Frank Gehry structures** are away from the boringness of modernism and have asymmetrical lines.
*   He frequently uses industrial metals such as titanium and stainless steel as the facade cladding in his large-scale [deconstructivist buildings](https://archeetect.com/deconstructivism/).

### A List of Frank Gehry Buildings

#### 1. Danziger House

This building he designed in 1965 is designer Louis Danziger’s own studio. This house is the leading functional and simple designs frequently seen in early period **Frank Gehry works**. With the white concrete surfaces and the low amount of glass surfaces in accordance with the degree of privacy inside, the building has a minimalist appearance. Moreover, it is possible to see traces of Louis Kahn’s pure functionalist style in the design.

#### 2. Gehry House

[![Image 5: Frank Gehry House located in Santa Monica](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/gehry-house-archeetect.com_.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/gehry-house-archeetect.com_.jpg)

Gehry House – ©IK’s World Trip, Wikimedia

It is Gehry’s design, which he completed in 1977-78 by removing the carriers and many elements of an existing house. For this reason, it has a messy appearance. Although it received a lot of backlash at first, it later began to be seen as one of the most successful examples of the Deconstructivism movement. This **Frank Gehry House in Santa Monica**, California was named after its owner.

Thanks to this work, he got many low-budget residential building projects. He had been turning architecture into an art in narrow plots, complex environments and low-budget projects.

#### 3. Walt Disney Concert Hall

**Architect Frank Gehry** designed the Walt Disney Concert Hall in downtown Los Angeles in 1988. During the design phase, he wanted the building to have a stone cladding. He even explained in an interview that the stone would shine at night and make the building look more beautiful and friendly. Metal cladding, on the other hand, will turned dark when it got dark. But things changed during the design process, and worked stainless steel claddings enveloped the facade.

[![Image 6: Walt Disney Concert Hall design by Frank Gehry](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/walt-disney-concert-hall-buildings-by-frank-gehry-architecture.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/walt-disney-concert-hall-buildings-by-frank-gehry-architecture.jpg)

Walt Disney Concert Hall

However, when the building was completed, a big problem arose. The facade covered with reflective metal panels, had been focalising sunlight on some of the surrounding buildings due to its sloping surfaces. This case created irresistible room temperatures in neighboring buildings and showed that architecture was not an issue independent of the environment.

In 2005, Gehry identified the problematic panels with the help of computer programs to solve this problem. Then, he mattified these panels by sanding. Walt Disney Concert Hall by Frank Gehry is host to the Los Angeles Philharmonic Orchestra.

#### 4. Bilbao Guggenheim Museum

Because of the splinter organization ETA in Spain, the light in the eyes of the city of Bilbao went out and the Port of Bilbao became unusable. As a remedy, the Spanish government initiated a cultural and economic transformation program in the 1990s. The port was the most important part of this renovation project.

[![Image 7: One of the most famous buildings by Frank Gehry, Bilbao Guggenheim Museum](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/bilbao-guggenheim-museum-design-by-frank-gehry-archeetect.com_.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/bilbao-guggenheim-museum-design-by-frank-gehry-archeetect.com_.jpg)

Bilbao Guggenheim Museum

A museum with Gehry’s signature was built in the port, which was renovated with the donations of Solomon R. Guggenheim. By this means, Gehry presented the Guggenheim Museum, which refers to the history of the port city of Bilbao and resembles a sailing ship, to the history of architecture. [Bilbao Guggenheim Museum](https://archeetect.com/bilbao-guggenheim-museum/) is frank gehry’s most famous building in Spain since then.

#### 5. Dancing House

[![Image 8: Dancing House, the famous architecture of Frank Gehry](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/dancing-house-frank-gehry-architecture-buildings.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/dancing-house-frank-gehry-architecture-buildings.jpg)
**Dancing House by Frank Gehry** is located in Prag. It is a building that stands out among historical buildings with its dynamic stance. Gehry makes the structure dance with the curving retreat in the middle of the building. Actually, the project consists of 2 buildings. The graceful and curved glass building on the left represents a dancing woman, and the more solemn one with a cylindrical mass on the right represents the male dancer. You can learn more about Dancing House by click [here](https://archeetect.com/dancing-house/).

#### 6. Vitra Design Museum

[![Image 9: Frank Gehry architecture example Vitra Design Museum](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/vitra-design-museum-architecture-of-frank-gehry-archeetect.com_.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/vitra-design-museum-architecture-of-frank-gehry-archeetect.com_.jpg)

Vitra Design Museum – ©Opalsson, Flickr

The museum, which belongs to the Vitra Foundation, is the first building designed by Frank Gehry in Europe. When we look at the form of the building, the sloping facades used by Gehry in his designs leap out in this building as well. Gehry has integrated these sloping facades with curvilinear surfaces. Unlike most of his buildings, Gehry used plaster on the facade and covered some parts of the exterior with a titanium alloy material.

The museum exhibites furnitures designed by designers such as Zaha Hadid and various works. Inside, there are exhibition halls, a library, a restoration laboratory and different workshop areas.

#### 7. Louis Vuitton Foundation

[![Image 10: Louis Vuitton Foundation building of Frank Gehry](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/louis-vuitton-foundation-building-architecture-of-frank-gehry.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/louis-vuitton-foundation-building-architecture-of-frank-gehry.jpg)

Louis Vuitton Foundation – ©Iwan Baan

Located in the second largest nature park in Paris, the Louis Vuitton Foundation has a dynamic mass. This deconstructivist structure formed by curved shells of various sizes has become a modern part of the city skyline. Although the Louis Vitton is at the center of criticism in terms of the context where it was built, Frank Gehry has done a successful job in the design of the building, depending on its [sustainable architecture](https://archeetect.com/sustainable-architecture/) strategies.

#### 8. Stata Center

The Ray and Maria Stata Center is the research center that architect Frank Gehry designed for MIT in 2000. The building with an area of 67 thousand square meters includes 2 different structures rising on 4 floors. One of them is called Gates Tower and the other is called Dreyfoos Tower or simply G Tower and D Tower.

[![Image 11: MIT Stata Center building](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/mit-stata-center-building-frank-gehry-architecture.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/mit-stata-center-building-frank-gehry-architecture.jpg)

MIT Stata Center

According to architecture critic Robert Campbell, the Stata Center has a design that looks as if it was never completed. Additionally, Campbell states that the building gives the impression that like it is about to collapse. The walls of the building are not perpendicular to the ground, but have different angles. For this reason, the facade you see changes depending on where you look at the building. Because the metal claddings have different illuminance levels according to the amount of exposure to the sun’s rays.

#### 9. Weisman Art Museum

Lastly, the Weisman Art Museum at the University of Minnesota, USA is a 1993 design by Frank Gehry. The exterior of the building is covered with stainless steel, which we can see frequently in the architecture of Frank Gehry. This facade overlooks the Mississippi River. And the back facade has brick claddings in harmony with the surrounding buildings.

# Architecture of Frank Gehry | Top 9 Gehry Works

By

[Archeetect](https://archeetect.com/author/kzxm241l-sadx/)

 - 

21 April 2022

Frank Gehry, whose real name is Ephraim Goldberg, is a Canadian born architect of Jewish origin. He had moved with his family to California before he went to college. After completing his undergraduate education at the University of Southern California, he was accepted to the Harvard School of Architecture. However, he abandoned his education and started to create a furniture series called Easy Edges. This design experiment he got in early ages has made a powerful impact on the **architecture of Frank Gehry**.

At his Easy Edges business, he was designing furniture from thick cardboard. Later, he released a second furniture design series and named it Experimental Edges.

## Architecture of Frank Gehry

[![Image 4: Life and buildings of Frank Gehry, famous Canadian architect](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/architecture-of-frank-gehry-works-buildings-archeetect.com_.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/architecture-of-frank-gehry-works-buildings-archeetect.com_.jpg)

Architect Frank Gehry – ©Eager, Flickr

Gehry started his professional architectural career by founding his own office, [Frank Gehry and Associates](https://foga.com/), in 1963. In 1989 he won the Pritzker Architecture Prize, the most prestigious award in the field of architecture. Then, he received a gold medal from the American Society of Architects in 1999 and from the British Royal Family in 2000. Throughout his career, he has produced designs in various typologies such as museums, public buildings, residences and concert halls.

### Characteristics of Frank Gehry Architecture

*   Frank Gehry has outstanded with the architectural designs he produced in the neo-modern period. Gehry started his career by designing furnitures. There, he was designing furnitures that was far from the usual forms by shaping cardboard. By this way, he had been disclosing his reaction against the usual and static designs of the modernism.
*   Gehry used to love functionalism and admired Louis Kahn, one of the leading architects in this field.
*   At the end of the 70’s, he designed various buildings by blending his architectural experience and mentality with deconstructivist thought.
*   In buildings of Frank Gehry, the form is freely shaped by cutting loose from the norms.
*   Frank Gehry often prefers to use curvy and fluid forms in his structures.
*   His designs leave a sculptural impact.
*   **Frank Gehry structures** are away from the boringness of modernism and have asymmetrical lines.
*   He frequently uses industrial metals such as titanium and stainless steel as the facade cladding in his large-scale [deconstructivist buildings](https://archeetect.com/deconstructivism/).

### A List of Frank Gehry Buildings

#### 1. Danziger House

This building he designed in 1965 is designer Louis Danziger’s own studio. This house is the leading functional and simple designs frequently seen in early period **Frank Gehry works**. With the white concrete surfaces and the low amount of glass surfaces in accordance with the degree of privacy inside, the building has a minimalist appearance. Moreover, it is possible to see traces of Louis Kahn’s pure functionalist style in the design.

#### 2. Gehry House

[![Image 5: Frank Gehry House located in Santa Monica](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/gehry-house-archeetect.com_.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/gehry-house-archeetect.com_.jpg)

Gehry House – ©IK’s World Trip, Wikimedia

It is Gehry’s design, which he completed in 1977-78 by removing the carriers and many elements of an existing house. For this reason, it has a messy appearance. Although it received a lot of backlash at first, it later began to be seen as one of the most successful examples of the Deconstructivism movement. This **Frank Gehry House in Santa Monica**, California was named after its owner.

Thanks to this work, he got many low-budget residential building projects. He had been turning architecture into an art in narrow plots, complex environments and low-budget projects.

#### 3. Walt Disney Concert Hall

**Architect Frank Gehry** designed the Walt Disney Concert Hall in downtown Los Angeles in 1988. During the design phase, he wanted the building to have a stone cladding. He even explained in an interview that the stone would shine at night and make the building look more beautiful and friendly. Metal cladding, on the other hand, will turned dark when it got dark. But things changed during the design process, and worked stainless steel claddings enveloped the facade.

[![Image 6: Walt Disney Concert Hall design by Frank Gehry](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/walt-disney-concert-hall-buildings-by-frank-gehry-architecture.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/walt-disney-concert-hall-buildings-by-frank-gehry-architecture.jpg)

Walt Disney Concert Hall

However, when the building was completed, a big problem arose. The facade covered with reflective metal panels, had been focalising sunlight on some of the surrounding buildings due to its sloping surfaces. This case created irresistible room temperatures in neighboring buildings and showed that architecture was not an issue independent of the environment.

In 2005, Gehry identified the problematic panels with the help of computer programs to solve this problem. Then, he mattified these panels by sanding. Walt Disney Concert Hall by Frank Gehry is host to the Los Angeles Philharmonic Orchestra.

#### 4. Bilbao Guggenheim Museum

Because of the splinter organization ETA in Spain, the light in the eyes of the city of Bilbao went out and the Port of Bilbao became unusable. As a remedy, the Spanish government initiated a cultural and economic transformation program in the 1990s. The port was the most important part of this renovation project.

[![Image 7: One of the most famous buildings by Frank Gehry, Bilbao Guggenheim Museum](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/bilbao-guggenheim-museum-design-by-frank-gehry-archeetect.com_.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/bilbao-guggenheim-museum-design-by-frank-gehry-archeetect.com_.jpg)

Bilbao Guggenheim Museum

A museum with Gehry’s signature was built in the port, which was renovated with the donations of Solomon R. Guggenheim. By this means, Gehry presented the Guggenheim Museum, which refers to the history of the port city of Bilbao and resembles a sailing ship, to the history of architecture. [Bilbao Guggenheim Museum](https://archeetect.com/bilbao-guggenheim-museum/) is frank gehry’s most famous building in Spain since then.

#### 5. Dancing House

[![Image 8: Dancing House, the famous architecture of Frank Gehry](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/dancing-house-frank-gehry-architecture-buildings.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/dancing-house-frank-gehry-architecture-buildings.jpg)
**Dancing House by Frank Gehry** is located in Prag. It is a building that stands out among historical buildings with its dynamic stance. Gehry makes the structure dance with the curving retreat in the middle of the building. Actually, the project consists of 2 buildings. The graceful and curved glass building on the left represents a dancing woman, and the more solemn one with a cylindrical mass on the right represents the male dancer. You can learn more about Dancing House by click [here](https://archeetect.com/dancing-house/).

#### 6. Vitra Design Museum

[![Image 9: Frank Gehry architecture example Vitra Design Museum](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/vitra-design-museum-architecture-of-frank-gehry-archeetect.com_.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/vitra-design-museum-architecture-of-frank-gehry-archeetect.com_.jpg)

Vitra Design Museum – ©Opalsson, Flickr

The museum, which belongs to the Vitra Foundation, is the first building designed by Frank Gehry in Europe. When we look at the form of the building, the sloping facades used by Gehry in his designs leap out in this building as well. Gehry has integrated these sloping facades with curvilinear surfaces. Unlike most of his buildings, Gehry used plaster on the facade and covered some parts of the exterior with a titanium alloy material.

The museum exhibites furnitures designed by designers such as Zaha Hadid and various works. Inside, there are exhibition halls, a library, a restoration laboratory and different workshop areas.

#### 7. Louis Vuitton Foundation

[![Image 10: Louis Vuitton Foundation building of Frank Gehry](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/louis-vuitton-foundation-building-architecture-of-frank-gehry.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/louis-vuitton-foundation-building-architecture-of-frank-gehry.jpg)

Louis Vuitton Foundation – ©Iwan Baan

Located in the second largest nature park in Paris, the Louis Vuitton Foundation has a dynamic mass. This deconstructivist structure formed by curved shells of various sizes has become a modern part of the city skyline. Although the Louis Vitton is at the center of criticism in terms of the context where it was built, Frank Gehry has done a successful job in the design of the building, depending on its [sustainable architecture](https://archeetect.com/sustainable-architecture/) strategies.

#### 8. Stata Center

The Ray and Maria Stata Center is the research center that architect Frank Gehry designed for MIT in 2000. The building with an area of 67 thousand square meters includes 2 different structures rising on 4 floors. One of them is called Gates Tower and the other is called Dreyfoos Tower or simply G Tower and D Tower.

[![Image 11: MIT Stata Center building](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/mit-stata-center-building-frank-gehry-architecture.jpg)](https://archeetect.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/mit-stata-center-building-frank-gehry-architecture.jpg)

MIT Stata Center

According to architecture critic Robert Campbell, the Stata Center has a design that looks as if it was never completed. Additionally, Campbell states that the building gives the impression that like it is about to collapse. The walls of the building are not perpendicular to the ground, but have different angles. For this reason, the facade you see changes depending on where you look at the building. Because the metal claddings have different illuminance levels according to the amount of exposure to the sun’s rays.

#### 9. Weisman Art Museum

Lastly, the Weisman Art Museum at the University of Minnesota, USA is a 1993 design by Frank Gehry. The exterior of the building is covered with stainless steel, which we can see frequently in the architecture of Frank Gehry. This facade overlooks the Mississippi River. And the back facade has brick claddings in harmony with the surrounding buildings.
