## Unrealized projects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Unrealized projects")]

### 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: 1990s")]

*   _**Gilligan's Island**_: In the late 1990s, Gunn and [Charlie Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Kaufman "Charlie Kaufman") attempted to make a film adaptation of the 1960s television series _[Gilligan's Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilligan's\_Island "Gilligan's Island")_, but as a [cannibal film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannibal_film "Cannibal film"). Although the project was supported by [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros."), the film was never made because [Sherwood Schwartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherwood_Schwartz "Sherwood Schwartz"), who created the show, disapproved.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-125)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-126)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-127)
*   _**Silver Surfer**_: In 1999, an executive from [20th Century Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Studios "20th Century Studios") offered to hire Gunn to write and direct a film about the [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics") superhero [Silver Surfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Surfer "Silver Surfer").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-accardo-128)
*   _**Spy vs. Spy**_: Also in 1999, Gunn wrote an unproduced screenplay adaptation of _[Spy vs. Spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy\_vs.\_Spy "Spy vs. Spy")_. According to Gunn, [Jay Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Roach "Jay Roach") was to have directed and [Nicolas Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Cage "Nicolas Cage") and [Eddie Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Murphy "Eddie Murphy") were to have starred.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-129)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-130)

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: 2000s")]

*   _**Plastic Man**_: While much is not known about this project or how far it got, Gunn pitched a basic idea back in the early 2000s where [Matthew Lillard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Lillard "Matthew Lillard") would have starred as the [titular, wise cracking hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_Man "Plastic Man").[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-131)
*   _**The Newlyweds**_: In a 2002 interview with _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_, Gunn revealed that one of his next projects was a script called _The Newlyweds_ for [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros."),[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-ign-132) which ultimately was not produced.
*   **_Pure_ stage musical**: Gunn also revealed that he and _[Tromeo and Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tromeo\_and\_Juliet "Tromeo and Juliet")_ composer Willie Wisely were working on a [stage musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theatre "Musical theatre") called _Pure_. Gunn described said project as "a love story revolving around a guy who kills and tortures people because he thinks it helps him write and draw better children's books."[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-ign-132)
*   _**Scooby-Doo 3**_: Gunn was to have helmed _Scooby-Doo 3_, which would have been the third film of _[Scooby-Doo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooby-Doo\_(film) "Scooby-Doo (film)")_ (2002). However, due to the critical and financial failure of _[Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooby-Doo\_2:\_Monsters\_Unleashed "Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed")_ (2004), [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.") cancelled the project.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-williams-133)
*   **_Creature from the Black Lagoon_ remake**: In 2004, Gunn pitched to [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") his screenplay that was intended to be a remake of the 1954 film _[Creature from the Black Lagoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creature\_from\_the\_Black\_Lagoon "Creature from the Black Lagoon")_, but the studio turned down the pitch.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-williams-133)
*   **Untitled Satan film**: While promoting his film _[Slither](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slither\_(2006\_film) "Slither (2006 film)")_ (2006), Gunn revealed to _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_ that he was in the process of writing a "much darker" movie about [Satan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan "Satan"). "I feel good about it," he said of the project at the time. "I think it's something special. [_Slither_] is really a call back to the '80s films and I think what I'm doing now, it's kind of its own thing."[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-134)
*   _**Pets**_: In 2007, it was reported that Gunn was to write and direct a comedy film for [New Regency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Regency "New Regency") titled _Pets_, with [Ben Stiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Stiller "Ben Stiller") serving as one of the producers.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-accardo-128)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-135) Gunn left the project due to creative differences.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-accardo-128)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-136)
*   _**The Belko Experiment**_: Main article: [The Belko Experiment §Production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Belko_Experiment#Production "The Belko Experiment")

**James Francis Gunn Jr.** (born August 5, 1966[[n 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-born-1)) is an American filmmaker. He began his career as a screenwriter in the mid-1990s, starting at [Troma Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troma_Entertainment "Troma Entertainment") with _[Tromeo and Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tromeo\_and\_Juliet "Tromeo and Juliet")_ (1996). He then began working as a director, starting with the horror-comedy film _[Slither](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slither\_(2006\_film) "Slither (2006 film)")_ (2006), and moving to the superhero genre with _[Super](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_(2010\_American\_film) "Super (2010 American film)")_ (2010), _[Guardians of the Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardians\_of\_the\_Galaxy\_(film) "Guardians of the Galaxy (film)")_ (2014), _[Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardians\_of\_the\_Galaxy\_Vol.\_2 "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2")_ (2017), _[The Suicide Squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Suicide\_Squad\_(film) "The Suicide Squad (film)")_ (2021), and _[Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardians\_of\_the\_Galaxy\_Vol.\_3 "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3")_ (2023).

In 2022, [Warner Bros. Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Discovery "Warner Bros. Discovery") hired Gunn and his longtime producer [Peter Safran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Safran "Peter Safran") to become co-chairmen and co-CEOs of [DC Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Studios "DC Studios").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-dc_studios-2) Under DC Studios, Gunn co-produced and executive produced every film and television series under the [DC Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Universe_(franchise) "DC Universe (franchise)") (DCU) media franchise alongside Safran, which acts as a soft-reboot of the [DC Extended Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Extended_Universe "DC Extended Universe") (DCEU). In the DCU, he is the creator of the series _[Creature Commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creature\_Commandos\_(TV\_series) "Creature Commandos (TV series)")_ (2024–present) and the writer-director of the film _[Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman\_(2025\_film) "Superman (2025 film)")_ (2025).

He also wrote and directed the web series _[James Gunn's PG Porn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James\_Gunn's\_PG\_Porn "James Gunn's PG Porn")_ (2008–2009), the [HBO Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO_Max "HBO Max") original series _[Peacemaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacemaker\_(TV\_series) "Peacemaker (TV series)")_ (2022–2025) and the [Disney+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney+ "Disney+") original special _[The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardians\_of\_the\_Galaxy\_Holiday\_Special "The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special")_ (2022). Other work for which he is known include writing for [the 2004 remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_of_the_Dead_(2004_film) "Dawn of the Dead (2004 film)") of [George A. Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_A._Romero "George A. Romero")'s _[Dawn of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn\_of\_the\_Dead\_(1978\_film) "Dawn of the Dead (1978 film)")_ (1978), writing the live-action adaptation of _[Scooby-Doo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooby-Doo\_(film) "Scooby-Doo (film)")_ (2002), and its sequel _[Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooby-Doo\_2:\_Monsters\_Unleashed "Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed")_ (2004), writing and producing the horror-action film _[The Belko Experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Belko\_Experiment "The Belko Experiment")_ (2016), producing the superhero-horror film _[Brightburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brightburn "Brightburn")_ (2019), contributing to comedy-anthology film _[Movie 43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie\_43 "Movie 43")_ (2013) (directing the segment "Beezel") and the 2012 hack-and-slash video game _[Lollipop Chainsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lollipop\_Chainsaw "Lollipop Chainsaw")_, and also co-producing and co-developing the story for the comedy-legal film [_Coyote Vs. Acme_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyote_vs._Acme "Coyote vs. Acme") (2026).

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

James Francis Gunn Jr.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-3) was born on August 5, 1966[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-LA_Times-4)[[n 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-born-1) in [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis"), Missouri,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-tribute-5) to parents James F. Gunn, an attorney, and Leota "Lee" (Hynek).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-stltoday.com-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-GunnNoClose-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-11) He was raised [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-12) in the St. Louis suburb of [Manchester, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester,_Missouri "Manchester, Missouri").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-14) He has five siblings — actor [Sean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Gunn "Sean Gunn"), actor and political writer [Matt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Gunn "Matt Gunn"), screenwriter [Brian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Gunn "Brian Gunn"), Patrick, and Beth.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-17) Gunn is of [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") descent,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-18) his father coming from an Irish immigrant family.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-19) Gunn has stated that his family's surname was originally the [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") name MacGilgunn and that it means "sons to the servants of the god of the dead"; it actually means "son of the brown youth."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-22)

Growing up, Gunn was influenced by low-budget films such as _[Night of the Living Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night\_of\_the\_Living\_Dead "Night of the Living Dead")_ and _[Friday the 13th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friday\_the\_13th\_(1980\_film) "Friday the 13th (1980 film)")_. He read magazines like _[Fangoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fangoria "Fangoria")_ and attended genre movie screenings, including the original _[Dawn of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn\_of\_the\_Dead\_(1978\_film) "Dawn of the Dead (1978 film)")_ at the [Tivoli Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tivoli_Theatre_(University_City,_Missouri) "Tivoli Theatre (University City, Missouri)") in St. Louis. At the age of 12, he began making [8 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8_mm_film "8 mm film")[zombie films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie_film "Zombie film") with his brothers in the woods near their home.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-stlmag.com-23)

Gunn and his brothers all attended the [Jesuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit "Jesuit")[St. Louis University High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_University_High_School "St. Louis University High School"), where he graduated in 1984.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-alumni-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-stltoday.com-9) He went on to earn a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") from [Saint Louis University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Louis_University_(United_States) "Saint Louis University (United States)").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-24) While at Saint Louis University, Gunn created political cartoons for the school's student weekly, _The University News_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-unewsonline.com-25) Gunn said that, at an unspecified time in his college education, "I went to two years undergraduate film school at [Loyola Marymount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyola_Marymount "Loyola Marymount") in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). But I was pretty screwed up at the time, and had to leave. Years later I went to graduate school at the [Columbia University School of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_Fine_Arts "Columbia University School of Fine Arts") but I studied prose writing, not film writing."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-26) He earned a [Master of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Fine_Arts "Master of Fine Arts") from Columbia University in 1995.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-27)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music")]

While living in St. Louis, Gunn founded a band, The Icons, in 1989, serving as lead vocalist. The group released the album _Mom, We Like It Here on Earth_ in 1994, and its songs "Sunday" and "Walking Naked" were featured in the film _[Tromeo and Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tromeo\_and\_Juliet "Tromeo and Juliet")_. The Icons disbanded in the mid-1990s.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Gunn has continued to work in music, composing songs for _[Scooby-Doo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooby-Doo\_(film) "Scooby-Doo (film)")_, _[Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooby-Doo\_2:\_Monsters\_Unleashed "Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed")_, and _[Movie 43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie\_43 "Movie 43")_.

### Film and television

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Film and television")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/James_Gunn_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg/250px-James_Gunn_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Gunn_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg)

Gunn in 2013

Gunn began his career in filmmaking with [Troma Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troma_Entertainment "Troma Entertainment") in 1996, for which he co-wrote the independent film _[Tromeo and Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tromeo\_and\_Juliet "Tromeo and Juliet")_. Working alongside his mentor [Lloyd Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Kaufman "Lloyd Kaufman"), the co-founder of Troma, Gunn learned how to write screenplays, produce films, scout locations, direct actors, distribute films, and create his own poster art.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-stlmag.com-23) After contributing to several other Troma films, Gunn in 2000 wrote, produced and performed in the superhero comedy _[The Specials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Specials\_(2000\_film) "The Specials (2000 film)")_, directed by [Craig Mazin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Mazin "Craig Mazin") and featuring [Rob Lowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Lowe "Rob Lowe"), [Thomas Haden Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Haden_Church "Thomas Haden Church"), [Paget Brewster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paget_Brewster "Paget Brewster"), [Judy Greer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Greer "Judy Greer") and [Jamie Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_Kennedy "Jamie Kennedy").

Gunn's first major Hollywood screenplay was _Scooby-Doo_ in 2002. In 2004, he wrote the screenplays for the remake of _[Dawn of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn\_of\_the\_Dead\_(2004\_film) "Dawn of the Dead (2004 film)")_ and the sequel _Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed_. With these films, Gunn became the first screenwriter to have two films top the box office in consecutive weeks.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-28) That same year, he executive produced and starred in the mockumentary _[LolliLove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LolliLove "LolliLove")_, directed by and starring his then-wife [Jenna Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jenna_Fischer "Jenna Fischer"). His film directorial debut was the 2006 horror-comedy _[Slither](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slither\_(2006\_film) "Slither (2006 film)")_, which was included on Rotten Tomatoes' list of the 50 Best Ever Reviewed Horror Movies.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-29)

Gunn's next projects included the comedy short film "Humanzee!" which was originally intended exclusively for the Xbox Live's _Horror Meets Comedy_ series of short comedy films by horror directors, it was replaced with "Sparky and Mikaela" which debuted on Xbox Live on December 31, 2008. In an April 2009 interview on _The [Jace Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jace\_Hall "Jace Hall") Show_, Gunn described "Sparky and Mikaela" as being "about a human [and] racoon crime fighting team and they fight crime in both the forest world, among the furry animals, and in the human world".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-30) Gunn also has a short-form web series for [Spike.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike.com "Spike.com") titled _[James Gunn's PG Porn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James\_Gunn's\_PG\_Porn "James Gunn's PG Porn")_.

In 2008, Gunn was a judge on the [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1") reality television show _[Scream Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scream\_Queens\_(2008\_TV\_series) "Scream Queens (2008 TV series)")_, where 10 unknown actresses compete for a role in the film _[Saw VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saw\_VI "Saw VI")_.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-31)

In 2009, Gunn announced he was going to write and direct _Pets_, a comedy about a man who is abducted by aliens who want to turn him into a household pet, with [Ben Stiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Stiller "Ben Stiller"), [Stuart Cornfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Cornfeld "Stuart Cornfeld") and Jeremy Kramer producing.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-32) However, by March 2009, Gunn announced, "_Pets_ unfortunately, is done. I'm gone. I left the project for various reasons. I hope it sees the light of day somehow, but it won't be with me attached as director."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-33)

In 2010, Gunn released _[Super](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_(2010\_American\_film) "Super (2010 American film)")_, a [dark comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_comedy "Dark comedy") and [superhero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superhero "Superhero") satire starring [Rainn Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainn_Wilson "Rainn Wilson") and [Elliot Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliot_Page "Elliot Page"). He also directed a segment of the 2013 comedy anthology film _[Movie 43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie\_43 "Movie 43")_ (2013); the segment starred [Elizabeth Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Banks "Elizabeth Banks") and [Josh Duhamel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Duhamel "Josh Duhamel"). The film was critically panned.

Gunn co-wrote and directed the [Marvel Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Studios "Marvel Studios") adaptation of _[Guardians of the Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardians\_of\_the\_Galaxy\_(film) "Guardians of the Galaxy (film)")_, which was released on August 1, 2014.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-GunnGotG-34) His brother, Sean, has a role in the film. > Popular fare in any medium has always been snubbed by the self-appointed elite. ... What bothers me slightly is that many people assume because you make big films that you put less love, care, and thought into them than people do who make independent films or who make what are considered more serious Hollywood films. ... Gunn wrote and directed _[Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardians\_of\_the\_Galaxy\_Vol.\_2 "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2")_ (2017).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-43) Gunn was slated to direct _[Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardians\_of\_the\_Galaxy\_Vol.\_3 "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3")_ in July 2018, but before the project started, [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Studios_(division) "Walt Disney Studios (division)") severed ties with Gunn as the director amid controversy over [off-color jokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-color_humor "Off-color humor") he had [tweeted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-ReporterFired-44) Gunn was rehired in March 2019 after a mass public appeal, many saying he was the reason of the previous movies' successes.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-GunnRehired-45)

### DC Studios

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/James_Gunn_headshoot_photo_%28cropped%29_%281%29.jpg/250px-James_Gunn_headshoot_photo_%28cropped%29_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Gunn_headshoot_photo_(cropped)_(1).jpg)

Gunn and frequent producing partner [Peter Safran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Safran "Peter Safran") had advised [David Zaslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Zaslav "David Zaslav"), the CEO of the newly created [Warner Bros. Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Discovery "Warner Bros. Discovery"), during his search for a new head of [DC Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Films "DC Films"). The duo impressed Zaslav, who decided to appoint them as the co-chairpersons and CEOs of DC Films, rebranded as "DC Studios". The two were given control over films, animation and television projects based on characters from [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics"). Gunn was to oversee the creative aspects and will be exclusive to Warner Bros. Discovery during his tenure, except for his prior commitments to Disney. The two first worked together on the 2000 superhero comedy film _[The Specials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Specials\_(2000\_film) "The Specials (2000 film)")_ written by Gunn with Safran as co-executive producer, with subsequent collaborations including Gunn's 2008 short films _Sparky & Mikaela_ and _Humanzee!_, the television series _[James Gunn's PG Porn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James\_Gunn's\_PG\_Porn "James Gunn's PG Porn")_ (2008–2009), _[The Belko Experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Belko\_Experiment "The Belko Experiment")_ (2016) and the DCEU film _[The Suicide Squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Suicide\_Squad\_(film) "The Suicide Squad (film)")_ (2021). The two assumed their positions on November 1, 2022.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-77)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-78)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-79)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-80)

In December 2022, Gunn announced that he was writing a film about a young [Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman "Superman") during his early years in [Metropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis_(comics) "Metropolis (comics)"),[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-81) later revealed to be titled _[Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman\_(2025\_film) "Superman (2025 film)")_ and released in July 2025; in March 2023 it was confirmed Gunn would also direct the project.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-82) In January 2023, Gunn and Safran revealed their plans for future DCU films, with the first chapter being titled "Gods and Monsters". Gunn also wrote a seven-episode animated series titled _[Creature Commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creature\_Commandos\_(TV\_series) "Creature Commandos (TV series)")_, based on the [comic book team of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creature_Commandos "Creature Commandos"),[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-:0-83) and released ahead of _Superman_ in December 2024,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-peacemaker_canon-84) and also worked on the HBO Max series _Waller_, a spin-off of _[Peacemaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacemaker\_(TV\_series) "Peacemaker (TV series)")_ focusing on the character of [Amanda Waller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Waller_(DC_Extended_Universe) "Amanda Waller (DC Extended Universe)"), with Christal Henry writing and [Viola Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_Davis "Viola Davis") reprising her role from previous DCEU projects.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-85)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-86) Gunn is also involved in multiple other DC projects, including producing _[Supergirl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergirl\_(2026\_film) "Supergirl (2026 film)")_ released on June 26, 2026.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-87)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-GunnDCProjects-88)

Following the success of _Superman_, Gunn announced a follow-up film in September 2025, titled _[Man of Tomorrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man\_of\_Tomorrow\_(film) "Man of Tomorrow (film)")_, using new artwork from [Jim Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Lee "Jim Lee"). The film is set to be released in 2027, with [David Corenswet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Corenswet "David Corenswet") and [Nicholas Hoult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Hoult "Nicholas Hoult") expected to reprise their roles.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-89) The [second season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacemaker_season_2 "Peacemaker season 2") of _Peacemaker_ was also produced by the Gunn and Safran-led DC Studios. Most of the [first season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacemaker_season_1 "Peacemaker season 1") is [canon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_(fiction) "Canon (fiction)") to the DCU, but only the second season, written in 2023 and aired in August–October 2025, is part of the Gods and Monsters chapter.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-peacemaker_canon-84)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-90)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-91)

## Political views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Political views")]

In December 2017, Gunn publicly shifted from his previous apolitical stance on social media to openly criticize the [Donald Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump"). In one of his tweets, he described the situation as a "national crisis" and compared the president's approach to facts and journalism to the tactics employed by [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") and [Vladimir Putin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-92) In July 2018, after [Mark Duplass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Duplass "Mark Duplass") posted and deleted a tweet endorsing conservative commentator [Ben Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Shapiro "Ben Shapiro"), Gunn came in defense of him by referring to Shapiro as an "asshole" and stating that "There are a lot of traitors and racists in the country today. Perhaps save the outrage for them."[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-93) This led to right-wing personality [Mike Cernovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Cernovich "Mike Cernovich") and conservative website _[The Daily Caller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Caller "The Daily Caller")_ to highlight some of Gunn's past controversial tweets.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-94)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-95)

Some critics have interpreted the film _Superman_ (2025) as an allegory for the [Israeli–Palestinian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict"), particularly referencing the [2018–2019 Gaza border protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%932019_Gaza_border_protests "2018–2019 Gaza border protests") and the [2023 Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Gaza_war "2023 Gaza war"). However, James Gunn stated that the script was written prior to the outbreak of the war and was not intended as an allegory.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-96)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-97) Filming began on February 29, 2024.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-98)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Gunn&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Gunn married actress [Jenna Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jenna_Fischer "Jenna Fischer") on October 7, 2000.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-stltoday.com-9) After seven years of marriage, Gunn and Fischer announced their separation in a joint statement on September 5, 2007,[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-99) divorcing in 2008.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-100) The two remained friends. In 2010, Fischer persuaded Gunn to cast [Rainn Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainn_Wilson "Rainn Wilson"), her co-star on _[The Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Office\_(U.S.\_TV\_series) "The Office (U.S. TV series)")_, in Gunn's film _[Super](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_(2010\_American\_film) "Super (2010 American film)")_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-stlmag.com-23)

Gunn has been in a relationship with actress [Jennifer Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Holland "Jennifer Holland") since 2015.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-101) In February 2022, Holland and Gunn became engaged,[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-102) and were married at the end of September 2022.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-103)

He has a dog named Ozu, adopted from a shelter in 2022. Gunn has regularly shared photos of the dog and promoted the hashtag #AdoptDontShop.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-104) For that reason as well as his CGI work on _Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3_, [PETA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_for_the_Ethical_Treatment_of_Animals "People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals") declared Gunn to be their 2023 Person of the Year.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-105) Ozu served as the inspiration for the redesigned, CGI-animated [Krypto the Superdog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krypto "Krypto") in Gunn's 2025 adaptation of _Superman_.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-106)

Gunn was raised in a [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") family and has mentioned how prayer continues to play an important role in his life,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-107) but has also said that he is, "in some ways, anti-religion".[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-108)

*   _**The Newlyweds**_: In a 2002 interview with _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_, Gunn revealed that one of his next projects was a script called _The Newlyweds_ for [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros."),[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gunn#cite_note-ign-132) which ultimately was not produced.

# The New Town Movement: Three Towns that Helped Build Los Angeles, and What They Teach Us about Building Cities

## New towns and master-planned communities played a major role in the growth of the Los Angeles metropolitan area throughout the 20th century. With the invention of mass-produced housing in the 1940s—a factory in the field, as exemplified by Levittown in New York—Los Angeles developed rapidly after large ranches such as Palos Verdes and Bixby Ranch were master-planned for housing and neighborhood amenities.

New towns and master-planned communities played a major role in the growth of the Los Angeles metropolitan area throughout the 20th century. With the invention of mass-produced housing in the 1940s—a factory in the field, as exemplified by Levittown in New York—Los Angeles developed rapidly after large ranches such as Palos Verdes and Bixby Ranch were master-planned for housing and neighborhood amenities.

Soldiers returning from World War II got loan guarantees via the GI Bill that enabled them to purchase homes with low down payments, which created enormous demand for housing. Production homebuilders including Marlow-Burns (Toluca Lake, 1941), Kaiser Community Homes (Panorama City, 1948), and Weingart, Taper, and Boyar (Lakewood, 1950) laid the groundwork for Los Angeles’ dramatic growth throughout the rest of the 20th century and into the 21st century.

As the metropolitan area expanded into Orange, Riverside, San Bernadino, and Ventura counties, many of the ranches were developed by major corporations such as Philip Morris, Mobil Land, and Kaiser Aluminum, as well as the families who owned them, such as the O’Neill, Moiso, and Irvine families in

**Orange County**

_New Towns for the 21st Century_, a 2021 book I coedited with Ann Forsyth, catalogs 14 new towns and master-planned communities (ones built out with 30,000 or more residents) in the Los Angeles metro area. This article focuses on three of the new towns that are among the most famous—Lakewood, Valencia, and Irvine—and that represent different eras and different parts of the Los Angeles metropolitan area. Each of these new towns has lessons not just for Los Angeles but also for urban growth and development throughout the United States.

Lakewood is a suburb of Los Angeles, south of its downtown and bordered by Long Beach, Bellflower, Cerritos, Cypress, and Hawaiian Gardens. With a 2020 population of 82,500, it was developed as a post-World War II new town by production homebuilders Louis Boyar, Mark Taper, and Ben Weingart.

Valencia was conceived in 1965 as a 15,000-acre (6,070 ha) new town on the Newhall Ranch, designed by Los Angeles-based urban architect Victor Gruen. Nowadays, anyone who drives north from Los Angeles on Interstate 5 will recognize Six Flags Magic Mountain, renowned for its 20 roller coasters at the top of the first mountain pass.

Irvine Ranch was assembled—by James Irvine I, in 1864 and 1866, with 110,000 acres (44,500 ha) from the coast to the Orange County mountains—out of a Mexican land grant. The future new town stemmed from the process of designating land to be placed into an agricultural preservation zone created under California’s Williamson Act in 1966. The land that remained outside the zone—in Newport Beach, Laguna Beach, and Inland—became the new town.

**Lakewood**

Los Angeles County’s population exploded after World War II, growing from 2.78 million to 4.15 million between 1940 and 1950. Homebuilders and planners conceived of Westchester, Panorama City, and Lakewood as self-contained communities, rather than as bedroom suburbs dependent on the urban core, according to Alida Brill’s 1996 essay “Lakewood, California ‘Tomorrowland’ at 40.”

Lakewood, near the Los Angeles/Long Beach harbor, was developed in the early 1950s as the region’s first Levittown-like community. The developers created a town of “row after row of neatly sculpted individual lots, ready to become ‘front yards and backyards,’ with houses of the same shape, dimension, and scale, ” according to Brill’s essay. It was a town deeply rooted in the idealized family of _The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet_—the perfect place to raise a family, with churches of every denomination, and neighborhood schools and parks that children could walk to safely.

Like many a graying inner-ring suburb, Lakewood goes through cycles of decline and then recovery. When the defense industry downsized in the 1980s, many of its white middle-class breadwinners, who worked in the aircraft industry (Boeing and McDonnell Douglas), at the port, and on the Naval base, lost their jobs.

Today, Lakewood is recovering and benefiting from an influx of immigrants. Median house prices are $620,000, and the demographics are 46 percent white, 34.3 percent Hispanic, 8.6 percent Black, 18.4 percent Asian, and 11.1 percent biracial, according to the U.S. Census Bureau in 2022.

The city is undergoing redevelopment and revival driven, in part, by an overhaul of the main shopping area and the industrial area around the plants, and by residential development. More than 300 ”mother-in-law” units are under construction, thanks to the state of California’s accessory dwelling unit (ADU) law that allows a second unit to be built on every single-family-zoned parcel.

Community Development Director Abel Avalos notes that Lakewood is famous for being the first contract city—where government services were contracted from the county rather than being provided directly by the municipality.

Don Waldie, who retired as Lakewood’s public information officer after 30 years, says that Lakewood was made specifically for young working-class families. “It is designed on a rectilinear grid where homes, parks, schools, and shopping are unusually well integrated.” Early residents created a plethora of community organizations—"bowling together.” The community spirit contributed to the early incorporation of the new town as a municipality. Waldie says, “This illuminates the city today. An imperative exists to bring new residents into the fold to experience the spirit that the earliest residents had in 1954.”

Valencia Town Center was developed by JMB Realty’s Urban Shopping Centers and opened in 1992. Westfield bought it in 2002. The 60-acre, 1 million square feet mall sold in September 2023 for $195 million, $4 million over the debt, after Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield defaulted on the loan. The buyer, Centennial Real Estate, plans to turn it into a live-work-play destination with offices, apartments, and entertainment spaces. (City of Santa Clarita)

**Valencia, California**

Developed by Newhall Land and Farming Company north of the San Fernando Valley, along Interstate 5, Valencia opened in 1967. The Newhall Ranch was one of the last big parcels of undeveloped land near Los Angeles with 37,250 acres (15,070 ha).

Unlike its residential suburban precedent Levittown, where William Levitt built 17,447 nearly identical houses on Long Island, New York, Valencia had a large employment base and industrial park with more than 8,500 employees by 1988. It was incorporated into the new city of Santa Clarita, formed in 1987.By 1996, Newhall Land had developed 5,000 acres (2,000 ha) with 12,000 homes. Although most of the more recent development in Valencia is outside of the city, Santa Clarita today is one of the wealthier suburbs of Los Angeles, with 228,000 people.

Valencia exemplifies the difficulties of developing urban fringe land in highly contested, water-constrained metropolitan areas. The developers attempted to expand the new town on ranch land west of Interstate 5 in the early 2000s, and had hoped to break ground by 2012, but legal challenges by various environmental groups stopped development for another eight years.

FivePoint Communities, successor to Lennar, who had bought controlling interest in the ranch from Newhall in 2009, ultimately won the lawsuit and finally commenced development in 2017 on 18 initial neighborhoods. Emile Haddad, founder and chairman emeritus of FivePoint Holdings, states that the original new town has 20,000 homes and 20 million square feet (2 million sq m) of commercial.

The Valencia Town Center in Santa Clarita exemplifies its vibrant streetscape. The shopping mall anchors a mixed-use district with 551 luxury apartments, a 244 key Hyatt hotel, and a 57,000-square-foot medical facility.

The west side of Interstate 5 will have an additional 21,000 homes and 11 million square feet (1 million sq m) of commercial space. He attributes Valencia’s success to the fact that it draws people from four major employment centers—Burbank, San Fernando Valley, Downtown LA, and the local Valencia market.

Valencia remains a model of new town development. Critical to its success was offering housing simultaneously for as many different segments of the market as possible—segmented by tenure (for-sale and rental) and by density—large single-family, patio homes, duplexes, low-rise, and high-rise and multistory buildings. The neighborhood was designed to serve all age groups. Its integration into nature provides access to parks and hiking trails within a few blocks of almost every home. And the large employment base shortens commutes and serves one of the new town movement’s foremost objectives—to provide “self-contained” communities where one can live, work, and play without ever leaving the new town.

**Irvine**

If any new town in the United States was destined to be successful, it was Irvine Ranch, with its location along the coast of Orange County, one hour south of downtown Los Angeles. H. Pike Oliver and C. Michael Stockstill’s 2022 book, _Transforming the Irvine Ranch: Joan Irvine, William Pereira, Ray Watson and the Big Plan_, chronicles the history of Irvine’s development, including the fascinating story of how Joan Irvine, the “golden girl” and heir to the ranch, successfully fought against the foundation that was established to own the ranch by Joan’s grandfather to gain control of the Irvine Company.

The book includes the memoir of Ray Watson, who started with the Irvine Company in 1960 as a planner and served as president from 1973 until 1977. He oversaw the master planning of Irvine, led the creation of the new town, and is a beloved figure in the history of Irvine’s formation and success.

The Irvine Ranch was selected to be the site for the new University of California Irvine campus in 1959. It was also chosen over 21 other sites because it was the only one under single ownership, and it offered the possibility of creating a unique vision of “town and gown.” Watson, quoted in Oliver and Stockstill’s book, underscores the enormity of the decision: “In retrospect, a huge step had been taken by the Irvine Company; it was now preparing to not only aggressively attempt to attract the university, but to plan an orderly transition from ranching to urban development.”

The next battle was over cityhood. The ranch had created plans for a business and industrial park next to the Orange County Airport (now John Wayne Airport). The city of Santa Ana sought to annex a strip of land, 300 feet (90 m) wide and 8.5 miles (14 km) long, along the future route of the 405 Freeway, effectively dividing in half the ranch’s land for the new town.

![Image 7: irvine-1-619](https://cdn-ul.uli.org/dims4/default/c88da33/2147483647/strip/true/crop/619x484+0+0/resize/450x352!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fk2-prod-uli.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2Fsites%2F5%2F2023%2F10%2FIrvine-1-619.gif)

In this picture dated 1964, Daniel Aldrich, first Chancellor of University of California, Irvine, William Pereira, architect and founder of William L. Pereira & Associates, and Charles Thomas, president of the Irvine Company review an exhibit detailing anticipated development of the core of University Town Center and the central campus area of UC Irvine. (UC Irvine Special Collections and Archives AS-056)

The annexation ultimately failed because the city overlooked a parcel of land on the route which caused officials to not have enough votes for the annexation. Whereas many new towns do not enjoy the status of self-governance, the incorporation of the area around the new UC Irvine campus into the new city of Irvine helped to ensure the integrity of the future city plan and gave the new town control over its own destiny.

According to Oliver and Stockstill, Joan Irvine was the gadfly who forced the Irvine Company to give up control by lobbying for a change in the federal tax code within the Tax Reform Act of 1969. When the Irvine Foundation had to sell most of its Irvine Company stock, a bidding war ensued that included Mobil Oil, Cadillac Fairview, and shopping center developer Al Taubman.

Taubman invited Joan Irvine to join their consortium. She agreed. Although she would not have control, she would at least have a seat at the table. Taubman still needed more money for his bid. Donald Bren, a Southern California homebuilder, was offered 35 percent of the company for $100 million.

As the authors note, when Taubman inquired why they needed Bren, his marketing executive Robert Schout told him ”Because, Al, you and I look like a couple of gangsters from Detroit. This guy looks like he came from Hollywood.” Five years later, in 1977, Bren bought out his partners for $1 billion, after purchasing the ranch for $337 million.

Today, the new town of Irvine Ranch, largely incorporated into the city of Irvine, celebrates its 50th anniversary. It is home to 310,000 residents and approximately 130,000 workers. Irvine has become an exemplar of new town development thanks to its employment base, Asian influx, and mixed-density neighborhoods.

Like Valencia, its design provides direct access to an abundance of open space, with views from the mountains to the ocean. It pioneered higher-density mixed-use development by catering to demographic groups from young professionals to seniors, many of them working in the life-science and high-tech industries, health care, manufacturing, and import-export companies that have been drawn to Irvine.

New towns and master-planned communities played a major role in the growth of the Los Angeles metropolitan area throughout the 20th century. With the invention of mass-produced housing in the 1940s—a factory in the field, as exemplified by Levittown in New York—Los Angeles developed rapidly after large ranches such as Palos Verdes and Bixby Ranch were master-planned for housing and neighborhood amenities.

Soldiers returning from World War II got loan guarantees via the GI Bill that enabled them to purchase homes with low down payments, which created enormous demand for housing. Production homebuilders including Marlow-Burns (Toluca Lake, 1941), Kaiser Community Homes (Panorama City, 1948), and Weingart, Taper, and Boyar (Lakewood, 1950) laid the groundwork for Los Angeles’ dramatic growth throughout the rest of the 20th century and into the 21st century.

As the metropolitan area expanded into Orange, Riverside, San Bernadino, and Ventura counties, many of the ranches were developed by major corporations such as Philip Morris, Mobil Land, and Kaiser Aluminum, as well as the families who owned them, such as the O’Neill, Moiso, and Irvine families in

**Orange County**

_New Towns for the 21st Century_, a 2021 book I coedited with Ann Forsyth, catalogs 14 new towns and master-planned communities (ones built out with 30,000 or more residents) in the Los Angeles metro area. This article focuses on three of the new towns that are among the most famous—Lakewood, Valencia, and Irvine—and that represent different eras and different parts of the Los Angeles metropolitan area. Each of these new towns has lessons not just for Los Angeles but also for urban growth and development throughout the United States.

Lakewood is a suburb of Los Angeles, south of its downtown and bordered by Long Beach, Bellflower, Cerritos, Cypress, and Hawaiian Gardens. With a 2020 population of 82,500, it was developed as a post-World War II new town by production homebuilders Louis Boyar, Mark Taper, and Ben Weingart.

Valencia was conceived in 1965 as a 15,000-acre (6,070 ha) new town on the Newhall Ranch, designed by Los Angeles-based urban architect Victor Gruen. Nowadays, anyone who drives north from Los Angeles on Interstate 5 will recognize Six Flags Magic Mountain, renowned for its 20 roller coasters at the top of the first mountain pass.

Irvine Ranch was assembled—by James Irvine I, in 1864 and 1866, with 110,000 acres (44,500 ha) from the coast to the Orange County mountains—out of a Mexican land grant. The future new town stemmed from the process of designating land to be placed into an agricultural preservation zone created under California’s Williamson Act in 1966. The land that remained outside the zone—in Newport Beach, Laguna Beach, and Inland—became the new town.

**Lakewood**

Los Angeles County’s population exploded after World War II, growing from 2.78 million to 4.15 million between 1940 and 1950. Homebuilders and planners conceived of Westchester, Panorama City, and Lakewood as self-contained communities, rather than as bedroom suburbs dependent on the urban core, according to Alida Brill’s 1996 essay “Lakewood, California ‘Tomorrowland’ at 40.”

Lakewood, near the Los Angeles/Long Beach harbor, was developed in the early 1950s as the region’s first Levittown-like community. The developers created a town of “row after row of neatly sculpted individual lots, ready to become ‘front yards and backyards,’ with houses of the same shape, dimension, and scale, ” according to Brill’s essay. It was a town deeply rooted in the idealized family of _The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet_—the perfect place to raise a family, with churches of every denomination, and neighborhood schools and parks that children could walk to safely.

Like many a graying inner-ring suburb, Lakewood goes through cycles of decline and then recovery. When the defense industry downsized in the 1980s, many of its white middle-class breadwinners, who worked in the aircraft industry (Boeing and McDonnell Douglas), at the port, and on the Naval base, lost their jobs.

Today, Lakewood is recovering and benefiting from an influx of immigrants. Median house prices are $620,000, and the demographics are 46 percent white, 34.3 percent Hispanic, 8.6 percent Black, 18.4 percent Asian, and 11.1 percent biracial, according to the U.S. Census Bureau in 2022.

The city is undergoing redevelopment and revival driven, in part, by an overhaul of the main shopping area and the industrial area around the plants, and by residential development. More than 300 ”mother-in-law” units are under construction, thanks to the state of California’s accessory dwelling unit (ADU) law that allows a second unit to be built on every single-family-zoned parcel.

Community Development Director Abel Avalos notes that Lakewood is famous for being the first contract city—where government services were contracted from the county rather than being provided directly by the municipality.

Don Waldie, who retired as Lakewood’s public information officer after 30 years, says that Lakewood was made specifically for young working-class families. “It is designed on a rectilinear grid where homes, parks, schools, and shopping are unusually well integrated.” Early residents created a plethora of community organizations—"bowling together.” The community spirit contributed to the early incorporation of the new town as a municipality. Waldie says, “This illuminates the city today. An imperative exists to bring new residents into the fold to experience the spirit that the earliest residents had in 1954.”

Valencia Town Center was developed by JMB Realty’s Urban Shopping Centers and opened in 1992. Westfield bought it in 2002. The 60-acre, 1 million square feet mall sold in September 2023 for $195 million, $4 million over the debt, after Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield defaulted on the loan. The buyer, Centennial Real Estate, plans to turn it into a live-work-play destination with offices, apartments, and entertainment spaces. (City of Santa Clarita)

**Valencia, California**

Developed by Newhall Land and Farming Company north of the San Fernando Valley, along Interstate 5, Valencia opened in 1967. The Newhall Ranch was one of the last big parcels of undeveloped land near Los Angeles with 37,250 acres (15,070 ha).

Unlike its residential suburban precedent Levittown, where William Levitt built 17,447 nearly identical houses on Long Island, New York, Valencia had a large employment base and industrial park with more than 8,500 employees by 1988. It was incorporated into the new city of Santa Clarita, formed in 1987.By 1996, Newhall Land had developed 5,000 acres (2,000 ha) with 12,000 homes. Although most of the more recent development in Valencia is outside of the city, Santa Clarita today is one of the wealthier suburbs of Los Angeles, with 228,000 people.

Valencia exemplifies the difficulties of developing urban fringe land in highly contested, water-constrained metropolitan areas. The developers attempted to expand the new town on ranch land west of Interstate 5 in the early 2000s, and had hoped to break ground by 2012, but legal challenges by various environmental groups stopped development for another eight years.

FivePoint Communities, successor to Lennar, who had bought controlling interest in the ranch from Newhall in 2009, ultimately won the lawsuit and finally commenced development in 2017 on 18 initial neighborhoods. Emile Haddad, founder and chairman emeritus of FivePoint Holdings, states that the original new town has 20,000 homes and 20 million square feet (2 million sq m) of commercial.

The Valencia Town Center in Santa Clarita exemplifies its vibrant streetscape. The shopping mall anchors a mixed-use district with 551 luxury apartments, a 244 key Hyatt hotel, and a 57,000-square-foot medical facility.

The west side of Interstate 5 will have an additional 21,000 homes and 11 million square feet (1 million sq m) of commercial space. He attributes Valencia’s success to the fact that it draws people from four major employment centers—Burbank, San Fernando Valley, Downtown LA, and the local Valencia market.

Valencia remains a model of new town development. Critical to its success was offering housing simultaneously for as many different segments of the market as possible—segmented by tenure (for-sale and rental) and by density—large single-family, patio homes, duplexes, low-rise, and high-rise and multistory buildings. The neighborhood was designed to serve all age groups. Its integration into nature provides access to parks and hiking trails within a few blocks of almost every home. And the large employment base shortens commutes and serves one of the new town movement’s foremost objectives—to provide “self-contained” communities where one can live, work, and play without ever leaving the new town.

**Irvine**

If any new town in the United States was destined to be successful, it was Irvine Ranch, with its location along the coast of Orange County, one hour south of downtown Los Angeles. H. Pike Oliver and C. Michael Stockstill’s 2022 book, _Transforming the Irvine Ranch: Joan Irvine, William Pereira, Ray Watson and the Big Plan_, chronicles the history of Irvine’s development, including the fascinating story of how Joan Irvine, the “golden girl” and heir to the ranch, successfully fought against the foundation that was established to own the ranch by Joan’s grandfather to gain control of the Irvine Company.

The book includes the memoir of Ray Watson, who started with the Irvine Company in 1960 as a planner and served as president from 1973 until 1977. He oversaw the master planning of Irvine, led the creation of the new town, and is a beloved figure in the history of Irvine’s formation and success.

The Irvine Ranch was selected to be the site for the new University of California Irvine campus in 1959. It was also chosen over 21 other sites because it was the only one under single ownership, and it offered the possibility of creating a unique vision of “town and gown.” Watson, quoted in Oliver and Stockstill’s book, underscores the enormity of the decision: “In retrospect, a huge step had been taken by the Irvine Company; it was now preparing to not only aggressively attempt to attract the university, but to plan an orderly transition from ranching to urban development.”

The next battle was over cityhood. The ranch had created plans for a business and industrial park next to the Orange County Airport (now John Wayne Airport). The city of Santa Ana sought to annex a strip of land, 300 feet (90 m) wide and 8.5 miles (14 km) long, along the future route of the 405 Freeway, effectively dividing in half the ranch’s land for the new town.

![Image 7: irvine-1-619](https://cdn-ul.uli.org/dims4/default/c88da33/2147483647/strip/true/crop/619x484+0+0/resize/450x352!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fk2-prod-uli.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2Fsites%2F5%2F2023%2F10%2FIrvine-1-619.gif)

In this picture dated 1964, Daniel Aldrich, first Chancellor of University of California, Irvine, William Pereira, architect and founder of William L. Pereira & Associates, and Charles Thomas, president of the Irvine Company review an exhibit detailing anticipated development of the core of University Town Center and the central campus area of UC Irvine. (UC Irvine Special Collections and Archives AS-056)

The annexation ultimately failed because the city overlooked a parcel of land on the route which caused officials to not have enough votes for the annexation. Whereas many new towns do not enjoy the status of self-governance, the incorporation of the area around the new UC Irvine campus into the new city of Irvine helped to ensure the integrity of the future city plan and gave the new town control over its own destiny.

According to Oliver and Stockstill, Joan Irvine was the gadfly who forced the Irvine Company to give up control by lobbying for a change in the federal tax code within the Tax Reform Act of 1969. When the Irvine Foundation had to sell most of its Irvine Company stock, a bidding war ensued that included Mobil Oil, Cadillac Fairview, and shopping center developer Al Taubman.

Taubman invited Joan Irvine to join their consortium. She agreed. Although she would not have control, she would at least have a seat at the table. Taubman still needed more money for his bid. Donald Bren, a Southern California homebuilder, was offered 35 percent of the company for $100 million.

As the authors note, when Taubman inquired why they needed Bren, his marketing executive Robert Schout told him ”Because, Al, you and I look like a couple of gangsters from Detroit. This guy looks like he came from Hollywood.” Five years later, in 1977, Bren bought out his partners for $1 billion, after purchasing the ranch for $337 million.

Today, the new town of Irvine Ranch, largely incorporated into the city of Irvine, celebrates its 50th anniversary. It is home to 310,000 residents and approximately 130,000 workers. Irvine has become an exemplar of new town development thanks to its employment base, Asian influx, and mixed-density neighborhoods.

Like Valencia, its design provides direct access to an abundance of open space, with views from the mountains to the ocean. It pioneered higher-density mixed-use development by catering to demographic groups from young professionals to seniors, many of them working in the life-science and high-tech industries, health care, manufacturing, and import-export companies that have been drawn to Irvine.

## Introduction

### Welcome!

This is a guide to Planned Communities in the United States. The emphasis of this guide is to provide basic information about planned communities, as well as print and electronic resources that might be helpful to those who would like to learn more about them.

## Historical Overview

![Image 3: Black and white map insert illustrating the grid layout of a planned community.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/1_-_gen_info_-_miletus__greece.png)The idea of planning entire communities prior to their construction is an ancient one. According to _[**Greenbelt: History of a New Town**](https://usmai-umcp.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/permalink/01USMAI\_UMCP/4tm3c8/alma990015656100108238),_ one of the earliest such cities on record is Miletus, Greece, which was built in the 4th century B.C. Throughout the Middle Ages and Renaissance, various planned communities, both theoretical and actual, were conceived. Leonardo da Vinci designed several cities that were never constructed. Following the great fire of London in 1666, the architect Christopher Wren created a new master plan for the city that incorporated park land and urban space. Several 18th century cities, including Washington D.C., New York City, and St. Petersburg, Russia, were built according to comprehensive planning.

## Ebenezer Howard and the Garden City Movement

![Image 4: Black and white map illustrating the grid layout of a Garden City community.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/2.2_letchworth_garden_city.png)One of the most important planned city concepts, the Garden City Movement, arose in 19th century England as a reaction to the pollution and crowding of the Industrial Revolution. In 1898, Ebenezer Howard published the book,**[_To-Morrow: A Peaceful Path to Real Reform_](https://usmai-umcp.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/permalink/01USMAI_UMCP/4tm3c8/alma9963858259408238)**in which he laid out his ideas concerning the creation of new towns. Howard believed that these towns should be limited in size and density, and surrounded with a belt of undeveloped land. The idea gained enough attention and financial backing to lead to the creation of Letchworth, in Hertfordshire, England, the first such "Garden City." After the First World War the second town built following Howard's ideas, Welwyn Garden City, also in Hertfordshire, was constructed.

## The Movement Comes to America: Radburn, New Jersey

![Image 5: Black and white aerial-view rendering of  Radburn, New Jersey.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/3_radburn__new_jersey.png)In the early 1920's, American architects Clarence Stein and Henry Wright, inspired by Howard's ideas and the success of Letchworth and Welwyn, created the city of Radburn, New Jersey. Conceived as a community which would be safe for children, Radburn was intentionally designed so that the residents would not require automobiles. Several urban planning designs were pioneered at Radburn that would influence later planned communities, including the separation of pedestrian and vehicle traffic, and the use of "superblocks," each of which shared 23 acres of commonly held parkland.

## New Deal Towns

![Image 6: Black and white aerial-view rendering of Greendale, Wisconsin.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/greendale__wisconsin_2.png)Following the stock market crash of 1929 and the subsequent economic depression, there was great demand both for affordable housing and employment for workers who had lost their jobs. In response the Resettlement Administration, created in 1935 by President Roosevelt, brought about a total of three greenbelt towns: Greenbelt, Maryland; Greenhills, Ohio; and Greendale, Wisconsin. These towns contained many of the elements of the Garden City Movement developments, including the use of superblocks and a "greenbelt" of undeveloped land surrounding the community.

## Levittowns

![Image 7: Black and white aerial-view rendering of Levittown.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/5_levittowns.png)Housing shortages faced many returning World War II veterans. Building materials had been in short supply during the War and residential construction had all but ceased. To meet the demand, enterprising real estate developer Abraham Levitt and his sons decided to build simple, inexpensive, mass-produced houses on a tract of land on Long Island, New York. The Levitts erected the houses quickly, at the rate of 30 per day, but they were still unable to keep up with demand.

Based upon the success of Levittown, Abraham Levitt expanded his building plan from the original 17,447 house community on Long Island to suburban Philadelphia (Levittown, Pa.), Washington, D.C. (Bowie, Md.), and New Jersey (Levittown, N.J.). These communities were criticized for their cookie-cutter design by social critics such as Malvina Reynolds as typified in her song "Little Boxes" (From 2005 to 2012, the US dark-comedy television series Weeds used Reynold’s ditty as its theme song.) Despite such criticism, these communities provided much-needed housing for returning veterans, and remain touchstones in the history of planned community development.

## Reston, Virginia

![Image 8: Aerial view of green space and a winding waterway in Reston, Virginia.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/6_reston__virginia.png)Decades after the demographically-driven success of Abraham Levitt's developments, another developer, Robert Simon, planned and built the city of Reston Virginia. Erected in 1962, the city was designed with a number of elements taken from the Garden City movement of the early 20th century including a buffer of parkland surrounding the city and 10 acres of parkland for every 1,000 residents. Simon's goals for the new city included high standards for structural and natural beauty as well as opportunities for living and working in the same community.

Simon's vision for the city was faithfully executed although his goal of financial success for the city was not attained. Ownership of Reston was relinquished to Gulf Oil (later Mobil), one of the largest initial investors in 1967. Today Reston is considered a model utopian suburb and its central plan is a blend of urban activity with country beauty.

## New Urbanism

![Image 9: Aerial view of a New Urbanism community layout, showing a high-density grid of buildings and integrated green spaces. ](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/new-urbanism.png)After a period of dormancy, the idea of building idealized communities was re-born in the early 1980s as "New Urbanism." This movement emphasized livable, walkable communities that utilize mass transit and more intelligent use and reuse of previously developed buildings and land. Promoted in large part by the husband and wife architectural team of Andres Duany and Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk (winners of the 2001 Vincent Scully Prize), this movement has caused a readjustment in the way urban planners think of building cities.

## Columbia, Maryland

![Image 10: 1967 black and white photograph of James Rouse and Frazar Wilde at the  plaque unveiling for Wilde, Columbia Association archive.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/5_rouse_and_wilde.png)While Reston was being constructed, another developer across the Potomac, James W. Rouse, was planning the town of Columbia, Maryland approximately halfway between Baltimore, Maryland and Washington D.C. Rouse planned the city as a "garden for people to grow in," designed around clusters of villages that attempted to recreate small-town life. Columbia's founders made a conscious effort to encourage diversity among its citizens.

However, due to the vast start up expenses involved in building these towns and slow home sales, Columbia, like Reston, ended up in the hands of its major investor, Connecticut General Life Insurance Company.

## Seaside, Florida

![Image 11: Aerial view looking down at the colorful residential rooftops of Seaside, Florida.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/8_seaside__fl.png)The city of Seaside, Florida was designed, by Duany and Plater-Zyerbeck and was the first such community to be built using New Urbanist ideas. Other communities across the country such as Kentlands, Maryland and Laguna West, California followed shortly thereafter.

Just as its name implies, Seaside is a resort community. It is a relatively small community (80 acres) which is designed to be completely walkable. Although automobiles are permitted, the emphasis of many of the streets is on pedestrians.

## Celebration, Florida

![Image 12: Aerial view of Celebration, Florida, featuring residential homes and a lake.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/libapps/accounts/53574/images/9_celebration__fl.png)Built in 1994 by the Disney Corporation on the edge of their Walt Disney World property, Celebration Florida is one of the latest "New Urbanist" developments in the United States. Although currently only 3,500 residents live in Celebration, the city is planned for 12,000-15,000 residents. The city is designed, in accordance with "New Urbanist" ideals, with pedestrian friendly streets and walkways and a mixture of commercial and residential space allowing Celeberation's citizens to live and work in the same area.
