Kazakhstan has several planned cities, many of which were founded in recent history as part of the country's shift from its historically [nomadic pastoralism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomadic_Pastoralism_in_Central_Asia "Nomadic Pastoralism in Central Asia") to a more urbanized and industrialized society. This transition began particularly during the Soviet era, as the country developed its infrastructure and urban areas to support industrial growth and modernization.

Some of the most prominent planned cities in Kazakhstan reflect this shift, with their establishment linked to the growth of key industries such as energy, mining, and manufacturing:

*   [Astana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astana "Astana") was originally founded as Akmolinsk and was restructured to become the [planned capital city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_capitals "Planned capitals") of Kazakhstan in 1997. Its modern planning by Japanese architect [Kisho Kurokawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisho_Kurokawa "Kisho Kurokawa") reflects the shift towards urbanization and industrialization, focusing on government institutions, modern infrastructure, and green spaces.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-21)
*   [Turkistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkistan_(city) "Turkistan (city)") has recently started undergoing significant urbanization and development. Historically a center for cultural and religious importance, the city now enjoys special city status, with efforts to preserve its historical appearance through the establishment of a reserve of archaeological monuments, while new infrastructure is being built in a traditional design style.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-23)
*   [Ekibastuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ek%C4%B1bast%C5%ABz "Ekıbastūz") was planned during the Soviet era to support coal mining and energy production, serving as an industrial city built for the region's resource needs.
*   [Zhanaozen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhanaozen "Zhanaozen") was developed as a key hub for Kazakhstan's oil and gas industry, designed to support workers in this vital sector.
*   [Temirtau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temirtau "Temirtau") was a planned industrial city created in the 20th century to support Kazakhstan's steel production industry.
*   [Aktau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aktau "Aktau") was built as a planned center to support the growing oil industry, positioned along the [Caspian Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea "Caspian Sea") as a hub for Kazakhstan's energy sector.
*   [Karaganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karaganda "Karaganda") was initially developed as a mining town, later becoming a planned city with infrastructure to support coal mining and steel production.
*   [Shymkent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shymkent "Shymkent") though it has ancient roots, the modern development of Shymkent reflects Kazakhstan's post-Soviet urbanization, with the city growing around trade, industry, and administrative functions.
*   [Pavlodar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavlodar "Pavlodar") was developed as an industrial hub focused on chemical and energy industries.
*   [Atyrau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atyrau "Atyrau") was transformed from a fishing village into a planned city, primarily due to its proximity to Kazakhstan's key oil and gas reserves.
*   [Kyzylorda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyzylorda "Kyzylorda") was developed in response to the need for irrigation and agriculture in southern Kazakhstan.
*   [Saran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saran,_Kazakhstan "Saran, Kazakhstan") was a small industrial city developed during the Soviet era to support Kazakhstan's steel industry, particularly as a [satellite city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_city "Satellite city") of larger industrial centers like Karaganda.
*   [Aksu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksu_(Pavlodar_Region) "Aksu (Pavlodar Region)") was created as a planned industrial town to support the development of aluminum production.
*   [Kokshetau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kokshetau "Kokshetau") was a small town that evolved into a regional center, planned with a focus on agriculture and light industry.
*   [Baikonur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur "Baikonur") was established as the [Soviet Union's primary space launch facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur_Cosmodrome "Baikonur Cosmodrome") and remains a key planned city in Kazakhstan, designed to support space exploration and technology.

### Mainland China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Mainland China")]

Main articles: [New areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_areas "New areas") and [Special economic zones of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China "Special economic zones of China")

Many ancient [cities in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_China "Cities in China"), especially those on the [North China Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_China_Plain "North China Plain"), were carefully designed according to the [fengshui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feng_shui "Feng shui") theory, featuring square or rectangular city walls, rectilinear road grid, and symmetrical layout. Famous examples are [Chang'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang'an "Chang'an") in [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty") and [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").

An exception to that is an ancient town in [Tekes County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekes_County "Tekes County"), [Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ili_Kazakh_Autonomous_Prefecture "Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture"), Xinjiang, with a shape of a [ba gua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba_gua "Ba gua").

In modern China, many SEZs ([special economic zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China "Special economic zones of China")) are developed from scratch according to extensive planning, for example, [Pudong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pudong "Pudong"), a new district of Shanghai. There are also [new areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_area "New area") that showcase new visions for urban planning, which in some cases are SEZs in their own right. For example, [Xiong'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiong'an "Xiong'an") is a planned city being built in an area of former small towns and farm fields.

President [Elpidio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino "Elpidio Quirino") proclaimed Quezon City as the national capital on 17 July 1948, with President [Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos "Ferdinand Marcos") restoring Manila as the capital on 24 June 1976. He then created a metropolitan area called [Metro Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Manila "Metro Manila"), which remains congested today due to failed execution of the Quezon City plan as well as the Burnham Plan.

### Singapore

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Singapore")]

Main article: [New towns of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_towns_of_Singapore "New towns of Singapore")

The new town planning concept was introduced into Singapore with the building of the first New Town, [Queenstown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queenstown,_Singapore "Queenstown, Singapore"), from July 1952 to 1973 by the country's public housing authority, the [Housing and Development Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_and_Development_Board "Housing and Development Board"). Today, the vast majority of the approximately 11,000 public housing buildings are organised into 22 new towns across the country.

Each new town is designed to be completely self-sustainable. Helmed by a hierarchy of commercial developments, ranging from a town centre to precinct-level outlets, there is no need to venture out of town to meet the most common needs of residences. Employment can be found in industrial estates located within several towns. Educational, health care, and recreational needs are also taken care of with the provision of schools, hospitals, parks, sports complexes, and so on.

Singapore's expertise in successful new town design was internationally recognised when the Building and Social Housing Foundation (BSHF) of the United Nations awarded the [World Habitat Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Habitat_Awards "World Habitat Awards") to [Tampines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampines "Tampines") New Town, which was selected as a representative of Singapore's new towns, on 5 October 1992.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-30)

### Taiwan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Taiwan")]

After losing the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"), the central government of China and its government forces retreated to the former Qing province and later [Japanese colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_under_Japanese_rule "Taiwan under Japanese rule") of the island of Taiwan, which was still a Japanese territory under Allied occupation. As a result, [Nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuomintang "Kuomintang") forces constructed several [military dependents' villages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_dependents'_village "Military dependents' village") that were intended to be temporary housing for party members and their families to regain [Mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") from the [Communists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party"). Many of these neighborhoods became permanent and still exist today.

Beginning in the 1950s, the [Taiwan Provincial Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Provincial_Government "Taiwan Provincial Government") was moved out of [Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei "Taipei") to central Taiwan for security reasons. Several new planned communities were created to house these government employees. The first planned community under the background was [Guangfu New Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangfu_New_Village?action=edit&redlink=1 "Guangfu New Village (page does not exist)"), located in [Wufeng, Taichung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wufeng,_Taichung "Wufeng, Taichung"). After Guangfu New Village, other communities were created as well:[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-31)

*   [Zhongxing New Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhongxing_New_Village "Zhongxing New Village"), the seat of the provincial government, Nantou County
*   [Liming New Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liming_New_Village "Liming New Village"), Taichung City

In the 1970s, several new cities were planned to help alleviate the overpopulation in Taiwan's largest cities, including [Linkou New Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linkou_District#Linkou_New_Town "Linkou District") and [Danhai New Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danhai_New_Town "Danhai New Town") to alleviate Taipei downtown's overpopulation, Dapingding new town to alleviate Kaohsiung downtown.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-32) Most of the new city plans during the time did not succeed due to strong opposition from locals and negative responses from various government departments.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-udn-2010-34)

[Taichung's 7th Redevelopment Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taichung's_7th_Redevelopment_Zone "Taichung's 7th Redevelopment Zone"), which is located in [Taichung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taichung "Taichung"), Taiwan, was a major planned community. Before Taichung's 7th Redevelopment Zone Plan, only a few farmhouses were scattered along a limited number of narrow streets.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-35) Today, this area the new central business district (CBD) of Taichung, away from the city's [Central District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_District,_Taichung "Central District, Taichung").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-36) It features broad and widely spaced boulevards, large apartments complexes, department stores, and office towers. There are many universities nearby, such as [Tunghai University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunghai_University "Tunghai University") and [Feng Chia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feng_Chia_University "Feng Chia University").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-37)

### South Asia

#### Ancient history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Ancient history")]

An urban culture is evident in the mature phase of [Indus Valley civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilization "Indus Valley civilization") which thrived in present-day Pakistan and north western India from around 3300 BC. The quality of municipal city planning suggests knowledge of [urban planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_planning "Urban planning") and efficient municipal governments which placed a high priority on [hygiene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hygiene "Hygiene"). The streets of major cities in present-day Pakistan such as [Mohenjo-daro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro "Mohenjo-daro") and [Harappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harappa "Harappa"), the world's earliest planned cities, were laid out in a perfect [grid pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan "Grid plan") comparable to that of present-day New York City. The houses were protected from noise, odours, and thieves.

As seen in the ancient sites of [Harappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harappa "Harappa") and [Mohenjo-daro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro "Mohenjo-daro") in Pakistan and western border of India, this urban plan included the world's first urban [sanitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation "Sanitation") systems. Within the city, individual homes or groups of homes obtained water from [wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_well "Water well"). From a room that appears to have been set aside for bathing, [waste water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wastewater "Wastewater") was directed to covered drains, which lined the major streets. Houses opened only to inner [courtyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtyard "Courtyard") and smaller lanes.

The ancient Indus systems of [sewage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewage "Sewage") and [drainage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage "Drainage") that were developed and used in cities throughout the Indus Valley were far more advanced than any found in contemporary urban sites in the Middle East and even more efficient than those in some areas of modern South Asia today. The advanced architecture of the [Harappans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation "Indus Valley civilisation") is shown by their [dockyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dockyard "Dockyard"), [granaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granary "Granary"), [warehouses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warehouse "Warehouse"), brick platforms, and protective walls.

### Turkmenistan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Turkmenistan")]

[Arkadag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkadag "Arkadag"), named in honor of Turkmenistan's former President [Gurbanguly Berdymukhamedov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurbanguly_Berdimuhamedow "Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow"), is a new planned [smart city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_city "Smart city") in Turkmenistan. Situated to the southeast of Ashgabat, the city is designed to be a modern and innovative urban hub, reflecting Turkmenistan's aspirations for technological advancement and sustainable development. Arkadag is being developed with a focus on smart technologies, including energy efficiency, modern infrastructure, and eco-friendly solutions, while preserving Turkmen cultural heritage. This city is part of a broader vision to diversify the country's urban landscape and provide an advanced living environment for its residents.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-63)

[Ashgabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashgabat "Ashgabat"), the capital of Turkmenistan, is a city that has been thoughtfully planned, with its foundations laid during the Soviet era. After Turkmenistan gained independence in 1991, the city saw considerable expansion and development. Ashgabat's layout is distinguished by monumental structures, grand government buildings, and wide avenues, many of which are made of marble. The urban development aims to showcase the national pride and Turkmen heritage, combining modern infrastructure with elements of traditional culture.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-64)

[Türkmenbaşy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%BCrkmenba%C5%9Fy,_Turkmenistan "Türkmenbaşy, Turkmenistan"), formerly known as Krasnovodsk, was transformed into a [resort town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resort_town "Resort town") during the Soviet era. Located on the [Caspian Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea "Caspian Sea") coast, the city was developed as an important port and industrial center. In 1993, after Turkmenistan gained independence, the city was renamed Türkmenbaşy in honour of the country's first president, [Saparmurat Niyazov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saparmurat_Niyazov "Saparmurat Niyazov"), who oversaw its further development. The city is known for its modern infrastructure, including wide streets, government buildings, and beach hotels, and serves as a major hub for the country's oil and gas industries.

## Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: Europe")]

### History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: History")]

New settlements were planned in Europe at least since Greek antiquity (see article [History of urban planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_urban_planning "History of urban planning")). The Greeks built new colonial cities around the Mediterranean. The ancient Romans also founded many new colonial towns through their empire. There are, however, also traces of planned settlements of non-Roman origin in pre-historic northern Europe. Most planned settlements of medieval Europe were created in the period of about the 12th to 14th centuries. All kinds of landlords, from the highest to the lowest rank, tried to found new villages and towns on their estates, to gain economic, political or military power. The settlers generally were attracted by fiscal, economic and juridical advantages granted by the founding lord, or were forced to move from elsewhere from his estates. Most of the new towns were to remain rather small (as for instance the [bastides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastide "Bastide") of southwestern France), but some of them became important cities, such as [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff"), [Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds "Leeds"), ['s-Hertogenbosch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'s-Hertogenbosch "'s-Hertogenbosch"), [Montauban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montauban "Montauban"), [Bilbao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilbao "Bilbao"), [Malmö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malm%C3%B6 "Malmö"), [Lübeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCbeck "Lübeck"), [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"), [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), [Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bern "Bern"), [Klagenfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klagenfurt "Klagenfurt"), [Alessandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandria "Alessandria"), [Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw "Warsaw") and [Sarajevo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-65)

#### Roman Empire

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: Roman Empire")]

The [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") built a large number of towns throughout their empire, often as colonies for the settlement of citizens or veterans. These were generally characterised by a grid of streets and a planned water-supply; and many modern European towns of originally Roman foundation still retain part of the original street-grid.

### Belgium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=43 "Edit section: Belgium")]

As many Roman army camps, the settlement of _Atuatuca Tungrorum_, on the site of the modern town of [Tongeren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongeren "Tongeren"), grew into an important regional centre, laid out along a [grid plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan "Grid plan") and supplied with water by an [aqueduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqueduct_(water_supply) "Aqueduct (water supply)"). While Tongeren's administrative and military functions were moved to Maastricht in the wake of [Germanic invasions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_Period "Migration Period") in the 350s, given the latter's better strategic position, remains of the Roman town are visible up to this day.

Named after king [Charles II of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Spain "Charles II of Spain"), the town of [Charleroi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleroi "Charleroi") (or _Caroloregium_, in Latin) was founded in 1666 as a stronghold near the French border, to fend off potential invasions. A few years before, in 1659, the border between [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and the [Spanish Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Netherlands "Spanish Netherlands") had shifted northward due to the [Treaty of the Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_the_Pyrenees "Treaty of the Pyrenees"). This shift, and the consequent loss of fortified border towns such as [Cambrai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrai "Cambrai") and [Avesnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avesnes "Avesnes") had sparked the need to found new forts to defend the border. The original fortifications were destroyed between 1867 and 1871, making place for a quickly expanding industrial centre.

A **planned community**, **planned city**, **planned town**, or **planned settlement** is any community that was carefully planned from its inception and is typically constructed on previously undeveloped land. This contrasts with settlements that evolve organically.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-2)

The term _new town_ refers to planned communities of the [new towns movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_towns_movement "New towns movement") in particular, [mainly in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_towns_in_the_United_Kingdom "New towns in the United Kingdom"). It was also common during the [European colonization of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_colonization_of_the_Americas "European colonization of the Americas") to build according to a plan either on fresh ground or on the ruins of earlier [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") villages.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-3)

A **model city** is a type of planned city designed to a high standard and intended as a [model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model "Model") for others to imitate. The term was first used in 1854.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-4)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Butterfly_Estate_1.jpg/250px-Butterfly_Estate_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Butterfly_Estate_1.jpg)

The terrains of Hong Kong are mostly mountainous and many places in the [New Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Territories "New Territories") have limited access to roads. Hong Kong started developing new towns in the 1950s, to accommodate rapidly growing populations. In the early days the term "satellite towns" was used. The very first new towns included [Tsuen Wan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsuen_Wan_New_Town "Tsuen Wan New Town") and [Kwun Tong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwun_Tong "Kwun Tong"). [Wah Fu Estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wah_Fu_Estate "Wah Fu Estate") was built in a remote corner on [Hong Kong Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Island "Hong Kong Island"), with similar concepts in a smaller scale.

In the late 1960s and the 1970s, another stage of new town developments was launched. Nine new towns have been developed to date. Land use is carefully planned and development provides plenty of room for public housing projects. Rail transport is usually available at a later stage. The first towns are [Sha Tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sha_Tin_New_Town "Sha Tin New Town"), [Tsuen Wan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsuen_Wan_New_Town "Tsuen Wan New Town"), [Tuen Mun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuen_Mun_New_Town "Tuen Mun New Town") and [Tseung Kwan O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tseung_Kwan_O_New_Town "Tseung Kwan O New Town"). [Tuen Mun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuen_Mun_New_Town "Tuen Mun New Town") was intended to be self-reliant, but was not successful at the beginning and maintained as a [dormitory town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dormitory_town "Dormitory town") up until the recent decades like the other new towns. More recent developments are [Tin Shui Wai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin_Shui_Wai_New_Town "Tin Shui Wai New Town") and [North Lantau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Lantau_New_Town "North Lantau New Town"). The government also plans to build such towns in [Hung Shui Kiu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hung_Shui_Kiu "Hung Shui Kiu"), [Ping Che](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ping_Che "Ping Che")-[Ta Kwu Ling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Kwu_Ling "Ta Kwu Ling"), [Fanling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanling "Fanling") North and [Kwu Tung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwu_Tung "Kwu Tung") North. [Bandung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandung "Bandung") laid as a well-planned city, set as the new capital of the Dutch East Indies back in the 1920s.

*   [Jakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta "Jakarta")
    *   [Batavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batavia,_Dutch_East_Indies "Batavia, Dutch East Indies") (predecessor of modern [Jakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta "Jakarta")) was a planned city, modeled after Dutch 17th century coastal city architecture. First, in the 17th century as a planned fortified city, crisscrossed with Dutch-style canals dug in regular grid. The city served as the administrative center of [Dutch East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company").
    *   In the early 19th century, the Dutch colonial authority moved their administrative center from the dilapidated and unhealthy port town of Old Batavia (now [Kota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kota_Tua_Jakarta "Kota Tua Jakarta") area) several kilometres south to [Weltevreden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltevreden,_Java "Weltevreden, Java") area (now [Central Jakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Jakarta "Central Jakarta")). Old Batavia and Weltevreden were connected by the Molenvliet Canal and a road (now Gajah Mada Road) that ran alongside the waterway.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-Heritage6-109-15) It was a well-planned community around the [Koningsplein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medan_Merdeka "Medan Merdeka"), the [Waterlooplein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapangan_Banteng "Lapangan Banteng") and Rijswijk (Jalan Veteran). The area, then known as Weltevreden, which include the Koningsplein, Rijswijk, Noordwijk, Tanah Abang, Kebon Sirih, and Prapatan became a popular residential, entertainment and commercial district for the European colonial elite.
    *   [Menteng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menteng "Menteng"), today a sub-district in Central Jakarta, was first built as a well-planned community. An [urban design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_design "Urban design") developed in the 1910s set the area to become a residential area for Dutch people and high officials. At the time of its development, the area was the first planned [garden suburb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_suburb "Garden suburb") in colonial [Batavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batavia_(Dutch_East_Indies) "Batavia (Dutch East Indies)"). Supported by easy access to service centers and nearby to the central business district, this area has become one of the most expensive areas for residential real estate in modern Jakarta.

*   In the early 20th century, [Bandung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandung "Bandung") was planned by the [Dutch East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_Indies "Dutch East Indies") government as a new capital city to replace Batavia. The idea was to separate the busy trading port or the commercial center (Batavia) from the new administrative and political center (Bandung). By the 1920s the plan to transfer the capital to Bandung was underway. As the city began to laid the master plan of a well-planned new city, grid of streets and avenues were laid, and numbers of government buildings were constructed, such as [Gedung Sate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gedung_Sate "Gedung Sate") that was planned as the colonial administrative center of Dutch East Indies. The plan, however, failed due to the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") and the outbreak of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-Fanara-16)
*   Since [Palangkaraya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palangkaraya "Palangkaraya") was established as the capital of [Central Kalimantan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Kalimantan "Central Kalimantan") province in 1957, the first president of Indonesia, [Sukarno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukarno "Sukarno"), outlined a plan to develop Palangkaraya as the future capital of Indonesia. Palangkaraya is far larger in area than [Jakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta "Jakarta") and safe from the danger of earthquakes and [volcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcano "Volcano"), common on the island of [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java "Java").
*   In the late 1950s to the first half of the 1960s, [Sukarno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukarno "Sukarno"), Indonesia's first president, laid a master plan to build [Jakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta "Jakarta") as the planned national capital of the Republic of Indonesia. He filled Jakarta with numbers of monuments and statues. Numbers of monumental projects were conceived, planned and initiated during his administration, including [Monumen Nasional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Monument_(Indonesia) "National Monument (Indonesia)"), [Istiqlal mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istiqlal_Mosque,_Jakarta "Istiqlal Mosque, Jakarta"), [DPR/MPR Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DPR/MPR_Building "DPR/MPR Building"), and [Gelora Bung Karno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelora_Bung_Karno_Stadium "Gelora Bung Karno Stadium") stadium. Sukarno also filled Jakarta with nationalistic monuments and statues, including [Selamat Datang Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selamat_Datang_Monument "Selamat Datang Monument"), Pemuda Monument at Senayan, Dirgantara Monument at Pancoran, and Irian Jaya Liberation Monument at [Lapangan Banteng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapangan_Banteng "Lapangan Banteng"). Although many of this projects were completed later in his successor era ([Suharto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suharto "Suharto") administration), Sukarno is credited for shaping Jakarta's monuments and landmarks. He desired Jakarta to be the beacon of a powerful new nation.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-Megacity-Jakarta-17)
*   Because of Jakarta's environmental degradation and [overpopulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overpopulation_(biology) "Overpopulation (biology)") problems, there has been an idea to build a new proposed capital city to replace Jakarta.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-Inilah1-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-Oke1-19) In 2019, President [Joko Widodo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joko_Widodo "Joko Widodo") announced that Indonesia [will move its capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_of_Indonesia#Move_to_Nusantara "Capital of Indonesia") from Jakarta to the new planned city in the [East Kalimantan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Kalimantan "East Kalimantan") province which will be built in between the regencies of [Penajam North Paser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penajam_North_Paser "Penajam North Paser") and [Kutai Kartanegara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutai_Kartanegara "Kutai Kartanegara"). Its construction will commence in 2020.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-20) The new national capital will be called [Nusantara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nusantara_(planned_city) "Nusantara (planned city)") and it is set to be inaugurated in 2024 with the groundbreaking ceremony in March 2022. The capital is expected to form a new province separated from East Kalimantan, similar to Jakarta.

In modern-day Iran more than 20 planned cities have been developed or are under construction, mostly around Iran's main metropolitan areas such as [Tehran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehran "Tehran"), [Isfahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isfahan_(city) "Isfahan (city)"), [Shiraz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiraz "Shiraz") and [Tabriz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabriz "Tabriz"). Some of these new cities are built for special purposes such as:

*   [Poulad-Shahr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poulad-Shahr "Poulad-Shahr"), which is an industrial city built for the housing of Isfahan's steel industry workers.
*   [Shirin Shahr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirin_Shahr "Shirin Shahr") which is to provide housing for the sugar industry personnel.
*   [Tehranpars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehranpars "Tehranpars") which was built to house Tehran's additional population.
*   [Shahrak-e Gharb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shahrak-e_Gharb "Shahrak-e Gharb"), built as a massive project of modern apartment buildings.
*   [Parand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parand "Parand") which is intended to provide residences for the staff of [Imam Khomeini International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imam_Khomeini_International_Airport "Imam Khomeini International Airport").
*   [Shushtar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shushtar "Shushtar") New Town which was built to provide housing for the employees of a sugar cane processing plant.

576,000 people were planned to be settled in Iran's new towns by 2005.

[Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto "Kyoto") was built on a grid system, starting in 794.

The city of [Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto "Kyoto") was developed as a planned city in 794 as a new imperial capital (then called [Heian-kyō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heian-ky%C5%8D "Heian-kyō")), built on a grid layout and remained the capital for over a millennium. The grid layout remains, reflected in major east–west streets being numbered, such as 4th street (四条, _shi-jō_). In modern times, [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapporo "Sapporo") was built from 1868, following an American [grid plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan "Grid plan"), and is today the fifth-largest city in Japan. Both these cities have regular addressing systems (following the grid) unlike the usual subdivision-based [Japanese addressing system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_addressing_system "Japanese addressing system").

Borrowing from the New Town movement in the United Kingdom, some 30 new towns have been built all over Japan. Most of these constructions were initiated during the period of rapid economic growth in the 1960s, but construction continued into the 1980s. Most of them are located near Tokyo and the big cities in [Kansai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansai "Kansai") region. Some towns, ([Senri New Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senri_New_Town?action=edit&redlink=1 "Senri New Town (page does not exist)")[[jp](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%8D%83%E9%87%8C%E3%83%8B%E3%83%A5%E3%83%BC%E3%82%BF%E3%82%A6%E3%83%B3 "jp:千里ニュータウン")], [Tama New Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tama_New_Town "Tama New Town")) do not provide much employment, and many of the residents commute to the nearby cities. These towns fostered the infamous congestion of commuter trains (although as the metropolitan areas have grown, this commute has become relatively short in comparison to commutes from the new urban fringe).

Other New Towns act as industrial/academic agglomerations (_sangyo-shuseki_) ([Tsukuba Science City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsukuba,_Ibaraki "Tsukuba, Ibaraki"), Kashima Port Town). These areas attempt to create an all-inclusive environment for daily living, in accordance with [Uzō Nishiyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uz%C5%8D_Nishiyama "Uzō Nishiyama")'s "life-spheres" principle.

Japan has also developed the concept of new towns to what [Manuel Castells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Castells "Manuel Castells") and [Sir Peter Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Hall_(urbanist) "Peter Hall (urbanist)") call [technopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_park "Science park"). The technopolis program of the 1980s has precedents in the New Industrial Cities Act of the 1960s. These cities are largely modeled after Tsukuba Academic New Town (Tsukuba Science City) in that they attempt to agglomerate high-tech resources together in a campus-like environment.

In the past, the Japanese government had proposed relocating the capital to a planned city, but this plan was cancelled.

Overall, Japan's New Town program consists of many diverse projects, most of which focus on a primary function, but also aspire to create an all-inclusive urban environment. Japan's New Town program is heavily informed by the Anglo-American [Garden City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_city_movement "Garden city movement") tradition, American neighborhood design, as well as Soviet strategies of industrial development.

In 2002 Prime Minister [Junichiro Koizumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junichiro_Koizumi "Junichiro Koizumi") announced the end of new town construction, although the new towns continue to receive government funding and redevelopment.

Kazakhstan has several planned cities, many of which were founded in recent history as part of the country's shift from its historically [nomadic pastoralism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomadic_Pastoralism_in_Central_Asia "Nomadic Pastoralism in Central Asia") to a more urbanized and industrialized society. This transition began particularly during the Soviet era, as the country developed its infrastructure and urban areas to support industrial growth and modernization.

Some of the most prominent planned cities in Kazakhstan reflect this shift, with their establishment linked to the growth of key industries such as energy, mining, and manufacturing:

*   [Astana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astana "Astana") was originally founded as Akmolinsk and was restructured to become the [planned capital city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_capitals "Planned capitals") of Kazakhstan in 1997. Its modern planning by Japanese architect [Kisho Kurokawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisho_Kurokawa "Kisho Kurokawa") reflects the shift towards urbanization and industrialization, focusing on government institutions, modern infrastructure, and green spaces.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-21)
*   [Turkistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkistan_(city) "Turkistan (city)") has recently started undergoing significant urbanization and development. Historically a center for cultural and religious importance, the city now enjoys special city status, with efforts to preserve its historical appearance through the establishment of a reserve of archaeological monuments, while new infrastructure is being built in a traditional design style.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-23)
*   [Ekibastuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ek%C4%B1bast%C5%ABz "Ekıbastūz") was planned during the Soviet era to support coal mining and energy production, serving as an industrial city built for the region's resource needs.
*   [Zhanaozen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhanaozen "Zhanaozen") was developed as a key hub for Kazakhstan's oil and gas industry, designed to support workers in this vital sector.
*   [Temirtau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temirtau "Temirtau") was a planned industrial city created in the 20th century to support Kazakhstan's steel production industry.
*   [Aktau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aktau "Aktau") was built as a planned center to support the growing oil industry, positioned along the [Caspian Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea "Caspian Sea") as a hub for Kazakhstan's energy sector.
*   [Karaganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karaganda "Karaganda") was initially developed as a mining town, later becoming a planned city with infrastructure to support coal mining and steel production.
*   [Shymkent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shymkent "Shymkent") though it has ancient roots, the modern development of Shymkent reflects Kazakhstan's post-Soviet urbanization, with the city growing around trade, industry, and administrative functions.
*   [Pavlodar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavlodar "Pavlodar") was developed as an industrial hub focused on chemical and energy industries.
*   [Atyrau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atyrau "Atyrau") was transformed from a fishing village into a planned city, primarily due to its proximity to Kazakhstan's key oil and gas reserves.
*   [Kyzylorda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyzylorda "Kyzylorda") was developed in response to the need for irrigation and agriculture in southern Kazakhstan.
*   [Saran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saran,_Kazakhstan "Saran, Kazakhstan") was a small industrial city developed during the Soviet era to support Kazakhstan's steel industry, particularly as a [satellite city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_city "Satellite city") of larger industrial centers like Karaganda.

### Mainland China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Mainland China")]

Main articles: [New areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_areas "New areas") and [Special economic zones of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China "Special economic zones of China")

Many ancient [cities in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_China "Cities in China"), especially those on the [North China Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_China_Plain "North China Plain"), were carefully designed according to the [fengshui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feng_shui "Feng shui") theory, featuring square or rectangular city walls, rectilinear road grid, and symmetrical layout. Famous examples are [Chang'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang'an "Chang'an") in [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty") and [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").

An exception to that is an ancient town in [Tekes County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekes_County "Tekes County"), [Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ili_Kazakh_Autonomous_Prefecture "Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture"), Xinjiang, with a shape of a [ba gua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba_gua "Ba gua").

In modern China, many SEZs ([special economic zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China "Special economic zones of China")) are developed from scratch according to extensive planning, for example, [Pudong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pudong "Pudong"), a new district of Shanghai. There are also [new areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_area "New area") that showcase new visions for urban planning, which in some cases are SEZs in their own right. For example, [Xiong'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiong'an "Xiong'an") is a planned city being built in an area of former small towns and farm fields.

### Singapore

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Singapore")]

Main article: [New towns of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_towns_of_Singapore "New towns of Singapore")

The new town planning concept was introduced into Singapore with the building of the first New Town, [Queenstown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queenstown,_Singapore "Queenstown, Singapore"), from July 1952 to 1973 by the country's public housing authority, the [Housing and Development Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_and_Development_Board "Housing and Development Board"). Today, the vast majority of the approximately 11,000 public housing buildings are organised into 22 new towns across the country.

Each new town is designed to be completely self-sustainable. Helmed by a hierarchy of commercial developments, ranging from a town centre to precinct-level outlets, there is no need to venture out of town to meet the most common needs of residences. Employment can be found in industrial estates located within several towns. Educational, health care, and recreational needs are also taken care of with the provision of schools, hospitals, parks, sports complexes, and so on.

Singapore's expertise in successful new town design was internationally recognised when the Building and Social Housing Foundation (BSHF) of the United Nations awarded the [World Habitat Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Habitat_Awards "World Habitat Awards") to [Tampines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampines "Tampines") New Town, which was selected as a representative of Singapore's new towns, on 5 October 1992.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-30)

Beginning in the 1950s, the [Taiwan Provincial Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Provincial_Government "Taiwan Provincial Government") was moved out of [Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei "Taipei") to central Taiwan for security reasons. ### South Asia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: South Asia")]

#### Ancient history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Ancient history")]

An urban culture is evident in the mature phase of [Indus Valley civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilization "Indus Valley civilization") which thrived in present-day Pakistan and north western India from around 3300 BC. The quality of municipal city planning suggests knowledge of [urban planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_planning "Urban planning") and efficient municipal governments which placed a high priority on [hygiene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hygiene "Hygiene"). The streets of major cities in present-day Pakistan such as [Mohenjo-daro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro "Mohenjo-daro") and [Harappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harappa "Harappa"), the world's earliest planned cities, were laid out in a perfect [grid pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan "Grid plan") comparable to that of present-day New York City. The houses were protected from noise, odours, and thieves.

As seen in the ancient sites of [Harappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harappa "Harappa") and [Mohenjo-daro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro "Mohenjo-daro") in Pakistan and western border of India, this urban plan included the world's first urban [sanitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation "Sanitation") systems. Within the city, individual homes or groups of homes obtained water from [wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_well "Water well"). From a room that appears to have been set aside for bathing, [waste water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wastewater "Wastewater") was directed to covered drains, which lined the major streets. Houses opened only to inner [courtyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtyard "Courtyard") and smaller lanes.

The ancient Indus systems of [sewage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewage "Sewage") and [drainage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage "Drainage") that were developed and used in cities throughout the Indus Valley were far more advanced than any found in contemporary urban sites in the Middle East and even more efficient than those in some areas of modern South Asia today. The advanced architecture of the [Harappans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation "Indus Valley civilisation") is shown by their [dockyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dockyard "Dockyard"), [granaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granary "Granary"), [warehouses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warehouse "Warehouse"), brick platforms, and protective walls.

#### Medieval history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Medieval history")]

A number of medieval Indian cities were planned including:

*   [Ahmedabad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmedabad "Ahmedabad") in Gujarat. Established by Sultan Ahmad Shah in 1411.
*   [Jaipur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur "Jaipur") in Rajasthan. Established in 1727 by Maharaja Sawai [Jai Singh II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jai_Singh_II "Jai Singh II").It is the capital of [Rajasthan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajasthan "Rajasthan") state of India.
*   [Udaipur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udaipur "Udaipur") in Rajasthan. It was the historic capital of the former kingdom of [Mewar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mewar "Mewar").

### Turkmenistan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Turkmenistan")]

[Arkadag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkadag "Arkadag"), named in honor of Turkmenistan's former President [Gurbanguly Berdymukhamedov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurbanguly_Berdimuhamedow "Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow"), is a new planned [smart city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_city "Smart city") in Turkmenistan. Situated to the southeast of Ashgabat, the city is designed to be a modern and innovative urban hub, reflecting Turkmenistan's aspirations for technological advancement and sustainable development. Arkadag is being developed with a focus on smart technologies, including energy efficiency, modern infrastructure, and eco-friendly solutions, while preserving Turkmen cultural heritage. This city is part of a broader vision to diversify the country's urban landscape and provide an advanced living environment for its residents.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-63)

[Ashgabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashgabat "Ashgabat"), the capital of Turkmenistan, is a city that has been thoughtfully planned, with its foundations laid during the Soviet era. After Turkmenistan gained independence in 1991, the city saw considerable expansion and development. Ashgabat's layout is distinguished by monumental structures, grand government buildings, and wide avenues, many of which are made of marble. The urban development aims to showcase the national pride and Turkmen heritage, combining modern infrastructure with elements of traditional culture.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-64)

[Türkmenbaşy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%BCrkmenba%C5%9Fy,_Turkmenistan "Türkmenbaşy, Turkmenistan"), formerly known as Krasnovodsk, was transformed into a [resort town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resort_town "Resort town") during the Soviet era. Located on the [Caspian Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea "Caspian Sea") coast, the city was developed as an important port and industrial center. In 1993, after Turkmenistan gained independence, the city was renamed Türkmenbaşy in honour of the country's first president, [Saparmurat Niyazov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saparmurat_Niyazov "Saparmurat Niyazov"), who oversaw its further development. The city is known for its modern infrastructure, including wide streets, government buildings, and beach hotels, and serves as a major hub for the country's oil and gas industries.

## Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: Europe")]

### History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: History")]

New settlements were planned in Europe at least since Greek antiquity (see article [History of urban planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_urban_planning "History of urban planning")). The Greeks built new colonial cities around the Mediterranean. The ancient Romans also founded many new colonial towns through their empire. There are, however, also traces of planned settlements of non-Roman origin in pre-historic northern Europe. Most planned settlements of medieval Europe were created in the period of about the 12th to 14th centuries. All kinds of landlords, from the highest to the lowest rank, tried to found new villages and towns on their estates, to gain economic, political or military power. The settlers generally were attracted by fiscal, economic and juridical advantages granted by the founding lord, or were forced to move from elsewhere from his estates. Most of the new towns were to remain rather small (as for instance the [bastides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastide "Bastide") of southwestern France), but some of them became important cities, such as [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff"), [Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds "Leeds"), ['s-Hertogenbosch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'s-Hertogenbosch "'s-Hertogenbosch"), [Montauban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montauban "Montauban"), [Bilbao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilbao "Bilbao"), [Malmö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malm%C3%B6 "Malmö"), [Lübeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCbeck "Lübeck"), [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"), [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), [Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bern "Bern"), [Klagenfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klagenfurt "Klagenfurt"), [Alessandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandria "Alessandria"), [Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw "Warsaw") and [Sarajevo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-65)

#### Roman Empire

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: Roman Empire")]

The [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") built a large number of towns throughout their empire, often as colonies for the settlement of citizens or veterans. These were generally characterised by a grid of streets and a planned water-supply; and many modern European towns of originally Roman foundation still retain part of the original street-grid.

### Albania

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=41 "Edit section: Albania")]

During the communist period under Enver Hoxha, many towns and industrial centers were planned and built from scratch. The government aimed to distribute population and industry evenly across the country.

Some notable examples:

*   [Laç](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La%C3%A7 "Laç"), built in the 1960s as an industrial town focused on chemical and construction materials production.
*   [Ballsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballsh "Ballsh"), developed around its oil refinery; designed as a compact socialist industrial city.
*   [Patos (municipality)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patos_(municipality) "Patos (municipality)"), expanded in a planned manner around oil extraction sites.
*   [Rrëshen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rr%C3%ABshen "Rrëshen"), created as the administrative center of Mirditë District; planned in the 1950s–1960s.
*   [Pogradec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pogradec "Pogradec") (partially), had elements of socialist urban planning (wide boulevards, public housing, industrial zones).

### Belgium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=43 "Edit section: Belgium")]

As many Roman army camps, the settlement of _Atuatuca Tungrorum_, on the site of the modern town of [Tongeren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongeren "Tongeren"), grew into an important regional centre, laid out along a [grid plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan "Grid plan") and supplied with water by an [aqueduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqueduct_(water_supply) "Aqueduct (water supply)"). While Tongeren's administrative and military functions were moved to Maastricht in the wake of [Germanic invasions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_Period "Migration Period") in the 350s, given the latter's better strategic position, remains of the Roman town are visible up to this day.

Named after king [Charles II of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Spain "Charles II of Spain"), the town of [Charleroi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleroi "Charleroi") (or _Caroloregium_, in Latin) was founded in 1666 as a stronghold near the French border, to fend off potential invasions. A few years before, in 1659, the border between [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and the [Spanish Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Netherlands "Spanish Netherlands") had shifted northward due to the [Treaty of the Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_the_Pyrenees "Treaty of the Pyrenees"). This shift, and the consequent loss of fortified border towns such as [Cambrai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrai "Cambrai") and [Avesnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avesnes "Avesnes") had sparked the need to found new forts to defend the border. The original fortifications were destroyed between 1867 and 1871, making place for a quickly expanding industrial centre.

In 1923, the city of [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp") annexed the sparsely populated, marshy lands known as Vlaams Hoofd, with the intention of using the area for urban development. Over the following decades, the terrain was elevated and a new urban community, now called [Linkeroever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linkeroever "Linkeroever") (literally 'Left Bank'), was created. Notably, [Le Corbusier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Corbusier "Le Corbusier") submitted a plan along the lines of his _Cité radieuse_[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-VRT-Linkeroever-66) but neither his plan nor those of his colleagues were accepted. Instead, Linkeroever was developed gradually over the 20th and 21st centuries, inspired by a mix of [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_architecture "Modern architecture") and later ideas.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_community#cite_note-67)

When the [Catholic University of Leuven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_University_of_Leuven_(1834%E2%80%931968) "Catholic University of Leuven (1834–1968)") was split along linguistic lines in 1968, it was decided to move its French-speaking division, the [Université catholique de Louvain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_catholique_de_Louvain "Université catholique de Louvain"), from [Leuven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leuven "Leuven") (in the [Flemish Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_Region "Flemish Region")) to a new location, some 30 kilometers south, in the [Walloon Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walloon_Region "Walloon Region"). Construction on the town of [Louvain-la-Neuve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvain-la-Neuve "Louvain-la-Neuve") (literally 'New Louvain') began in the 1970s, in what had previously been the mostly empty countryside near the village of [Ottignies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottignies "Ottignies"). Its city centre is supported by a concrete structure, allowing car traffic to pass underneath and making the city centre a pedestrian zone.

### Croatia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Planned_community&action=edit&section=46 "Edit section: Croatia")]

[Červar-Porat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%8Cervar-Porat "Červar-Porat") is a [resort town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resort_town "Resort town") in western Croatia, located on the east coast of the [Adriatic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") on the Červar lagoon. **Robert Edward Simon Jr.** (April 10, 1914 – September 21, 2015) was an American real estate entrepreneur, most known for founding the community of [Reston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-NYT-obit-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Morello_2004-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-RestonBriefHistory-3) He was the maternal uncle of feminist historian and writer [Elizabeth Fox-Genovese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Fox-Genovese "Elizabeth Fox-Genovese").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-4)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_E._Simon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Simon was born in New York City in 1914,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-HJR_2009-5) the son of Robert Sr. and Elsa Weil Simon,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Marks-6) immigrants from [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-7) He was raised in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") along with his four siblings.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Marks-6) He was [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jews "American Jews").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Jackman-8)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_E._Simon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Reston

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_E._Simon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Reston")]

Further information: [Reston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia")

After graduating from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), Simon took over the family [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate") management and development business. In 1961, with the proceeds from the sale of a family property, [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"), Simon purchased 6,750 acres (27 km 2) of land in [Fairfax County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") and hired Conklin + [Rossant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Rossant "James Rossant")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-9) to develop a master plan for the new town of [Reston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia"), a planned community well known on the national level. (The town's name was derived from Simon's initials and the word "town".)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-RestonBriefHistory-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-McKeon_1999-10) Simon's [new town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_town "New town") concept emphasized quality of life for the individual and provided a community where people could live, work, and play without driving long distances.

Simon returned to live in an apartment near [Lake Anne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Anne "Lake Anne") in Reston in 1993[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-McKeon_1999-10) and helped celebrate Reston's 40th birthday in 2004.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-MyersPR_2009-11) In that same year a [bronze statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_sculpture "Bronze sculpture") of Simon was placed on a park bench in Washington Plaza on Lake Anne, the original heart of the community he built.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-RestonBriefHistory-3)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-MyersPR_2009-11)

A collection of Simon's donated materials is housed at the Special Collections Research Center at the [George Mason University Libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mason_University_Libraries "George Mason University Libraries").

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_E._Simon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Simon married four times.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Marks-6) He was married to author and environmentalist [Anne Wertheim Langman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_W._Simon "Anne W. Simon"), daughter of [Maurice Wertheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Wertheim "Maurice Wertheim"), and granddaughter of [Henry Morgenthau Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Morgenthau_Sr. "Henry Morgenthau Sr.")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-12)

He died in [Reston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia") in September 2015 at the age of 101.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-13) He was survived by his fourth wife (married 2004), Cheryl Terio-Simon; a daughter, Margo Prescott-Morris her 2 children (Robert's grandchildren) Christine Doolin, Noah Prescott along with great-grandchildren Sara Collier, Austin Ingram, Ashton Prescott and 8 great-great grandchildren. Also his six stepchildren, Karen Terio, Betsy Langman Schulberg (married and divorced from [Budd Schulberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Schulberg "Budd Schulberg")), Deborah Langman Lesser, Lucinda Zilk, Tom Langman, and Adam Terio.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Marks-6)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-15)

**Robert Edward Simon Jr.** (April 10, 1914 – September 21, 2015) was an American real estate entrepreneur, most known for founding the community of [Reston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-NYT-obit-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Morello_2004-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-RestonBriefHistory-3) He was the maternal uncle of feminist historian and writer [Elizabeth Fox-Genovese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Fox-Genovese "Elizabeth Fox-Genovese").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-4)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_E._Simon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Simon was born in New York City in 1914,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-HJR_2009-5) the son of Robert Sr. and Elsa Weil Simon,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Marks-6) immigrants from [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-7) He was raised in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") along with his four siblings.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Marks-6) He was [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jews "American Jews").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Jackman-8)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_E._Simon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Reston

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_E._Simon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Reston")]

Further information: [Reston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia")

After graduating from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), Simon took over the family [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate") management and development business. In 1961, with the proceeds from the sale of a family property, [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"), Simon purchased 6,750 acres (27 km 2) of land in [Fairfax County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") and hired Conklin + [Rossant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Rossant "James Rossant")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-9) to develop a master plan for the new town of [Reston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia"), a planned community well known on the national level. (The town's name was derived from Simon's initials and the word "town".)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-RestonBriefHistory-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-McKeon_1999-10) Simon's [new town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_town "New town") concept emphasized quality of life for the individual and provided a community where people could live, work, and play without driving long distances.

Simon returned to live in an apartment near [Lake Anne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Anne "Lake Anne") in Reston in 1993[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-McKeon_1999-10) and helped celebrate Reston's 40th birthday in 2004.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-MyersPR_2009-11) In that same year a [bronze statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_sculpture "Bronze sculpture") of Simon was placed on a park bench in Washington Plaza on Lake Anne, the original heart of the community he built.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-RestonBriefHistory-3)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-MyersPR_2009-11)

A collection of Simon's donated materials is housed at the Special Collections Research Center at the [George Mason University Libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mason_University_Libraries "George Mason University Libraries").

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_E._Simon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Simon married four times.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Marks-6) He was married to author and environmentalist [Anne Wertheim Langman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_W._Simon "Anne W. Simon"), daughter of [Maurice Wertheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Wertheim "Maurice Wertheim"), and granddaughter of [Henry Morgenthau Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Morgenthau_Sr. "Henry Morgenthau Sr.")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-12)

He died in [Reston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia") in September 2015 at the age of 101.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-13) He was survived by his fourth wife (married 2004), Cheryl Terio-Simon; a daughter, Margo Prescott-Morris her 2 children (Robert's grandchildren) Christine Doolin, Noah Prescott along with great-grandchildren Sara Collier, Austin Ingram, Ashton Prescott and 8 great-great grandchildren. Also his six stepchildren, Karen Terio, Betsy Langman Schulberg (married and divorced from [Budd Schulberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Schulberg "Budd Schulberg")), Deborah Langman Lesser, Lucinda Zilk, Tom Langman, and Adam Terio.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-Marks-6)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Simon#cite_note-15)

### About Us

Simon Center is designed to meet the emotional, social, physical and intellectual needs of children in a safe, child-oriented daycare environment.

[Learn more](https://simoncenter.org/about-us/)

### Our Center

We offer an active, in-person, full-day, comprehensive and all-inclusive program where children are respected, loved and accepted.

[Learn more](https://simoncenter.org/program/)

### Our Community

Simon Center organizes a number of events to build a strong feeling of connection and friendship among our families within the community.

[Learn more](https://simoncenter.org/about-us/community/)

![Image 8](https://simoncenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/LeilaK-Photo.png)

## Consistency You Can Trust

Your child deserves familiar faces, lasting relationships, and a team that truly knows them.

#### Experienced, Long-Tenured Teachers

Our teachers don’t just stop by — they build careers here. Many members of our team have been with us for years, bringing experience, confidence, and deep understanding to every classroom.

#### Stability That Supports Your Child

Children thrive when they see the same caring adults each day. We prioritize continuity so your child can form strong bonds and feel secure in a familiar environment.

#### A Team That Chooses to Stay

Low staff turnover reflects a positive, supportive workplace. When teachers feel valued and fulfilled, that care naturally extends to the children and families they serve.

### About Us

Simon Center is designed to meet the emotional, social, physical and intellectual needs of children in a safe, child-oriented daycare environment.

[Learn more](https://simoncenter.org/about-us/)

### Our Center

We offer an active, in-person, full-day, comprehensive and all-inclusive program where children are respected, loved and accepted.

[Learn more](https://simoncenter.org/program/)

### Our Community

Simon Center organizes a number of events to build a strong feeling of connection and friendship among our families within the community.

[Learn more](https://simoncenter.org/about-us/community/)

![Image 8](https://simoncenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/LeilaK-Photo.png)

## Consistency You Can Trust

Your child deserves familiar faces, lasting relationships, and a team that truly knows them.

#### Experienced, Long-Tenured Teachers

Our teachers don’t just stop by — they build careers here. Many members of our team have been with us for years, bringing experience, confidence, and deep understanding to every classroom.

#### Stability That Supports Your Child

Children thrive when they see the same caring adults each day. We prioritize continuity so your child can form strong bonds and feel secure in a familiar environment.

#### A Team That Chooses to Stay

Low staff turnover reflects a positive, supportive workplace. When teachers feel valued and fulfilled, that care naturally extends to the children and families they serve.

> You have all been so wonderful to our family over the last 6 years. We have been so humbled and impressed by the teachers who all exhibit patience and love towards our children as if they are their own. We are sad to see this part of our story end, but we are excited for what’s to come. Thank you for all that you have done for our family. We will miss you.

> Words can’t express how truly grateful we are to have been part of this amazing community for the past 7 years. Thank you so much for everything you have done for our family. We are sad to leave but excited about how well prepared both our children are for their elementary years.

> Thank you for all the kindness, generosity and love you have given our family during our time at RESCC! We have thought of you and all the wonderful, talented and caring teachers as part of our family over the past 8 years and it has been wonderful to watch our kids grow and thrive in the environment you have created. We are eternally grateful for all of the support we have received, and we will always know that our children got off to such a great start because of RESCC.

> Thank you so much for the wonderful experience you have given our son (and us) at the Simon Center. We have felt at home here since his very first day and have loved being a part of this community. While we are excited for his journey ahead, we will very much miss seeing you all and being here each day. We are truly very appreciative of this school and its staff, and hope this is not “goodbye” but “see you later”.
