**Wayne Morris** (born **Bert DeWayne Morris Jr.**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-Clarke-2) February 17, 1914 – September 14, 1959) was an American film and television actor, as well as a decorated [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II")[fighter ace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_ace "Flying ace"). He appeared in many films, including _[Paths of Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paths\_of\_Glory "Paths of Glory")_ (1957), _[The Bushwackers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bushwhackers\_(1952\_film) "The Bushwhackers (1952 film)")_ (1952), and the title role of _[Kid Galahad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Galahad\_(1937\_film) "Kid Galahad (1937 film)")_ (1937).

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Morris was born in [Los Angeles County, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County,_California "Los Angeles County, California"), to Bert DeWayne Morris and Anna Lorea Morris ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Fitzgerald). He attended [Los Angeles City College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_City_College "Los Angeles City College") and was a fullback on that school's varsity football team. He gained acting experience through his work at the [Pasadena Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena_Playhouse "Pasadena Playhouse").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-pi-3)

His film debut was in the _[China Clipper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China\_Clipper\_(1936\_film) "China Clipper (1936 film)")_ (1936).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-4) He played the title character of _[Kid Galahad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Galahad\_(1937\_film) "Kid Galahad (1937 film)")_ (1937), a story of a young prizefighter that featured some of Hollywood's biggest stars, [Bette Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bette_Davis "Bette Davis"), [Edward G. Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_G._Robinson "Edward G. Robinson") and [Humphrey Bogart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey_Bogart "Humphrey Bogart"). His career flourished in films like _[Brother Rat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brother\_Rat "Brother Rat")_, which starred [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan"), and in Bogart's only horror film, _[The Return of Doctor X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Return\_of\_Doctor\_X "The Return of Doctor X")_ (1939).

## Military service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military service")]

[![Image 19: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Wayne_Morris "Special:EditPage/Wayne Morris") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(November 2022)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

While filming _[Flight Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight\_Angels "Flight Angels")_ (1940), Morris became interested in flying and became a pilot. With war in the wind, he joined the [United States Naval Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Reserve "United States Naval Reserve") and became a [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") aviator in 1942, leaving his film career behind for the duration of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

Morris was considered by the Navy as physically 'too big' to fly [fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_aircraft "Fighter aircraft"). After being turned down several times as a fighter pilot, he went to his uncle-in-law, [Commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander_(United_States) "Commander (United States)")[David McCampbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_McCampbell "David McCampbell"), imploring him for the chance to fly fighters. McCampbell said "Give me a letter." He flew the [F6F Hellcat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grumman_F6F_Hellcat "Grumman F6F Hellcat") off the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Essex_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Essex_(CV-9) "USS Essex (CV-9)") with [Fighter Squadron 15 (VF-15)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VF-15 "VF-15"), the famed "McCampbell Heroes."

A December 15, 1944, [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") news story reported that Morris was "credited with 57 aerial [sorties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortie "Sortie"), shooting down seven Japanese [Zeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsubishi_A6M_Zero "Mitsubishi A6M Zero"), sinking an escort vessel and an [antiaircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiaircraft "Antiaircraft") gunboat and helping sink a [submarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine "Submarine") and damage a [heavy cruiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_cruiser "Heavy cruiser") and a [minelayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minelayer "Minelayer")."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-5) He was awarded four [Distinguished Flying Crosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinguished_Flying_Cross_(United_States) "Distinguished Flying Cross (United States)") and two [Air Medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Medal "Air Medal").

## Later career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later career")]

[![Image 20: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. After the war, Morris returned to films, but his nearly four-year absence had cost him his burgeoning stardom. He continued to act in movies, but the pictures, for the most part, sank in quality. Losing his boyish looks but not demeanor, Morris spent much of the 1950s in low-budget [westerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_(genre) "Western (genre)"), but also appeared as the cowardly [Lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant "Lieutenant") Roget, one of the main characters, in [Stanley Kubrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kubrick "Stanley Kubrick")'s _[Paths of Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paths\_of\_Glory "Paths of Glory")_ (1957).

In 1957, Morris made his [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") debut as a washed-up [boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") champ in [William Saroyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Saroyan "William Saroyan")'s _[The Cave Dwellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cave\_Dwellers "The Cave Dwellers")_.

On television, Morris starred in a 1956 episode of _[Science Fiction Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_Fiction\_Theater "Science Fiction Theater")_, "Beam of Fire". In 1958, Morris appeared in _[Gunsmoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunsmoke "Gunsmoke")_ as "Nat", a groom almost shot to death. Wayne Morris played "Captain Hathaway" in 1959 on _[The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Adventures\_of\_Ozzie\_and\_Harriet "The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet")_ (in the episode "The Sea Captain"), and posthumously as Sheriff Sam Cloggett in 1960 on _[New Comedy Showcase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Comedy\_Showcase "New Comedy Showcase")_ (in the episode "They Went Thataway").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Morris was first married to tobacco heiress Leonora (Bubbles) Schinasi; the couple later divorced. Eighteen months later, Morris married the 19-year-old Patricia Ann O'Rourke at the [Long Beach, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Beach,_California "Long Beach, California") Naval Air Base February 25, 1942.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-mns-6) He had two daughters and a son.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-pi-3)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Death")]

Aged 45, Morris died of a [coronary occlusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_occlusion "Coronary occlusion") on September 14, 1959, aboard the attack aircraft carrier [USS _Bon Homme Richard_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Bon_Homme_Richard_(CV-31) "USS Bon Homme Richard (CV-31)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-pi-3)

**Wayne Morris** (born **Bert DeWayne Morris Jr.**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-Clarke-2) February 17, 1914 – September 14, 1959) was an American film and television actor, as well as a decorated [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II")[fighter ace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_ace "Flying ace"). He appeared in many films, including _[Paths of Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paths\_of\_Glory "Paths of Glory")_ (1957), _[The Bushwackers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bushwhackers\_(1952\_film) "The Bushwhackers (1952 film)")_ (1952), and the title role of _[Kid Galahad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Galahad\_(1937\_film) "Kid Galahad (1937 film)")_ (1937).

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Morris was born in [Los Angeles County, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County,_California "Los Angeles County, California"), to Bert DeWayne Morris and Anna Lorea Morris ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Fitzgerald). He attended [Los Angeles City College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_City_College "Los Angeles City College") and was a fullback on that school's varsity football team. He gained acting experience through his work at the [Pasadena Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena_Playhouse "Pasadena Playhouse").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-pi-3)

His film debut was in the _[China Clipper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China\_Clipper\_(1936\_film) "China Clipper (1936 film)")_ (1936).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-4) He played the title character of _[Kid Galahad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Galahad\_(1937\_film) "Kid Galahad (1937 film)")_ (1937), a story of a young prizefighter that featured some of Hollywood's biggest stars, [Bette Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bette_Davis "Bette Davis"), [Edward G. Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_G._Robinson "Edward G. Robinson") and [Humphrey Bogart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey_Bogart "Humphrey Bogart"). His career flourished in films like _[Brother Rat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brother\_Rat "Brother Rat")_, which starred [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan"), and in Bogart's only horror film, _[The Return of Doctor X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Return\_of\_Doctor\_X "The Return of Doctor X")_ (1939).

## Military service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military service")]

[![Image 19: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(November 2022)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

While filming _[Flight Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight\_Angels "Flight Angels")_ (1940), Morris became interested in flying and became a pilot. With war in the wind, he joined the [United States Naval Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Reserve "United States Naval Reserve") and became a [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") aviator in 1942, leaving his film career behind for the duration of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

Morris was considered by the Navy as physically 'too big' to fly [fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_aircraft "Fighter aircraft"). After being turned down several times as a fighter pilot, he went to his uncle-in-law, [Commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander_(United_States) "Commander (United States)")[David McCampbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_McCampbell "David McCampbell"), imploring him for the chance to fly fighters. McCampbell said "Give me a letter." He flew the [F6F Hellcat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grumman_F6F_Hellcat "Grumman F6F Hellcat") off the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Essex_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Essex_(CV-9) "USS Essex (CV-9)") with [Fighter Squadron 15 (VF-15)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VF-15 "VF-15"), the famed "McCampbell Heroes."

A December 15, 1944, [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") news story reported that Morris was "credited with 57 aerial [sorties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortie "Sortie"), shooting down seven Japanese [Zeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsubishi_A6M_Zero "Mitsubishi A6M Zero"), sinking an escort vessel and an [antiaircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiaircraft "Antiaircraft") gunboat and helping sink a [submarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine "Submarine") and damage a [heavy cruiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_cruiser "Heavy cruiser") and a [minelayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minelayer "Minelayer")."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-5) He was awarded four [Distinguished Flying Crosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinguished_Flying_Cross_(United_States) "Distinguished Flying Cross (United States)") and two [Air Medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Medal "Air Medal").

## Later career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later career")]

[![Image 20: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(November 2022)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

After the war, Morris returned to films, but his nearly four-year absence had cost him his burgeoning stardom. He continued to act in movies, but the pictures, for the most part, sank in quality. Losing his boyish looks but not demeanor, Morris spent much of the 1950s in low-budget [westerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_(genre) "Western (genre)"), but also appeared as the cowardly [Lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant "Lieutenant") Roget, one of the main characters, in [Stanley Kubrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kubrick "Stanley Kubrick")'s _[Paths of Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paths\_of\_Glory "Paths of Glory")_ (1957).

In 1957, Morris made his [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") debut as a washed-up [boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") champ in [William Saroyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Saroyan "William Saroyan")'s _[The Cave Dwellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cave\_Dwellers "The Cave Dwellers")_.

On television, Morris starred in a 1956 episode of _[Science Fiction Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_Fiction\_Theater "Science Fiction Theater")_, "Beam of Fire". In 1958, Morris appeared in _[Gunsmoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunsmoke "Gunsmoke")_ as "Nat", a groom almost shot to death. Wayne Morris played "Captain Hathaway" in 1959 on _[The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Adventures\_of\_Ozzie\_and\_Harriet "The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet")_ (in the episode "The Sea Captain"), and posthumously as Sheriff Sam Cloggett in 1960 on _[New Comedy Showcase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Comedy\_Showcase "New Comedy Showcase")_ (in the episode "They Went Thataway").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Morris was first married to tobacco heiress Leonora (Bubbles) Schinasi; the couple later divorced. Eighteen months later, Morris married the 19-year-old Patricia Ann O'Rourke at the [Long Beach, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Beach,_California "Long Beach, California") Naval Air Base February 25, 1942.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-mns-6) He had two daughters and a son.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-pi-3)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Morris&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Death")]

Aged 45, Morris died of a [coronary occlusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_occlusion "Coronary occlusion") on September 14, 1959, aboard the attack aircraft carrier [USS _Bon Homme Richard_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Bon_Homme_Richard_(CV-31) "USS Bon Homme Richard (CV-31)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Morris#cite_note-pi-3)

[](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_sm)

American actor who had early success as a sunny juvenile, but whose career declined following World War II, in which he was a highly-decorated hero. A native of Los Angeles, Morris played football at Los Angeles Junior College, then worked as a forest ranger. Returning to school, he studied acting at Los Angeles Junior College and at the acclaimed Pasadena Playhouse. A Warner Bros. talent scout spotted him at the Playhouse and he signed with the studio in 1936. Blond and open-faced, he was a perfect type for boy-next-door parts and within a year had made a success in the title role of [Kid Galahad (1937)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0029080/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). While filming [Flight Angels (1940)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0032476/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), Morris became interested in flying and became a pilot. With war in the wind, he joined the Naval Reserve and became a Navy flier in 1942, leaving his film career behind for the duration of the war. Assigned to the carrier Essex in the Pacific, Morris shot down seven Japanese planes and contributed to the sinking of five ships. He was awarded four Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals. Following the war, Morris returned to films, but his nearly four-year absence had cost him his burgeoning stardom. He continued to topline movies, but the pictures, for the most part, sank in quality. Losing his boyish looks but not demeanor, Morris spent most of the Fifties in low-budget Westerns. A wonderful performance as a weakling in [Stanley Kubrick](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000040/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk)'s [Paths of Glory (1957)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0050825/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) might have given impetus to a new career as a character actor, had Morris lived. However, he suffered a massive heart attack while visiting aboard the aircraft carrier Bon Homme Richard in San Francisco Bay and was pronounced dead after being transported to Oakland Naval Hospital in Oakland, California. He was 45. His last film was not released until two years after his death.

## Did you know

Edit

*   [Trivia](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/trivia/?ref_=nm_dyk_trv)During World War II Morris was a Navy fighter pilot assigned to the aircraft carrier USS Essex. He flew 57 missions in an F6F Hellcat and shot down seven Japanese aircraft, becoming one of the war's first aces. He finished with the rank of Lieutenant Commander and was a recipient of four awards of the Distinguished Flying Cross and two awards of the Air Medal.     [](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/trivia/?ref_=nm_dyk_trv)

*   [Quotes](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/quotes/?ref_=nm_dyk_qu)As to what a fellow thinks when he's scared, I guess it's the same with anyone. You get fleeting glimpses in your mind of your home, your wife, the baby you want to see. You see so clearly all the mistakes you made. You want another chance to correct those mistakes. You wonder how you could have attached so much importance to ridiculous, meaningless things in your life. But before you get to thinking too much, you're off into action and everything else is forgotten. (on his wartime experiences)     [](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/quotes/?ref_=nm_dyk_qu)

[](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_sm)

American actor who had early success as a sunny juvenile, but whose career declined following World War II, in which he was a highly-decorated hero. A native of Los Angeles, Morris played football at Los Angeles Junior College, then worked as a forest ranger. Returning to school, he studied acting at Los Angeles Junior College and at the acclaimed Pasadena Playhouse. A Warner Bros. talent scout spotted him at the Playhouse and he signed with the studio in 1936. Blond and open-faced, he was a perfect type for boy-next-door parts and within a year had made a success in the title role of [Kid Galahad (1937)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0029080/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). While filming [Flight Angels (1940)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0032476/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), Morris became interested in flying and became a pilot. With war in the wind, he joined the Naval Reserve and became a Navy flier in 1942, leaving his film career behind for the duration of the war. Assigned to the carrier Essex in the Pacific, Morris shot down seven Japanese planes and contributed to the sinking of five ships. He was awarded four Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals. Following the war, Morris returned to films, but his nearly four-year absence had cost him his burgeoning stardom. He continued to topline movies, but the pictures, for the most part, sank in quality. Losing his boyish looks but not demeanor, Morris spent most of the Fifties in low-budget Westerns. A wonderful performance as a weakling in [Stanley Kubrick](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000040/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk)'s [Paths of Glory (1957)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0050825/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) might have given impetus to a new career as a character actor, had Morris lived. However, he suffered a massive heart attack while visiting aboard the aircraft carrier Bon Homme Richard in San Francisco Bay and was pronounced dead after being transported to Oakland Naval Hospital in Oakland, California. He was 45. His last film was not released until two years after his death.

## Did you know

Edit

*   [Trivia](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/trivia/?ref_=nm_dyk_trv)During World War II Morris was a Navy fighter pilot assigned to the aircraft carrier USS Essex. He flew 57 missions in an F6F Hellcat and shot down seven Japanese aircraft, becoming one of the war's first aces. He finished with the rank of Lieutenant Commander and was a recipient of four awards of the Distinguished Flying Cross and two awards of the Air Medal.     [](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/trivia/?ref_=nm_dyk_trv)

*   [Quotes](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/quotes/?ref_=nm_dyk_qu)As to what a fellow thinks when he's scared, I guess it's the same with anyone. You get fleeting glimpses in your mind of your home, your wife, the baby you want to see. You see so clearly all the mistakes you made. You want another chance to correct those mistakes. You wonder how you could have attached so much importance to ridiculous, meaningless things in your life. But before you get to thinking too much, you're off into action and everything else is forgotten. (on his wartime experiences)     [](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0606998/quotes/?ref_=nm_dyk_qu)

# The forgotten Hollywood war hero: Wayne Morris

Posted on May 27, 2013 by [Jnpickens](https://cometoverhollywood.com/author/hollywoodcomet/ "View all posts by Jnpickens")

[![Image 3: Warner Brothers star, Wayne Morris in he 1930s](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris3.jpg?w=278&h=346)](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris3.jpg)
Warner Brothers star, Wayne Morris in he 1930s

He can be seen playing alongside Bette Davis as a boxer in “[Kid Galahad](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B001IYPWNM/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B001IYPWNM&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20)” (1937) or a cadet running amok at the Virginia Military Institute in “[Brother Rat](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/6304288891/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=6304288891&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20).”

Wayne Morris may not be a name you’re familiar with but you have most likely seen the husky, affable blond in Warner Brothers 1930s and 1940s films.

But you may not be familiar with Morris’ war time record.  
 We frequently hear about Hollywood actors such as James Stewart, Clark Gable and Mickey Rooney who enlisted and were decorated for their bravery during World War II.

However, Morris is rarely recognized for his service and was one of World War II’s first flying aces.

His interest in flying started in Hollywood.

While filming “Flying Angles” (1940) with Jane Wyman and Dennis Morgan, Morris learned how to fly a plane.

[![Image 4: Morris in 1944 in his plane "Meatball." The decals show how many Japanese planes he shot down. ](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-1944.jpg?w=306&h=384)](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-1944.jpg)
Morris in 1944 in his plane “Meatball.” The decals show how many Japanese planes he shot down.

Once World War II began, Morris joined the Naval Reserve and became a Naval flier in 1942 on the U.S.S. Essex. He put his career on hold to fight. The same year he was married to Olympic swimmer Patricia O’Rourke.

“Every time they showed a picture aboard the Essex, I was scared to death it would be one of mine,” Morris said. “That’s something I could never have lived down.”

Morris flew 57 missions-while some actors only flew 20 or less- and made seven kills, which qualified him as an ace. He also helped sink five enemy ships.

He originally was told he was too big to fly fighter planes until he went to his uncle-in-law, Cdr. David McCampbell who wrote him a letter, allowing him to fly the VF-15, according to “McCampbell’s Heroes: the Story of the U.S. Navy’s Most Celebrated Carrier Fighter of the Pacific”, Edwin P. Hoyt.

Three of his planes were so badly damaged by enemy fire that they were deemed unfit to fly and were dumped in the ocean, according to IMDB.

Advertisement

“As to what a fellow thinks when he’s scared, I guess it’s the same with anyone. You get fleeting glimpses in your mind of your home, your wife, the baby you want to see,” Morris said. “You see so clearly all the mistakes you made. You want another chance to correct those mistakes. You wonder how you could have attached so much importance to ridiculous, meaningless things in your life. But before you get to thinking too much, you’re off into action and everything else is forgotten.”

For his duty, Morris was honored with four Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals.

When he returned to Hollywood after four year at war, his once promising career floundered and Warner Brothers did not allow him to act for a year.

[![Image 5: Jack Warner welcoming actors home from the war in 1945 including Wayne Morris, Ronald Reagan, Army Air Forces; Jack Warner; Gig Young, Coast Guard; and Harry Lewis, Army.](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris.jpg?w=584)](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris.jpg)
Jack Warner welcoming actors home from the war in 1945 including Wayne Morris, Ronald Reagan, Army Air Forces; Jack Warner; Gig Young, Coast Guard; and Harry Lewis, Army.

Morris’s most notable post-war films include “[The Voice of the Turtle](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B00A1AU6VC/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B00A1AU6VC&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20),” “[John Loves Mary](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B002EAYE1K/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B002EAYE1K&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20)” and “[Paths of Glory](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B001BO5B6C/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B001BO5B6C&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20).” His career ended with several B-westerns.

At the age of 45, Morris passed away in 1959 from a massive heart attack.

But his service to his country was not forgotten. Morris is buried in Arlington Cemetery and was given full military honors at his funeral.

[![Image 6: Morris with his wife Patricia and daughter Pamela in 1946.](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris2.jpg?w=231&h=300)](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris2.jpg)
Morris with his wife Patricia and daughter Pamela in 1946.

Though I am thankful for all men and women who serve our country, I wanted to recognize Wayne Morris.

For years I saw Wayne Morris in films and knew nothing about him except that I liked him. He is one of those character actors that can make a movie special.

Morris seemed like a regular guy. Before he started out in Hollywood, he played football at Los Angeles Junior College and worked as a forest ranger.

After I researched him and discovered his war record, I wanted to honor his service and his work in films.

Thank you to Wayne Morris and men and women in the military for serving our country.

# The forgotten Hollywood war hero: Wayne Morris

Posted on May 27, 2013 by [Jnpickens](https://cometoverhollywood.com/author/hollywoodcomet/ "View all posts by Jnpickens")

[![Image 3: Warner Brothers star, Wayne Morris in he 1930s](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris3.jpg?w=278&h=346)](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris3.jpg)
Warner Brothers star, Wayne Morris in he 1930s

He can be seen playing alongside Bette Davis as a boxer in “[Kid Galahad](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B001IYPWNM/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B001IYPWNM&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20)” (1937) or a cadet running amok at the Virginia Military Institute in “[Brother Rat](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/6304288891/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=6304288891&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20).”

Wayne Morris may not be a name you’re familiar with but you have most likely seen the husky, affable blond in Warner Brothers 1930s and 1940s films.

But you may not be familiar with Morris’ war time record.  
 We frequently hear about Hollywood actors such as James Stewart, Clark Gable and Mickey Rooney who enlisted and were decorated for their bravery during World War II.

However, Morris is rarely recognized for his service and was one of World War II’s first flying aces.

His interest in flying started in Hollywood.

While filming “Flying Angles” (1940) with Jane Wyman and Dennis Morgan, Morris learned how to fly a plane.

[![Image 4: Morris in 1944 in his plane "Meatball." The decals show how many Japanese planes he shot down. ](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-1944.jpg?w=306&h=384)](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-1944.jpg)
Morris in 1944 in his plane “Meatball.” The decals show how many Japanese planes he shot down.

Once World War II began, Morris joined the Naval Reserve and became a Naval flier in 1942 on the U.S.S. Essex. He put his career on hold to fight. The same year he was married to Olympic swimmer Patricia O’Rourke.

“Every time they showed a picture aboard the Essex, I was scared to death it would be one of mine,” Morris said. “That’s something I could never have lived down.”

Morris flew 57 missions-while some actors only flew 20 or less- and made seven kills, which qualified him as an ace. He also helped sink five enemy ships.

He originally was told he was too big to fly fighter planes until he went to his uncle-in-law, Cdr. David McCampbell who wrote him a letter, allowing him to fly the VF-15, according to “McCampbell’s Heroes: the Story of the U.S. Navy’s Most Celebrated Carrier Fighter of the Pacific”, Edwin P. Hoyt.

Three of his planes were so badly damaged by enemy fire that they were deemed unfit to fly and were dumped in the ocean, according to IMDB.

Advertisement

“As to what a fellow thinks when he’s scared, I guess it’s the same with anyone. You get fleeting glimpses in your mind of your home, your wife, the baby you want to see,” Morris said. “You see so clearly all the mistakes you made. You want another chance to correct those mistakes. You wonder how you could have attached so much importance to ridiculous, meaningless things in your life. But before you get to thinking too much, you’re off into action and everything else is forgotten.”

For his duty, Morris was honored with four Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals.

When he returned to Hollywood after four year at war, his once promising career floundered and Warner Brothers did not allow him to act for a year.

[![Image 5: Jack Warner welcoming actors home from the war in 1945 including Wayne Morris, Ronald Reagan, Army Air Forces; Jack Warner; Gig Young, Coast Guard; and Harry Lewis, Army.](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris.jpg?w=584)](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris.jpg)
Jack Warner welcoming actors home from the war in 1945 including Wayne Morris, Ronald Reagan, Army Air Forces; Jack Warner; Gig Young, Coast Guard; and Harry Lewis, Army.

Morris’s most notable post-war films include “[The Voice of the Turtle](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B00A1AU6VC/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B00A1AU6VC&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20),” “[John Loves Mary](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B002EAYE1K/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B002EAYE1K&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20)” and “[Paths of Glory](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B001BO5B6C/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B001BO5B6C&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20).” His career ended with several B-westerns.

At the age of 45, Morris passed away in 1959 from a massive heart attack.

But his service to his country was not forgotten. Morris is buried in Arlington Cemetery and was given full military honors at his funeral.

[![Image 6: Morris with his wife Patricia and daughter Pamela in 1946.](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris2.jpg?w=231&h=300)](https://cometoverhollywood.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/wayne-morris2.jpg)
Morris with his wife Patricia and daughter Pamela in 1946.

Though I am thankful for all men and women who serve our country, I wanted to recognize Wayne Morris.

For years I saw Wayne Morris in films and knew nothing about him except that I liked him. He is one of those character actors that can make a movie special.

Morris seemed like a regular guy. Before he started out in Hollywood, he played football at Los Angeles Junior College and worked as a forest ranger.

After I researched him and discovered his war record, I wanted to honor his service and his work in films.

Thank you to Wayne Morris and men and women in the military for serving our country.

## Robert Wayne Morris Obituary

Share

Please share a memory of Robert to include in a keepsake book for family and friends. 

 View Tribute Book 

Robert Wayne Morris passed peacefully into the loving arms of his Heavenly Father Saturday afternoon. His earthy struggles are now over. "For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with Him those who sleep in Jesus" 1 Thes 4:14. Born February 20, 1930 to Joseph and Ermina Morris. Most of his early life was spent in or near Taft, CA where he graduated from high school. Born into a family of hard workers he and his brothers worked in the oil fields early on in their careers. Drafted into the US Army during the Korean Conflict He served with distinction earning the Bronze Star. Back home he lived with distinction, Marrying Marieta Neubauer whom he spent 69 years with as wife. They had three children Robert, Lynne, and Candace who he loved and cared greatly for. He has 7 grandchildren and 5 great grandchildren who brought him great joy. A large portion of his career was spent working for Pacific Bell telephone company as a phone technician and linesman. Later He would start his own telephone repair company "Telephone Service Technicians." Many Salinas business had a phone system installed or maintained by this patient and hardworking man. A service will be held 1:40pm Friday, March 6th at San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery. He is dearly missed by his family who remember him for his hard work, quiet demeanor, love of family, and faithfulness over the years.

## Robert Wayne Morris Obituary

Share

Please share a memory of Robert to include in a keepsake book for family and friends. 

 View Tribute Book 

Robert Wayne Morris passed peacefully into the loving arms of his Heavenly Father Saturday afternoon. His earthy struggles are now over. "For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with Him those who sleep in Jesus" 1 Thes 4:14. Born February 20, 1930 to Joseph and Ermina Morris. Most of his early life was spent in or near Taft, CA where he graduated from high school. Born into a family of hard workers he and his brothers worked in the oil fields early on in their careers. Drafted into the US Army during the Korean Conflict He served with distinction earning the Bronze Star. Back home he lived with distinction, Marrying Marieta Neubauer whom he spent 69 years with as wife. They had three children Robert, Lynne, and Candace who he loved and cared greatly for. He has 7 grandchildren and 5 great grandchildren who brought him great joy. A large portion of his career was spent working for Pacific Bell telephone company as a phone technician and linesman. Later He would start his own telephone repair company "Telephone Service Technicians." Many Salinas business had a phone system installed or maintained by this patient and hardworking man. A service will be held 1:40pm Friday, March 6th at San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery. He is dearly missed by his family who remember him for his hard work, quiet demeanor, love of family, and faithfulness over the years.

## Robert Wayne Morris, Sr. Obituary

Share

_Robert Wayne “Bobby” “BJ” Morris, Sr., 77, of Elkton, passed away Tuesday, November 25, 2025 in Crozet, Va. He was born June 28, 1948 in Harrisonburg and was the son of the late Malcolm Ray Morris and Nancy Jewel Wright Berry._

_In addition to his parents, he was preceded in death by his brothers, David Johnson and Donnie Morris._

_Bobby retired from R.R. Donnelley working as a Tool and Die Maker and Maintenance Planner. He also worked for Sperry Marine, North Anna and Westinghouse. He was a former member of the Elkton Volunteer Fire Company. Bobby loved hunting, camping and tinkering around on things in his garage and was a “Jack of all trades”. He was a member of the Harrisonburg 1st Church of Nazarene. He will be missed by all those who knew and loved him._

_Bobby is survived by his wife, Sheila Hensley Morris; son, Bobby Morris Jr. and wife, Mary Beth; a daughter, Teresa Rogers and husband, Charles; step-daughters, Jennifer Lawhon and husband, Brian, Emily Keesling, Cicely Hedrick and husband, Jon; brothers, Glen Edward Johnson, Patrick Morris; sisters, Peggy Rae Silvious, Sandra Ray Coffman, Carol Helmintoller, Toni Ray; grandchildren, Hailey, Tanner, Sarah Paige, Evee, Megan, Chase, Elliot, Delaney, Shane, Seth and wife, Allison, Zachary and wife, Grace and Kyle._

_A Funeral Service will be conducted 2 p.m., Wednesday, December 3, 2025 at Kyger Funeral Home in Elkton, with Pastor Jim Harrison and Pastor Joe Stoner officiating. Burial to follow at Elk Run Cemetery._

_Visitation will be 6 to 8 p.m., Tuesday, December 2, 2025 at the funeral home._

_Memorial contributions may be made to the hospice of the donors choice or_[_“All Blessings Flow”_](https://www.allblessingsflow.org/)_._

## Robert Wayne Morris, Sr. Obituary

Share

_Robert Wayne “Bobby” “BJ” Morris, Sr., 77, of Elkton, passed away Tuesday, November 25, 2025 in Crozet, Va. He was born June 28, 1948 in Harrisonburg and was the son of the late Malcolm Ray Morris and Nancy Jewel Wright Berry._

_In addition to his parents, he was preceded in death by his brothers, David Johnson and Donnie Morris._

_Bobby retired from R.R. Donnelley working as a Tool and Die Maker and Maintenance Planner. He also worked for Sperry Marine, North Anna and Westinghouse. He was a former member of the Elkton Volunteer Fire Company. Bobby loved hunting, camping and tinkering around on things in his garage and was a “Jack of all trades”. He was a member of the Harrisonburg 1st Church of Nazarene. He will be missed by all those who knew and loved him._

_Bobby is survived by his wife, Sheila Hensley Morris; son, Bobby Morris Jr. and wife, Mary Beth; a daughter, Teresa Rogers and husband, Charles; step-daughters, Jennifer Lawhon and husband, Brian, Emily Keesling, Cicely Hedrick and husband, Jon; brothers, Glen Edward Johnson, Patrick Morris; sisters, Peggy Rae Silvious, Sandra Ray Coffman, Carol Helmintoller, Toni Ray; grandchildren, Hailey, Tanner, Sarah Paige, Evee, Megan, Chase, Elliot, Delaney, Shane, Seth and wife, Allison, Zachary and wife, Grace and Kyle._

_A Funeral Service will be conducted 2 p.m., Wednesday, December 3, 2025 at Kyger Funeral Home in Elkton, with Pastor Jim Harrison and Pastor Joe Stoner officiating. Burial to follow at Elk Run Cemetery._

_Visitation will be 6 to 8 p.m., Tuesday, December 2, 2025 at the funeral home._

_Memorial contributions may be made to the hospice of the donors choice or_[_“All Blessings Flow”_](https://www.allblessingsflow.org/)_._

# Robert 'Bob' Wayne Morris' Obituary

Robert (Bob) Wayne Morris, beloved husband, father, grandfather and great-grandfather, passed away peacefully on September 28, 2025.

Born in the Bronx, NY on January 22, 1940 to Harold Morris and Mary Virginia Morris (Kenney), Bob attended Samuel Gompers High School and spent many afternoons canoeing near Orchard Beach with his cousins. His interest in military history and his patriotism inspired Bob to enlist in the United States Army when he was seventeen years old.

He proudly served in the United States Army for six years and met the love of his life, Ruth shortly after he was stationed in Germany. Bob and Ruth enjoyed 53 wonderful years of marriage together. They were never apart for more than Bob's eight hour shifts (8-4, 4-12 or 12-8) during his career as a police officer. During his tenure at the OPD, he was often called "Abe" (short for Honest Abe, a nickname associated with Abraham Lincoln due to his personal integrity and honesty). After 31 years of distinguished service Bob retired from the Orangetown Police Department on February 4 , 2001.

Bob is survived by his daughter, Britta Green (Christopher), grandson, Timothy Rothschild, great-granddaughter Alma Rothschild and brother James Morris as well as his nieces and nephews, Brenda Holohan, Joan Grosser, James Morris and Jason Morris.

He is predeceased by his devoted wife Ruth (Grosser) Morris, grandson, Robert Rothschild , sister Denice Thurmes and brother-in-law Werner Grosser.

"Die Liebe höret nimmer auf"

Family will receive visitors at Moritz Funeral Home in Tappan, NY on Sunday, October 5 from 1-3 pm. A Mass of Christian burial will take place on Monday October 6 at 10:00am at St. Catharine's Church in Blauvelt, NY. Internment will follow at Rockland Cemetery in Sparkill, NY. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the charity of your choice.

# Robert 'Bob' Wayne Morris' Obituary

Robert (Bob) Wayne Morris, beloved husband, father, grandfather and great-grandfather, passed away peacefully on September 28, 2025.

Born in the Bronx, NY on January 22, 1940 to Harold Morris and Mary Virginia Morris (Kenney), Bob attended Samuel Gompers High School and spent many afternoons canoeing near Orchard Beach with his cousins. His interest in military history and his patriotism inspired Bob to enlist in the United States Army when he was seventeen years old.

He proudly served in the United States Army for six years and met the love of his life, Ruth shortly after he was stationed in Germany. Bob and Ruth enjoyed 53 wonderful years of marriage together. They were never apart for more than Bob's eight hour shifts (8-4, 4-12 or 12-8) during his career as a police officer. During his tenure at the OPD, he was often called "Abe" (short for Honest Abe, a nickname associated with Abraham Lincoln due to his personal integrity and honesty). After 31 years of distinguished service Bob retired from the Orangetown Police Department on February 4 , 2001.

Bob is survived by his daughter, Britta Green (Christopher), grandson, Timothy Rothschild, great-granddaughter Alma Rothschild and brother James Morris as well as his nieces and nephews, Brenda Holohan, Joan Grosser, James Morris and Jason Morris.

He is predeceased by his devoted wife Ruth (Grosser) Morris, grandson, Robert Rothschild , sister Denice Thurmes and brother-in-law Werner Grosser.

"Die Liebe höret nimmer auf"

Family will receive visitors at Moritz Funeral Home in Tappan, NY on Sunday, October 5 from 1-3 pm. A Mass of Christian burial will take place on Monday October 6 at 10:00am at St. Catharine's Church in Blauvelt, NY. Internment will follow at Rockland Cemetery in Sparkill, NY. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the charity of your choice.

**(Pressbook ads below courtesy of Les Adams)** ![Image 3](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris3.jpg) **1950** ![Image 4](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris4.jpg) **1953** ![Image 5](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris1.jpg) **1953** ![Image 6](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris2.jpg) **1954** ![Image 7](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris6.jpg) **1955** **It's a dubious distinction or honor, perhaps, but most Western film historians and fans generally agree that Wayne Morris was the last of the B-Western heroes, and TWO GUNS AND A BADGE (Allied Artists, 1954), was the last of the low-budget series Westerns. While this distinction may be questioned, there is no debating the fact that the big, likeable, laid-back actor was one of the true heroes of World War II. Born February 17, 1914 in Los Angeles, he attended Los Angeles High where he was a member of the cheerleading squad. Contrary to popular belief and probably studio hype, he did not play football. After graduating, he attended Los Angeles City College before entering the famous Pasadena Playhouse on a scholarship. A screen test with Warner Brothers' Studio led to a contract and a bit part as a navigator in the 1936 CHINA CLIPPER, an aviation yarn starring Pat O'Brien. Other small roles followed between 1936 and 1937. His big break finally came in May of '37 when the studio selected him for the title role in KID GALAHAD. Directed by Sam Bischoff, it was a major film with an impressive cast that included Bette Davis and Humphrey Bogart. In fact, KID GALAHAD is considered Morris' best film and definitely boosted him to near-star status. That year also found Morris in his first Western, supporting Dick Foran in LAND BEYOND THE LAW. Then came good performances in other roles including VALLEY OF THE GIANTS ('38), a Peter B. Kyne tale starring Chester Morris and Claire Trevor (two actors who would also become familiar with the Western genre) about lumberjacks and their many brawls. Unfortunately, the following year, Morris would appear in only two films for the studio - THE KID FROM KOKOMO and THE RETURN OF DOCTOR X (which starred Bogart in the ludicrous role of Doctor X). Meanwhile, over at the Republic lot, changes were being made in their THREE MESQUITEERS' lineup. John Wayne, who had replaced Robert Livingston for the '38-'39 season, was moving up to bigger and better things (thanks, of course, to his starring role in STAGECOACH). This left a vacancy in the Stony Brooke role. Morris, interested in the role, and currently unsigned, inquired about the role, but to no avail. Discouraged, he then went back to Warners, who offered him another contract, which he signed. Republic then re-signed Livingston to portray Stony Brooke. Then began one of Morris's busiest seasons, appearing in seven titles, none of them Westerns. Of the seven, FLIGHT ANGELS (starring Dennis Morgan and Jane Wyman), undoubtedly set the stage for Wayne Morris's future. During the shooting of the film, he took up flying lessons, a decision that would make a significant impact on his life. Morris' first Western of note came in 1941 in the Warner Brothers' BAD MEN OF MISSOURI in which he plays one of the notorious Younger brothers. With war clouds hanging over much of Europe and Asia, Morris became one of the first Hollywood actors to enter the service, joining the Naval Reserves and receiving a commission. Following flight training and a year as an instructor, he was thrust immediately in the Pacific air war, flying an F6F Hellcat off the carrier, the USS Essex. He would go on to fly 57 missions, shooting down seven Japanese aircraft, making him one of the early American aces of the war. Of the 57 missions he flew, three of his Hellcats were so full of holes when he returned to his carrier, they were rendered "unfit for duty" and dumped overboard. Returning to Hollywood after the war, Morris attempted to pick up where he left off but things were not the same. He had difficulty getting roles; for some reason the studio kept him on ice for over a year before his next film appearance, on loan to Fox for the film, DEEP VALLEY, starring Ida Lupino and Dane Clark. Back to Warner's he began to receive good, co-starring roles in 1947-48 and in 1949 mounted up for his third Western, THE YOUNGER BROTHERS, another accounting of the outlaw brothers with Morris essaying the role of Cole in this one (he played Bob Cole in the '41 film). Further adventure-type roles followed until 1951 when he returned to the Western genre again with star Rod Cameron for the routine but efficient Columbia oater, STAGE TO TUCSON. Then came SIERRA PASSAGE for Monogram with a good cast featuring Lola Albright and I. Stanford Jolley (Jim Bannon, a former Red Ryder appeared briefly in the film). Closing out 1951 was YELLOWFIN (Monogram), and THE BUSHWHACKERS, a Jack Broder Western that starred John Ireland in his first starring role. In 1952, Morris began his series of pictures for Monogram/Allied Artists, leading off with DESERT PURSUIT, an off-beat Western which takes place in Death Valley with Morris and ingénue Virginia Grey being chased by Arab-like characters on camels. Morris' B-Western run officially began in December 1952 with TEXAS BADMAN, although STAR OF TEXAS (issued the following month) is often listed as the first of the series. A cut above the average B-Western, it was directed in documentary style by Lewis Collins and is unique in that no females are in the cast. As put by the late Don Miller in his unsurpassed HOLLYWOOD CORRAL, there was "no timeout for obligatory romantic byplay". It was all action. Still possessing an athletic build and the good looks of his earlier days, unfortunately, the years had taken its toll in the weight department, making him a little beefier than the average sagebrush hero. Nevertheless, he handled himself well in the action department and although doubled in most fight scenes, in close-ups he looked realistic enough throwing a punch. His Western garb was more on the conservative side and his horse had no name, an average looking cayuse that he rode with more or less convincing ability. Several of his Allied Artists' pictures could be in the B-plus category rather than true, low-budgeted, formatted and programmed Westerns of the 30's and 40's. Running times were generally longer. THE DESPERADO ('54), next to last in the series ran for 82 minutes. THE FIGHTING LAWMAN ('53) clocked in at 71 minutes while STAR OF TEXAS ('53) and the last, TWO GUNS AND A BADGE ('54) were in the 68-69 minute range. The other two - TEXAS BADMAN ('52) and THE MARKSMAN ('53) - ran the standard 60-minute format. Of the six, THE DESPERADO is by far the strongest and best of the series. The final film in the series, and considered the last B-Western produced, TWO GUNS AND A BADGE, released September 12, 1954, was more true to B-Western standards. Replete with a strong cast that included Beverly Garland, Morris Ankrum, Roy Barcroft, and I. Stanford Jolley, it has ex-con Morris mistaken for a lawman who arrives in town to face corrupt rancher Barcroft. It was the last gasp for the B-Western series and the end of an era that brought thrills and chills to millions of fans growing up in the 1930s-1950s. Morris returned to Warner Brothers in 1954 to take second lead in the Randolph Scott, RIDING SHOTGUN and later that year traveled to England where he made five films for release in the U.S. Throughout 1955, Morris appeared or starred in several adventure-oriented films and for reasons unknown, was inactive the following year, or at least no credits have turned up. The following year he appeared as cowardly "Lieutenant Roget" in the somber and disturbing PATHS OF GLORY ('57), the Stanley Kubrick directed story about an action in World War I. Morris' last screen appearance came in 1961 in BUFFALO GUN, a low-budget Globe production that featured singers Marty Robbins. Webb Pierce, and Carl Smith. It was not released until three years after it was filmed, and ironically, two years following Morris' death. In the late 1950s, Morris, like so many other actors of the day, turned to the TV medium for work. From 1957 until his death, he appeared in a number of TV Westerns, and starred in an unsold TV pilot called THEY WENT THATAWAY. During this period, he made his Broadway debut in the William Saroyan play "The Cave Dwellers". He was "the Duke", a washed up prizefighter, and the play ran for 97 performances from October, 1957 to January, 1958. Wayne Morris' tragic death on September 14, 1959 at the age of 45 was a bizarre and ironic one. While visiting his old wartime commander and watching aerial maneuvers on the bridge of a carrier off the coast of Monterey, he collapsed and died of a heart attack. He was buried at Arlington National Cemetery with full military honors. His younger brother, Richard, a B-17 pilot shot down during World War II, also reposes at Arlington. In February, 1942, Morris married Patricia O'Rourke, an Olympic swimmer and sister of Republic Pictures leading lady Peggy Stewart, and they had two daughters, Patricia and Melinda. Tragedy struck in May, 1946 when their newborn son passed away hours after birth. Prior to that pairing, there was a 1939 - 1941 marriage to tobacco heiress Leonora 'Bubbles' Schinasi, who, in later life, became newspaper writer and book author Leonora Hornblow. Whether or not Wayne Morris was the last of the B-Western heroes is irrelevant and of little consequence when you consider his fighter pilot experiences in World War II. Americans should never forget his military service.**

>  Guessing that most fans of the ol' B western might recall Wayne Morris for his films at Warners, but have little or no recollection of him doing low budget sagebrush adventures. His TWO GUNS AND A BADGE (1954) was the last SERIES westerns at Monogram / Allied Artists. But the genre was near death ... and TV had arrived. Columbia Pictures ended their Charles Starrett / Durango Kids in 1952. That same year, the end came for whip cracking Lash LaRue and Johnny Mack Brown concluded his starring career in CANYON AMBUSH (Monogram, 1952). At Republic Pictures, Roy, Dale and Trigger did their finale, PALS OF THE GOLDEN WEST (Republic, 1951) and 'Rocky' Lane rode Black Jack for the last time in EL PASO STAMPEDE (Republic, 1953). The LAST OF THE PONY RIDERS (Columbia, 1953) was an appropriate title for Gene Autry's last starring feature. The assembly line at Republic also ground to a halt - their last series oater was Rex Allen's THE PHANTOM STALLION (Republic, 1954), and KING OF THE CARNIVAL (Republic, 1955) was their 66th and final cliffhanger. In 1956, Columbia released two chapterplays, BLAZING THE OVERLAND TRAIL and PERILS OF THE WILDERNESS, and quit serial production.   
>   
>  Grumman F6F Hellcat pilot Wayne Morris was a member of VF-15 on the aircraft carrier USS Essex and he shot down seven planes and destroyed/help destroy five ships during his 57 missions. As best I can determine, he was awarded four Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals for acts of valor and courage. His other medals and decorations were the American Campaign Medal, National Defense Medal, Philippines Liberation Medal, China Service Medal, Asiatic Pacific Theater Medal, and Overseas Service Bar. His final Navy rank was Lieutenant Commander.**

**(Pressbook ads below courtesy of Les Adams)** ![Image 3](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris3.jpg) **1950** ![Image 4](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris4.jpg) **1953** ![Image 5](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris1.jpg) **1953** ![Image 6](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris2.jpg) **1954** ![Image 7](https://www.b-westerns.com/pic_u-z/wmorris6.jpg) **1955** **It's a dubious distinction or honor, perhaps, but most Western film historians and fans generally agree that Wayne Morris was the last of the B-Western heroes, and TWO GUNS AND A BADGE (Allied Artists, 1954), was the last of the low-budget series Westerns. While this distinction may be questioned, there is no debating the fact that the big, likeable, laid-back actor was one of the true heroes of World War II. Born February 17, 1914 in Los Angeles, he attended Los Angeles High where he was a member of the cheerleading squad. Contrary to popular belief and probably studio hype, he did not play football. After graduating, he attended Los Angeles City College before entering the famous Pasadena Playhouse on a scholarship. A screen test with Warner Brothers' Studio led to a contract and a bit part as a navigator in the 1936 CHINA CLIPPER, an aviation yarn starring Pat O'Brien. Other small roles followed between 1936 and 1937. His big break finally came in May of '37 when the studio selected him for the title role in KID GALAHAD. Directed by Sam Bischoff, it was a major film with an impressive cast that included Bette Davis and Humphrey Bogart. In fact, KID GALAHAD is considered Morris' best film and definitely boosted him to near-star status. That year also found Morris in his first Western, supporting Dick Foran in LAND BEYOND THE LAW. Then came good performances in other roles including VALLEY OF THE GIANTS ('38), a Peter B. Kyne tale starring Chester Morris and Claire Trevor (two actors who would also become familiar with the Western genre) about lumberjacks and their many brawls. Unfortunately, the following year, Morris would appear in only two films for the studio - THE KID FROM KOKOMO and THE RETURN OF DOCTOR X (which starred Bogart in the ludicrous role of Doctor X). Meanwhile, over at the Republic lot, changes were being made in their THREE MESQUITEERS' lineup. John Wayne, who had replaced Robert Livingston for the '38-'39 season, was moving up to bigger and better things (thanks, of course, to his starring role in STAGECOACH). This left a vacancy in the Stony Brooke role. Morris, interested in the role, and currently unsigned, inquired about the role, but to no avail. Discouraged, he then went back to Warners, who offered him another contract, which he signed. Republic then re-signed Livingston to portray Stony Brooke. Then began one of Morris's busiest seasons, appearing in seven titles, none of them Westerns. Of the seven, FLIGHT ANGELS (starring Dennis Morgan and Jane Wyman), undoubtedly set the stage for Wayne Morris's future. During the shooting of the film, he took up flying lessons, a decision that would make a significant impact on his life. Morris' first Western of note came in 1941 in the Warner Brothers' BAD MEN OF MISSOURI in which he plays one of the notorious Younger brothers. With war clouds hanging over much of Europe and Asia, Morris became one of the first Hollywood actors to enter the service, joining the Naval Reserves and receiving a commission. Following flight training and a year as an instructor, he was thrust immediately in the Pacific air war, flying an F6F Hellcat off the carrier, the USS Essex. He would go on to fly 57 missions, shooting down seven Japanese aircraft, making him one of the early American aces of the war. Of the 57 missions he flew, three of his Hellcats were so full of holes when he returned to his carrier, they were rendered "unfit for duty" and dumped overboard. Returning to Hollywood after the war, Morris attempted to pick up where he left off but things were not the same. He had difficulty getting roles; for some reason the studio kept him on ice for over a year before his next film appearance, on loan to Fox for the film, DEEP VALLEY, starring Ida Lupino and Dane Clark. Back to Warner's he began to receive good, co-starring roles in 1947-48 and in 1949 mounted up for his third Western, THE YOUNGER BROTHERS, another accounting of the outlaw brothers with Morris essaying the role of Cole in this one (he played Bob Cole in the '41 film). Further adventure-type roles followed until 1951 when he returned to the Western genre again with star Rod Cameron for the routine but efficient Columbia oater, STAGE TO TUCSON. Then came SIERRA PASSAGE for Monogram with a good cast featuring Lola Albright and I. Stanford Jolley (Jim Bannon, a former Red Ryder appeared briefly in the film). Closing out 1951 was YELLOWFIN (Monogram), and THE BUSHWHACKERS, a Jack Broder Western that starred John Ireland in his first starring role. In 1952, Morris began his series of pictures for Monogram/Allied Artists, leading off with DESERT PURSUIT, an off-beat Western which takes place in Death Valley with Morris and ingénue Virginia Grey being chased by Arab-like characters on camels. Morris' B-Western run officially began in December 1952 with TEXAS BADMAN, although STAR OF TEXAS (issued the following month) is often listed as the first of the series. A cut above the average B-Western, it was directed in documentary style by Lewis Collins and is unique in that no females are in the cast. As put by the late Don Miller in his unsurpassed HOLLYWOOD CORRAL, there was "no timeout for obligatory romantic byplay". It was all action. Still possessing an athletic build and the good looks of his earlier days, unfortunately, the years had taken its toll in the weight department, making him a little beefier than the average sagebrush hero. Nevertheless, he handled himself well in the action department and although doubled in most fight scenes, in close-ups he looked realistic enough throwing a punch. His Western garb was more on the conservative side and his horse had no name, an average looking cayuse that he rode with more or less convincing ability. Several of his Allied Artists' pictures could be in the B-plus category rather than true, low-budgeted, formatted and programmed Westerns of the 30's and 40's. Running times were generally longer. THE DESPERADO ('54), next to last in the series ran for 82 minutes. THE FIGHTING LAWMAN ('53) clocked in at 71 minutes while STAR OF TEXAS ('53) and the last, TWO GUNS AND A BADGE ('54) were in the 68-69 minute range. The other two - TEXAS BADMAN ('52) and THE MARKSMAN ('53) - ran the standard 60-minute format. Of the six, THE DESPERADO is by far the strongest and best of the series. The final film in the series, and considered the last B-Western produced, TWO GUNS AND A BADGE, released September 12, 1954, was more true to B-Western standards. Replete with a strong cast that included Beverly Garland, Morris Ankrum, Roy Barcroft, and I. Stanford Jolley, it has ex-con Morris mistaken for a lawman who arrives in town to face corrupt rancher Barcroft. It was the last gasp for the B-Western series and the end of an era that brought thrills and chills to millions of fans growing up in the 1930s-1950s. Morris returned to Warner Brothers in 1954 to take second lead in the Randolph Scott, RIDING SHOTGUN and later that year traveled to England where he made five films for release in the U.S. Throughout 1955, Morris appeared or starred in several adventure-oriented films and for reasons unknown, was inactive the following year, or at least no credits have turned up. The following year he appeared as cowardly "Lieutenant Roget" in the somber and disturbing PATHS OF GLORY ('57), the Stanley Kubrick directed story about an action in World War I. Morris' last screen appearance came in 1961 in BUFFALO GUN, a low-budget Globe production that featured singers Marty Robbins. Webb Pierce, and Carl Smith. It was not released until three years after it was filmed, and ironically, two years following Morris' death. In the late 1950s, Morris, like so many other actors of the day, turned to the TV medium for work. From 1957 until his death, he appeared in a number of TV Westerns, and starred in an unsold TV pilot called THEY WENT THATAWAY. During this period, he made his Broadway debut in the William Saroyan play "The Cave Dwellers". He was "the Duke", a washed up prizefighter, and the play ran for 97 performances from October, 1957 to January, 1958. Wayne Morris' tragic death on September 14, 1959 at the age of 45 was a bizarre and ironic one. While visiting his old wartime commander and watching aerial maneuvers on the bridge of a carrier off the coast of Monterey, he collapsed and died of a heart attack. He was buried at Arlington National Cemetery with full military honors. His younger brother, Richard, a B-17 pilot shot down during World War II, also reposes at Arlington. In February, 1942, Morris married Patricia O'Rourke, an Olympic swimmer and sister of Republic Pictures leading lady Peggy Stewart, and they had two daughters, Patricia and Melinda. Tragedy struck in May, 1946 when their newborn son passed away hours after birth. Prior to that pairing, there was a 1939 - 1941 marriage to tobacco heiress Leonora 'Bubbles' Schinasi, who, in later life, became newspaper writer and book author Leonora Hornblow. Whether or not Wayne Morris was the last of the B-Western heroes is irrelevant and of little consequence when you consider his fighter pilot experiences in World War II. Americans should never forget his military service.**

**Notes from the Old Corral webmaster:**

> **While I agree with Bill Russell's comments about Wayne Morris being the last of the B western series heroes, I realize that some have different opinions and views. In order to reduce controversy and promote domestic tranquility, please click [HERE](https://www.b-westerns.com/johnnyc.htm) to find out the western film lead who some believe represents the end of the B western genre.   
>   
>  Guessing that most fans of the ol' B western might recall Wayne Morris for his films at Warners, but have little or no recollection of him doing low budget sagebrush adventures. His TWO GUNS AND A BADGE (1954) was the last SERIES westerns at Monogram / Allied Artists. But the genre was near death ... and TV had arrived. Columbia Pictures ended their Charles Starrett / Durango Kids in 1952. That same year, the end came for whip cracking Lash LaRue and Johnny Mack Brown concluded his starring career in CANYON AMBUSH (Monogram, 1952). At Republic Pictures, Roy, Dale and Trigger did their finale, PALS OF THE GOLDEN WEST (Republic, 1951) and 'Rocky' Lane rode Black Jack for the last time in EL PASO STAMPEDE (Republic, 1953). The LAST OF THE PONY RIDERS (Columbia, 1953) was an appropriate title for Gene Autry's last starring feature. The assembly line at Republic also ground to a halt - their last series oater was Rex Allen's THE PHANTOM STALLION (Republic, 1954), and KING OF THE CARNIVAL (Republic, 1955) was their 66th and final cliffhanger. In 1956, Columbia released two chapterplays, BLAZING THE OVERLAND TRAIL and PERILS OF THE WILDERNESS, and quit serial production.   
>   
>  Grumman F6F Hellcat pilot Wayne Morris was a member of VF-15 on the aircraft carrier USS Essex and he shot down seven planes and destroyed/help destroy five ships during his 57 missions. As best I can determine, he was awarded four Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals for acts of valor and courage. His other medals and decorations were the American Campaign Medal, National Defense Medal, Philippines Liberation Medal, China Service Medal, Asiatic Pacific Theater Medal, and Overseas Service Bar. His final Navy rank was Lieutenant Commander.**

**John Brooker adds some further info on Morris and his mid 1950s work on films and TV in the UK:**

> **The British films Morris starred in between 1953 and 1957 were THE MASTER PLAN (1953), CROSS CHANNEL (1955), THE GREEN BUDDHA (1955), THE GELIGNITE GANG (1956, US title: THE DYNAMITERS) and THE CROOKED SKY (1957). Possibly the reason he appeared to be "inactive" in 1956 is because he was in the UK starring in 26 half hour episodes of THE ADVENTURES OF THE BIG MAN in which he played Bill Pierce, a troubleshooter for a big department store. It was a Charles Wick presentation for Trinity Productions. Admittedly it wasn't very good but I always liked Morris (I found his voice particularly interesting) and I remember enjoying them. I can't find any reference to the series in the books I checked. He also appeared in a SCIENCE FICTION THEATRE episode "Beam of Fire" in 1956, an ALFRED HITCHCOCK "A Personal Matter" (shown January 1959 in US) and "The Archer's Ring" episode of ADVENTURES IN PARADISE. His TV western series appearances include GUNSMOKE, MAVERICK, WAGON TRAIN, LAWMAN, WANTED DEAD OR ALIVE, BAT MASTERSON and BRONCO. For me, TWO GUNS AND A BADGE is the last of the B westerns although I know there are those who would disagree.**

## Wayne Morris

This actor had a very distinguished war record followed by a pretty good career in films which was cut short by his sudden death at a very young age. In fact his film career had started well before the War but from 1941 he did not make any more until hostilities had ended and he was back in business.

[![Image 1: Marksman LC](https://fiftieswesterns.files.wordpress.com/2016/02/marksman-lc.jpg?w=500&h=382)](https://fiftieswesterns.files.wordpress.com/2016/02/marksman-lc.jpg)

**Wayne Morris**  
 (February 17, 1914 – September 14, 1959)

Warner Archive have released on DVD quite a few Wayne Morris films. He gave tremendous service to his country during World War II — seven Japanese planes shot down, five ships sunk.

Above in **_The Marksman_ (1953),** one of the Westerns Morris made for Allied Artists, which is part of Warner Archive’s Wayne Morris double feature.

One of his later appearances was in the TV Series **Bat Masterson** starring **Gene Barry.**

[![Image 2: Warner Brothers star, Wayne Morris in he 1930s](https://jnpickens.files.wordpress.com/2013/05/wayne-morris3.jpg?w=278&h=346)](https://jnpickens.files.wordpress.com/2013/05/wayne-morris3.jpg)

He can be seen playing alongside Bette Davis as a boxer in “Kid Galahad” (1937) or a cadet running amok at the Virginia Military Institute in “[Brother Rat](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/6304288891/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=6304288891&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20).”

Wayne Morris may not be a name you’re familiar with but you have most likely seen the husky, affable blond in Warner Brothers 1930s and 1940s films.

But you may not be familiar with Morris’ war time record.  
 We frequently hear about Hollywood actors such as James Stewart, Clark Gable and Mickey Rooney who enlisted and were decorated for their bravery during World War II.

However, Wayne Morris is rarely recognised for his service and was one of World War II’s first flying aces.

His interest in flying started in Hollywood.

While filming “Flying Angles” (1940) with Jane Wyman and Dennis Morgan, Morris learned how to fly a plane.

[![Image 3: Morris in 1944 in his plane "Meatball." The decals show how many Japanese planes he shot down. ](https://jnpickens.files.wordpress.com/2013/05/wayne-1944.jpg?w=306&h=384)](https://jnpickens.files.wordpress.com/2013/05/wayne-1944.jpg)

Once World War II began, Morris joined the Naval Reserve and became a Naval flier in 1942 on the U.S.S. Essex. He put his career on hold to fight. The same year he was married to Olympic swimmer Patricia O’Rourke.

“Every time they showed a picture aboard the Essex, I was scared to death it would be one of mine,” Morris said. “That’s something I could never have lived down.”

Morris flew 57 missions-while some actors only flew 20 or less- and made seven kills, which qualified him as an ace. He also helped sink five enemy ships.

He originally was told he was too big to fly fighter planes until he went to his uncle-in-law, Cdr. David McCampbell who wrote him a letter, allowing him to fly the VF-15, according to “McCampbell’s Heroes: the Story of the U.S. Navy’s Most Celebrated Carrier Fighter of the Pacific”, Edwin P. Hoyt.

Three of his planes were so badly damaged by enemy fire that they were deemed unfit to fly and were dumped in the ocean, according to IMDB.

“As to what a fellow thinks when he’s scared, I guess it’s the same with anyone. You get fleeting glimpses in your mind of your home, your wife, the baby you want to see,” Morris said. “You see so clearly all the mistakes you made. You want another chance to correct those mistakes. You wonder how you could have attached so much importance to ridiculous, meaningless things in your life. But before you get to thinking too much, you’re off into action and everything else is forgotten.”

For his duty, Morris was honoured with four Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals.

When he returned to Hollywood after four year at war, his once promising career floundered and Warner Brothers did not allow him to act for a year.

[![Image 4: Jack Warner welcoming actors home from the war in 1945 including Wayne Morris, Ronald Reagan, Army Air Forces; Jack Warner; Gig Young, Coast Guard; and Harry Lewis, Army.](https://jnpickens.files.wordpress.com/2013/05/wayne-morris.jpg?w=584)](https://jnpickens.files.wordpress.com/2013/05/wayne-morris.jpg)

Morris’s most notable post-war films include “**[The Voice of the Turtle](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B00A1AU6VC/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B00A1AU6VC&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20),”** “**[John Loves Mary](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B002EAYE1K/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B002EAYE1K&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20)”** and “**[Paths of Glory](http://www.amazon.com/gp/offer-listing/B001BO5B6C/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=211189&creative=373493&creativeASIN=B001BO5B6C&link_code=am3&tag=comeoverholl-20).”** His career ended with several B-westerns.

At the age of 45, Morris passed away in 1959 from a massive heart attack.

But his service to his country was not forgotten. Morris is buried in Arlington Cemetery and was given full military honors at his funeral.

[![Image 5: Morris with his wife Patricia and daughter Pamela in 1946.](https://jnpickens.files.wordpress.com/2013/05/wayne-morris2.jpg?w=231&h=300)](https://jnpickens.files.wordpress.com/2013/05/wayne-morris2.jpg)

Before he started out in Hollywood, he played football at Los Angeles Junior College and worked as a forest ranger.
